Rotorua company Hickey Contractors has folded one month before it would have celebrated its 50th birthday.

The company, based in Te Ngae Rd, wound up at the end of June, seven months after a new Auckland-based owner took it over.

Twelve full-time employees and an estimated eight sub-contracted workers lost their jobs.

The company’s founders, Stan and Sonja Hickey, sold it more than 25 years ago, but Stan continued working there until about seven years ago, when he turned 70.

Stan Hickey told the Rotorua Daily Post he would still pop in from time to time over the past few years.

While it was sad to see the company go, it was probably for the best, he said. His views were taken into consideration before the closure, given his name was associated with the business.

“It’s a sign of the times. It is tough out there.”

Hickey Contractors, which specialised in infrastructure development, subdivisions, site works and commercial and residential contracting, had its boom periods in the 1980s and 1990s.

Stan and Sonja Hickey – key figures in Rotorua’s successful speedway scene – were involved in big developments such as Countdown and Novotel Rotorua, as well as knocking down buildings such as the Majestic Theatre.

Stan Hickey said that, in its heyday, its success was built on great relationships, including a solid contract with the Rotorua Lakes Council.

He credited his wife as the driving force behind the business.

Hickey said the beginning of the end came when out-of-town contractors started moving into Rotorua when their work dried up, undercutting the locals.

“I believe that’s a lot of the problem. They come in and take the work off the local contractors.”

Most people still associated him with the business, despite him not being the owner for many years, he said. He continued to own the land and buildings at Te Ngae Rd until about seven years ago.

Subsequent owners of the business have included former managing director Andrew Shrimpton and Te Puke businessman Seth Pardoe.

Pardoe, who took over in 2018, sold it to Auckland-based Mark Long in November last year, according to New Zealand Companies Office records.

Long, who has a doctorate in business administration, is linked to troubled company Du Val Property Group as a high-performance coach and observer.

He was reportedly set to become a director of that company not long before it went into receivership in 2024. Du Val Property Group was reported in 2025 as owing $268 million.

Long told the Rotorua Daily Post that Hickey Contractors had a great team and it was never easy to put people out of work.

His options were to sell the business to someone who wanted to keep the name, or sell the branding and plant separately.

He spoke to Hickey about what he wanted to do, “out of respect”.

It was Hickey’s preference to sell the plant separately and therefore wind up what was known as Hickey Contractors, Long said.

The loss of “a couple of people quite close to us” was also a factor in the decision.

“My priority was to be with my family and prioritise other businesses.”

Former manager Geoff Kitson, who was with Hickey Contractors for more than seven years, said the market was tough and Long could not sustain running the business how it was.

“Once I knew he was trying to sell it again, I resigned. I could see the writing was on the wall.”

He said the staff’s mood went from that of a close-knit business family to one of disappointment.

Kitson had now set up another contracting business with a former Hickey Contractors staff member.

Another former staff member, who asked not to be named, said some of the workers had found work elsewhere while others were now unemployed. He said about 20 people were left out of work, including full-timers and what he estimated were about eight sub-contractors.

Property owner Mark Rendall said the site on Te Ngae Rd was now for lease.

“We have an interested party. It’s set up as a contractors’ yard so it appeals only to a certain group.”

Rendall, who bought the land and buildings from the Hickeys around the time of the Covid-19 pandemic, said it was sad that the 50-year-old business with such an attachment to Rotorua would no longer exist.

Meanwhile, Stan Hickey is proving he’s still got what it takes on a bobcat after playing a large part in a team that won a major speedway track award at the weekend.

Paradise Valley Speedway was named Speedway of the Year in the Private or Professionally Promoted Venue category announced at the New Zealand Speedway Awards at the Christchurch Town Hall on July 18.

Rotorua also won the award for National Event of the Year with the New Zealand Stockcar Teams Championships.

Hickey again credited his wife for the club’s success.

He said he was a proud member of what was affectionately known at the track as “Dad’s Army”, which was a group of people like him who helped to build and maintain the speedway track.

Given the family’s passion for speedway in Rotorua, it was a proud moment to come away with the awards, he said.

“We were really proud of winning those awards. I have spent all my life up there [at Paradise Valley Speedway].”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

A phone ban for kids is not a rethink of my solution for social media harm – David Seymour

New Zealand Herald August 01, 2026

David Seymour supports a ban on smartphones for those under 16 rather than a social media ban. Photo / Getty Images

Cecilia Robinson of the lobby group “Before 16” praises Act for our “rethink” on social media harm. This in response to a speech where I suggested it might be more practical for the Government to ban smartphones for under-16s than social media. She even offered her own theories about why we’ve changed our minds.

Not to split hairs, but there has been no rethink. I’ve been worried about social media since at least 2018 when I had dinner with one of its main critics, Jonathan Haidt. Haidt was out on a limb with his theories back then, but more and more people have shared his worry since.

Mental distress has quadrupled among the young, according to the Ministry of Health’s surveys. It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that ubiquitous smartphones and social media apps they carry are a big part of the problem, when the same trends follow their introduction, all over the world.

It doesn’t help that social media companies employ extremely smart people to figure out how to keep children locked to the screen. Kids are not merely social media users. They are the product. It’s no surprise that social media companies are very effective at keeping children on their platforms.

That is why my party called for, and got, a select committee inquiry into the problem last year. It’s why one of our MPs, Laura McClure, has successfully brought about a bill banning deepfake porn with universal support across Parliament.

Unfortunately, Before 16 have rightly identified this problem, but hitched their wagon to a terrible solution. The ban they propose won’t work, and the side effects will leave us worse off. Act has been consistent in this position, too. It is possible to agree there’s a problem without diving into the solution.

Australia’s ban is almost totally ineffective. Almost all the kids who were on social media before are still on it after the ban.

Advocates of the ban are now saying things like “oh, you just need to give it five years” and “it’s not really about the ban, it’s about the changing the platforms’ behaviour”. Suffice to say, these arguments don’t square with the earnest, urgent tones they took before the Australian experiment.

The next proposal is to double down. Ban Virtual Private Networks. Require every adult to share a Government ID with every platform they log on to.

Extreme? Sure. North Korean, yep. But these ideas are the logical destination of a ban. Motivated teenagers are generally better at using the internet than adults. So, anything draconian enough to stop them will need to be restrictive and intrusive for adults. You can have the ban, or a free society, but not both.

The unintended consequences aren’t finished. Without such overreach, young people will still access social media, but feel less able to talk to adults about what they encounter if they believe they’ve done something illegal.

Or perhaps the ban will eventually push children off mainstream platforms, to worse places on the internet. TikTok may not be great, but it’s not the worst place online.

The social media ban is dying before our eyes. It will make a terrible problem worse, not better. The core problem is that the Government is no match for teenagers when it comes to using software, unless it goes to draconian lengths most adults will never accept.

The argument might end there, but parents feel under siege from social media and smartphones, or at least their children’s attachment to them. Parental responsibility is all well and good, but there is a first mover problem. No parent wants their child to become a social outcast if every other child is on the platforms.

The first mover problem is why Government might have a role here. Government could regulate the sale and supply of smartphones to under-16s. We already do similar things with vapes, cigarettes and alcohol, and it generally works.

An alternative law would forbid the sale and supply of any “smart” device that could fit in a pocket to children under 16. That is, any device with internet access, a touch screen and a camera.

Children under 16 wouldn’t be able to buy them, and parents who bought their children a “smart” device could be liable in the same way they would be for supplying their child with cigarettes.

This would wipe out much of the current harm because social media wouldn’t be ever-present. Perhaps it is nostalgia for my own millennial childhood, but there’s nothing wrong with a “dumb” phone. No touch screen, camera or internet access, just calling and texting to arrange pick-ups and meet-ups.

Children might still hassle Mum to use TikTok on her iPad. I concede that’s a problem, but not nearly as bad as carrying around an addictive supercomputer with a high-definition video camera for your entire childhood. Here’s to saving childhood with a practical, achievable policy all can agree on.

Child poverty report a devastating reflection of our values – Editorial

New Zealand Herald August 01, 2026

About 20% of New Zealand children live below the poverty line, with another 13% struggling in what the Child Poverty Action Group calls "extreme poverty".

THE FACTS

A report by the Ministry of Social Development has just been published and it is by any measure, devastating reading: one in seven children, 169,300 – roughly the population of Kirikiriroa (Hamilton) or Tauranga – are living in material hardship, in households earning 50% less than the median income.

Material hardship – a key poverty measure – means going without essentials: fresh fruit and vegetables, doctors, heating.

In low-income households, 17.8% of children – 210,600 – are living in poverty, roughly the population of Pōneke (Wellington City).

Māori and Pasifika children are disproportionately impacted, with 31.0% of Pacific children and 25.1% of tamariki Māori experiencing material hardship.

How on earth did a nation that prides itself on being egalitarian get here?

Political history and policies provide insight and reveal just how important they are, beyond rhetoric. In 2017, the Labour Government led by Dame Jacinda Ardern introduced the Child Poverty Reduction portfolio. The changes were incremental, addressing poverty alongside increasing core benefits by about $30-$50 a week. This came on top of other benefit increases, such as the Families Package and the winter energy payment. The minimum wage, increased by every government since 2014, also went up.

But after three years of the Ardern Government, the annual child poverty monitor found 148,000 children lived in homes experiencing material hardship, the same number as when Labour took power. Children’s Commissioner at the time, Andrew Becroft, said the efforts had failed and the numbers had remained unchanged since the first report into child poverty in 2012.

Bolder action was required, Becroft said.

There was some hope in 2021 when it was reported that 43,300 children had been lifted out of poverty when using the after-housing-costs measure and compared to 2017. That is roughly the population of Whanganui.

But since then, child poverty has got worse.

This week the Minister for Child Poverty Reduction, Louise Upston, managed to apply impoverished logic to a miserable reality, saying there was no radical increase in child poverty, ergo nothing to see here. Except there is.

In the coalition Government’s first year, child poverty numbers rose to 170,000 from 160,000 post-pandemic.

At best it suggests a blind spot; at worst, casual disregard for the welfare of our most vulnerable and for the big picture, which all New Zealanders should be acutely concerned about.

New Zealand’s rates of child poverty are three times worse than those that affect children in other developed countries. In Denmark, a wealthy European country for example, one-third fewer children live in material poverty compared with New Zealand.

There are multiple elements to poverty and there is no single measurement. It’s highly complex, but if we look at the bigger picture, how does child poverty impact in a broader societal and economic way?

Much like the interest on a debt with a loan shark, because you can’t afford to pay a surprise $500 bill, the wretchedness compounds. Poorer nutrition; lower education outcomes; compounding harm through health issues; worse mental health in a country that already ranks third in the world for child and adolescent suicide rates; homelessness; and ultimately, less economic growth.

Gone, too, the dreams and ambitions; the skills and tools to develop and grow. If the poorest children aren’t supported, they won’t have the tools to not only get through life but to thrive.

In 1980s New Zealand, Rogernomics championed the “neo-liberal” shift in politics – championed hyper individualism; the market will decide. In 1982, child poverty sat at around 14% – by 2013 it was 24%.

Homelessness nationally is at record rates and according to the Affordable Housing Database, New Zealand now has one of the highest rates among developed countries.

New Zealand is ranking high in all the wrong places. These statistics are eye-watering, and they make the Prime Minister’s political rhetoric about “Kiwis doing it tough” sound bafflingly out of touch. For material poverty we need material solutions – housing affordability, fairer tax and pay equity.

On Friday Christopher Luxon told the Rotorua business community that if businesses were not “retooling and radically disrupting” their business, “you ain’t doing your job”. This Government could say the same about itself on child poverty, and the lack of a radical or even gradual shift for the better in relation to child poverty.

The 1% should not reflect the wealthiest – that statistic should pertain to a low number of the poorest New Zealanders. That is radical thinking; that is disruption. When we can cite that statistic, then and only then can we say we are a fair society, and only then can we hold our heads high.

Letters: Fireworks ban decision flies in face of public opinion; wealth tax perspectives

New Zealand Herald August 01, 2026

Fireworks go on sale as debate reignites over banning private Guy Fawkes displays. Photo / 123rf

The Government’s decision this week not to ban the public sale of fireworks flies in the face of public opinion. Three petitions, bearing a combined total of nearly 100,000 signatures, were ignored, as was the expert advice of the SPCA’s chief scientific officer, Dr Arnja Dale.

Queensland banned the public sale of fireworks in 1972, and the populous Australian states of New South Wales and Victoria followed suit in the 1980s.

Our Government’s justification – that a ban would remove access to “a long-standing and widely used lawful activity” – is unconvincing. It overlooks the distress caused to animals, the risk of injury and property damage, and the ongoing nuisance of fireworks being set off late at night for weeks after November 5. It also ignores the unnecessary cost of importing fireworks, adding to New Zealand’s trade deficit.

The Government should show some leadership, listen to the overwhelming public sentiment, and do the right thing by banning the public sale of fireworks.

Randal Lockie, Rothesay Bay.

Reading Thomas Coughlan’s and Phil Whittington’s perspective (July 29) on the Greens’ super-rich tax, I couldn’t help noticing it was not once mentioned – even in the worst-case scenario – that it would still bring in billions for spending on ordinary Kiwis.

Despite being chock-full of numbers and doubt-casting, it failed to mention anywhere that, whether the 1000-odd affected households stiffed us by a (modelled) 28% or a (speculated) 43.75%, through tax avoidance, it would still reduce inequality and convert the asset inflation that benefits just 0.3% of us into collective productivity and wellbeing for the remaining 97.7%.

But it wasn’t until the bafflingly unrelatable example of the couple suffering from their $200m wealth burden that I literally laughed out loud. If they want to leave behind family, friends, community, and a New Zealand lifestyle, to live with the dust and dangerous wildlife of Australia, let them. But let’s not worry about their tax bill: wealth like that dependably grows by $200,000+ a week, tax-free, so I think they’ll be fine.

Tim Barlow, Hillcrest.

Winston Aldworth’s article (July 23) on ditching the Commonwealth Games, because of its anachronistic link to another era, suggests he does not know what it is like to represent his country in sport.

Many people who are seriously involved in sport have a lifelong ambition to wear the silver fern at international level. The Commonwealth Games helps fulfil that ambition. Dame Valerie Adams first showed her talent at these games before going on to Olympic glory.

The Games also showcase sports that normally don’t receive much public attention. These include lawn bowls, squash and parasports. Also, young people watching these Games might be inspired to become involved in sport at the community level, which could lead to the ultimate goal of representing New Zealand.

If Aldworth wants to ditch the Commonwealth Games because of its odorous connection to a colonial past, then he should perhaps interview some of our current medallists in Glasgow to see what they think.

Bernard Walker, Mt Maunganui.

Richard Prebble’s characterisation of Ōwairaka Boys’ Home as a cross between a hotel and a holiday camp cannot go unchallenged. I had some professional knowledge of the place in the 1970s, but would refer sceptical readers to the report of the Royal Commission on Abuse in Care. It speaks of “savage beatings”, and “runaways” being “beaten to a pulp” on their return.

Either Prebble claims that the survivors and staff who gave evidence are all lying; or he approves of the deterrent value of such abuse.

Colin Jones, Redvale.

It seems that NZ First just keeps embarrassing itself and our country. I refer to it as the “The Time Warp Party”. Still stuck in 70s’ archaic ways and views, plus: “it’s just a jump to the left, and a step to the right”.

Dean McIlroy, Ngahinapouri.

Calls for Winston Peters’ resignation or dismissal are perfectly reasonable. His tirade against Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan in the House was unforgivable, particularly for someone who holds the title of Foreign Affairs Minister.

Not only did this insult reach the ears of all New Zealanders, which was bad enough, but also those of the Chinese Ambassador to New Zealand and, from there, without any doubt, the Chinese Government. Peters has lost any respect, credibility and trust as a suitable representative for our country as a valued member of government, not just here but across the globe.

Christopher Luxon gave the portfolio to Peters. Now it’s time to take it back. Anything less would bring Luxon’s ability to act as leader of Aotearoa New Zealand into question.

Jeremy Coleman, Hillpark.

I read with interest, and ultimately concern, the article (July 29) on the NZ sports anti-doping programme. Any reader of the article would have been left with a clear impression that New Zealand has an unreliable and sub-standard programme.

The article emphasised three areas where the programme was deemed non-compliant with mandatory international standards. The issues were ones of partial or incomplete application of standards rather than total failure.

While not inaccurate, the article gave no sense of context. To have only three (easily, and apparently now remedied) “critical” issues to address amid the hundreds of mandatory requirements is an extraordinarily low number for such a thorough audit to identify and, by this measure, places the organisation among the highest-performing such organisations in the world. The overall conclusions of the WADA audit were highly complementary of the programme, but received only a cursory late reference. While it is important to keep our public authorities under scrutiny, it needs to be done with research, balance and perspective.

Graeme Steel, Pakuranga.

The hidden cost of raising a young competitor in Hawke’s Bay – nearly $44k and counting

New Zealand Herald August 01, 2026

When Paula Wilson sat down and added up what she had spent supporting her teenage son’s competitive chess over the past two-and-a-half years, she was shocked.

Airfares: about $13,400.

Accommodation: $19,000.

Tournament entries: $3300.

Coaching: $7200.

Transport and extras: $800.

The total was about $43,700, excluding food, petrol and other day-to-day travel costs.

Her son, Dion Wilson, 17, placed second at the New Zealand under-20 Junior Championship in Invercargill in January and represented the country at the under-16 Fide Olympiad in Colombia last year.

Dion has played about 23 tournaments over the past two-and-a-half years. None of them were in Hawke’s Bay.

Unlike competitors in larger centres, every event needed to improve Dion ‘s rating required travel, Paula said.

A single mother and hairdresser, she had borrowed money, relied on her parents’ support and downsized their home to keep funding Dion’s progress.

“We have done a lot of sacrifices for him to do what he is doing,” Paula said.

“The commitment is just pretty much 100%.”

Dion recently missed a chance to represent New Zealand at the Commonwealth Chess Championships in Sri Lanka because the family could not afford the travel.

“He’s missed out on numerous trips because we just can’t afford it,” Paula said.

She had faced similar costs with her older son, Jayden Wilson, who was a competitive swimmer.

“This is just carrying on from one expense to now another,” Paula said.

She said funding for individual competitors was difficult to access, with most support aimed at team sports.

“People don’t know that chess games go for four to five hours twice a day, and it can be up to 10 days when you go to Congress.”

Families across Hawke’s Bay are facing similar pressures in other sports.

Koryo Taekwondo Hawke’s Bay owner and head instructor Camille Pruckmuller has spent more than 30 years coaching athletes and has also experienced the costs as a parent – and now a grandparent.

Her 14-year-old grandson, Lennix Pruckmuller-Brown, is preparing for a month-long training trip to Thailand, aimed at helping him make the New Zealand team next year.

He comes from a family with six children and is one of twins.

Pruckmuller said his parents could not afford the costs, so she funded much of his pathway herself.

She estimated supporting a serious taekwondo competitor cost between $6000 and $7000 a year, excluding international flights, with expenses including training fees, uniforms, compulsory camps, travel, accommodation and specialist sparring equipment.

Electronic socks alone could cost about $120 a pair and may need replacing, while different competitions can require different electronic systems.

“And they don’t last very long because they’re on your feet. And of course, the kids are growing,” Pruckmuller said.

This year, a Gold Coast competition cost them just under $4000.

The Hastings Boys’ High School student also worked as a dishwasher and mowed lawns to help fund his journey.

His twin brother also trains in taekwondo but does not compete because Pruckmuller couldn’t afford to support both boys at that level.

Fundraising through raffles, sausage sizzles and markets had become part of club life.

One junior, Jake Champion, was fundraising to travel to the World Poomsae Championships in South Korea in September, while another para-athlete qualified for the world championships but could not afford to go.

Another family, with three children in the club, had paused the training because of the cumulative cost of fees, gear and competition travel.

A Central Hawke’s Bay family has also faced the financial challenge of supporting more than one high-performing teenage athlete.

Kiri Kirk said she had organised raffles, quiz nights, sales, sought sponsorship and relied on support from the Waipukurau community to help fund daughter Caitlin’s athletics and multisport career and son Lachie’s trampolining.

“You name it. I’ve done it all over the past five years,” Kiri said.

Caitlin’s current trip to the World Under-20 Athletics Championships in the United States cost about $12,000, following Gold Coast and Spain campaigns last year costing about $5000 and $12,000 respectively for each child.

“There is no funding for them, though I’ve tried everywhere around the country,” Kiri said.

Sport Hawke’s Bay chief executive Ryan Hambleton said cost was increasingly one of the biggest barriers once young people progressed into representative pathways.

“We are seeing more families having to make difficult decisions about which opportunities they can realistically afford to pursue,” he said.

“In many cases, it isn’t a lack of talent, commitment or potential that limits progress, it is affordability.”

He said demand for funding exceeded available resources despite support from gaming trusts, community foundations, councils and national initiatives.

Hawke’s Bay families also faced extra costs because most high-performance competitions, camps and specialist training were outside the region.

He said there was no single solution, with rising travel, accommodation, equipment and living costs combining to put increasing pressure on families.

“No single organisation can solve that challenge alone. What is needed is a collective effort across our system.”

Pastures Past: Saleyard locations debated as towns expanded

New Zealand Herald August 01, 2026

The location of saleyards became an issue as towns grew. Photo / John Stone

Kem Ormond takes a look at farming back in the day. In this week’s Pastures Past, she’s found newspaper articles on saleyards.

The location of saleyards has long been a subject of debate, as seen in the articles below.

In many districts, communities carefully weighed up the advantages and disadvantages before deciding where to establish them.

Early saleyards were often located near the heart of a township, where they were convenient for farmers and stock agents.

As towns grew, however, difficulties emerged.

Livestock being driven through the streets posed risks to pedestrians and cyclists, while effluent from the yards could contaminate nearby waterways.

Increasing traffic volumes also made it more dangerous to move stock between farms and saleyards via roads and highways.

Below is a selection of historical stories from the Hawke’s Bay Tribune (1928), Central Hawke’s Bay Press (1941) and the Northern Advocate (1944 and 1945).

Hawke’s Bay Tribune, July 6, 1928

(To the Editor.)

Sir, —Have the gentlemen who oppose the removal of the saleyards site any children attending the nearby school?

Only on Wednesday last a lady teacher was thrown from her bicycle when passing a mob of cattle between the saleyards and the school.

About the same time, a small girl suffered the same fate and had to be conveyed home.

These are two instances. No doubt there are plenty more.

Also, do any of the aforesaid gentlemen live anywhere near the saleyards?

If so, probably an alarm clock is not much use to them.

—Yours etc. QUERY.

Hastings, 6/7/28.

(Per Press Association)

Pollution of stream

Central Hawke’s Bay Press, February 25, 1941

Feilding, Last Night.

The existence of the Feilding live stock saleyards is threatened by legal proceedings which have been started.

It is understood that the Manawatu Live Stock Auctioneers have been served with a legal process claiming damages and applying for an injunction restraining the concern, as proprietors of the saleyards, from creating an alleged nuisance.

The legal process has been instituted because of alleged injuries suffered by a landowner who claims that the drainage from the saleyards is polluting the Makino Stream.

The damages claimed are understood to be in the vicinity of £800.

The situation arising from these proceedings must be of some concern to Feilding because of the importance of the saleyards to the town and district.

For 50 years or more the saleyards have served a wide district and have grown to paramount importance in the realm of live stock selling in the North Island.

Thousands of heads of stock pass through these yards every year, and their central situation affords unusual facilities for the quick handling of all offerings.

The Feilding Borough Council, it is understood, has considered the situation, for it knew that there was some complaint about the alleged pollution of the Makino Stream.

Northern Advocate, August 11, 1944

Support for the removal of the saleyards at Kamo was sought by the Kamo Town Board of the Whangarei County Council today.

The board considered that the saleyards were too near the town area.

The chairman (Mr J. Morrison) moved that the council should support any move to meet the position.

Stating that the present was not an opportune time for removal of the two saleyards as a great amount of timber and concrete would be required, Cr. R. Feaver moved an amendment that the council should support the removal of the saleyards but considered the work should not be done until after the war.

Plans could be made now for the future, he considered.

Cr. W. C. B. Powell doubted if it was the function of local bodies to endeavour to bring about community yards.

Explaining that he had not thought the motion would embarrass anybody, the chairman withdrew his motion as he considered the amendment on the right lines.

Councillors supported Cr. Feaver’s suggestion, which was adopted.

Northern Advocate, June 14, 1945

Controlling the building of saleyards on State highways was advocated to No. 1 Highways Board meeting in Whangarei yesterday by the chairman (Mr W. L. Bell).

He said that with saleyards on highways, traffic congestion occurred not only with stock but also through parked cars.

He suggested that saleyards should be set back from the road to allow of a parking ground.

This suggestion was supported by members who considered that some form of regulations should be framed to control the erection of saleyards on highways.

It was stated by Mr Bell that the stock firms were prepared to co-operate and a resolution was carried asking the Highways Board, in consultation with stock firms, to bring down regulations governing the erection of saleyards on highways.

- Source: Papers Past

The draw, the brawl and the buried curse: The wild story behind Collingwood’s 1990 flag

Sydney Morning Herald August 02, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

For 32 years, between the premiership of 1958 and the drought-breaker of 1990, Collingwood were a laughing stock for opposition supporters because of a mythical curse. It was known as the “Colliwobbles”, a term coined during a phase in which the Magpies went to nine grand finals and came away with not a single victory.

Their draw against North Melbourne in 1977 was as close as they came to triumph. It became a crushing weight to carry, only growing with each successive failure on the big stage.

Back when Collingwood surprised Melbourne in the 1958 VFL grand final, denying the Demons a fourth straight flag, the Magpies had 13 premierships and sat three ahead of any other club, Essendon being next best with 10.

But for three decades they could not add to their tally – eight times runner-up in that period including the fadeout from 44 points ahead at half-time against Carlton in 1970. In one stretch, the Magpies were runners-up in four of five seasons from 1977.

This is what makes the 1990 grand final, the first under the banner of the Australian Football League, so famous. I don’t think there could have been a wilder night in Melbourne, such was the emotion that spilled into the streets.

Yet Collingwood was not the best team in the competition that year – Essendon was, quite comfortably. That Collingwood won came down to the ability of Leigh Matthews’ side to perform when it counted, but also to a quirk of the finals system that has since been adjusted.

Essendon, coached by Kevin Sheedy and boasting Tim Watson, Terry Daniher, Simon Madden, Mark Thompson, Paul Vander Haar, Michael Long, Derek Kickett, Mark Harvey, Paul Salmon, Gary O’Donnell and Darren Bewick, to name but a few, went 17–5 for the season to finish a game clear on top of the ladder. When the Bombers beat St Kilda in the final round on September 1, they were firm favourites for the flag.

Under the system at the time, they had week one of the finals off so they could tend to their wounds. But three weeks after that game at Waverley, they still had not played a final. The delay occurred because Collingwood and West Coast played a draw in the qualifying final, forcing a replay the next week and pushing all the other games back.

It was such a mess that the AFL introduced extra time for finals from 1991 (the extra-time rules did not apply to grand finals until 2016). Too late for Essendon in 1990, the Bombers had to wait until September 23 – a full 22 days – to play Collingwood in a semi-final. Players are creatures of habit, and the several weeks off stole their momentum; they were never the same team.

Collingwood smashed Essendon in the semi-final to win direct entry to the grand final.(The Bombers reached the grand final after beating West Coast in the preliminary by 10 goals.)

The Magpies were match-hardened and running at full tilt. But they still had to deal with the Colliwobbles. In charge of this project were two fierce competitors in Matthews and Tony Shaw, the Collingwood captain. Matthews was in his first stint as a head coach and had brought a calm to Collingwood that was epitomised by the lack of streamers or balloons in the dressing room before the grand final. He reasoned that no player needed extra motivation or adrenaline flow for this match.

Shaw had a day job as a gardener with the Collingwood Council and was the younger brother of a former Collingwood captain, Ray Shaw. He had Collingwood in his blood, but he had seen his elder brother play in five grand finals without a win, as well as experiencing it twice himself in 1980 and 1981. Enough was enough.

Matthews recalled hearing Shaw drive his players with the message: “I’ve played in two losing grand finals. There’s not going to be a third.”

Meanwhile, across town, Essendon was worried, producing a slipshod final training session at Windy Hill and having to endure a club function at the Flemington Racecourse the night before the match.

On the day, Collingwood was much better, covering all its deficiencies. While the 205-centimetre Paul Salmon threatened early for the Dons, Matthews sent Michael Christian to curb him. Peter Daicos conjured a trademark miracle goal from the boundary to get his team up and running. Shaw beavered and bullocked through the middle on his way to a Norm Smith Medal.

Kevin Sheedy has said that Collingwood was not a great side in 1990, but the Magpies did have an all-time great in Daicos, who kicked 97 goals that season, plus Darren Millane, Gavin Brown, Graham Wright, Mick McGuane and a two-time Copeland Trophy winner in Shaw, plus numerous other outstanding players. Missing a legitimate tall forward because of Brian Taylor’s absence through injury, regular half-back Gavin Crosisca had to play at centre half-forward in a patch-up role. He thrived on the challenge.

At quarter-time of the grand final, with Collingwood three points ahead, there was a ferocious brawl. As was their wont in that era, the players unloaded.

Denis Banks, Collingwood’s centre half-forward, has acknowledged that he started it by ankle-tapping Kieran Sporn of Essendon. Sporn belted Banks, Gavin Brown king-hit Sporn, and an offended Terry Daniher defended his teammate’s honour and knocked out Brown with a punch to the head.

At the first break, Matthews implored his players to keep their eyes on the ball and “be the victims”. Paul Salmon has said that Sheedy delivered the same message, but it was Collingwood’s players who settled better. Essendon conceded three 50-metre penalties with ill-discipline and the Magpies ran away to a good lead.

The tension simmered all day – and particularly at half-time, as the players left the field. In those days, the two races were side by side, and Matthews was looking for something he could use as a powerful motivational tool.

He grabbed Brown, who had spent the second quarter off the field, by the arm, and walked him towards Terry Daniher.

As they headed up the race, an extraordinary scene unfolded: Matthews was screaming that Brown was “coming back for you”, while Daniher was throwing punches at Collingwood’s coach through the wire netting.

Brown did come back onto the field in the third quarter, sprinting straight up to confront Daniher in the Collingwood forward line. He doubtless was suffering from some concussion – he had not moved for some time after Daniher clocked him – but his return seemed to symbolise Collingwood’s resilience and resolve.

The Magpies pulled away but the players never relaxed. Shaw would not allow them the luxury. Doug Barwick’s goal at the 19-minute mark of the final quarter sealed it, but even then, Matthews waited until Damian Monkhorst bombed one home after 25 minutes before he left the box.

He almost broke the neck of his football manager, Graeme ‘Gubby’ Allan, in the embrace they shared down on the boundary. By then the crowd was singing the Collingwood theme song.

Darren Millane had the football in defence when the siren signalled a 48-point win and the end of the great drought. Millane, who had played the finals’ series with a broken right thumb – having it replastered after each successive match – threw the Sherrin in the air, leaving us with an image that has lingered. He died in a car accident in Albert Park just a year on.

At the siren, Tony Shaw went down on all fours. At 170 centimetres and 80 kilograms, with an abbreviated left-foot kick and no leg speed, he had defied the physical odds to be best afield. “Mentally and physically, I was shot,” he said. “I had nothing left.”

Tim Watson, his opposing captain and a class act in every way, embraced Shaw, acknowledging the workload he had carried. “He was like a wind-up doll, just going and going,” Watson later said. “He was going to take his last breath on the MCG to make sure they had victory on that day.”

It was a missed opportunity for Essendon, but the AFL’s system is not first-past-the-post, as is common in, say, soccer. Part of the beauty of this game is that the premiership has to be won on the day.

Matthews had his first premiership as a coach, on his way to four – and Australian football immortality. His record as a player and coach is remarkable, with eight flags. “I’m just so pleased for those 20 blokes who’ve written their name in history and cut down a folklore of Australian sport,” he told Channel 7.

The aftermath of the 1990 grand final matched the gravity of the occasion with some irreverence and a lot of fun. Collingwood’s players celebrated at a formal function at the Southern Cross Hotel in the city and then took the team bus to Victoria Park, their home ground, amid chaotic scenes.

It took aeons to get to the ground, where tens of thousands of supporters were already celebrating. Hoddle Street was choked with traffic; at each traffic light, Collingwood fans could be seen standing on the roofs of cars, with people milling all over the road, oblivious to danger. The bus ultimately had to take every side street to spirit the players to Vic Park.

Driving home to Clifton Hill that night, I witnessed the chaos first-hand. Kevin Sheedy had to as well, heading to his northern suburbs home. A friend and colleague who was covering the celebrations found his way onto the Collingwood bus; he said he had never witnessed a scene like it in Melbourne.

At Vic Park, the players were treated like rock stars as they made their way to the stage. “It was like being in heaven,” said Tony Shaw.

A few weeks later, Collingwood called its supporters back to Victoria Park for a funeral. Lou Richards, media personality and former club captain, was dressed as an undertaker, complete with top hat. Ten thousand people showed up to see Richards place a wooden coffin containing the Colliwobbles in the ground out on the playing arena. “It’s ashes to ashes, dust to dust, the Colliwobbles are buried, and once again, it’s them against us,” he said.

This is an edited extract from Martin Blake’s book Why We Love Footy: An Aussie Rules History in 50 Great Moments, published by Allen & Unwin; available August 4.

Can testosterone improve your sex life and boost your mood – and what are the risks? Here’s what the science says

Sydney Morning Herald August 02, 2026

Both men and women are seeking out testosterone for a host of reasons. Why the buzz? And what do the experts want you to know?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It’ll put a spring in your step, improve your sex life and lift your mood, its proponents claim. Testosterone is in demand – among both men and women –but not everyone is excited. “Muscle strength, mood, brain fog, cognition, general vitality, wellbeing, dementia – you name it, someone will have said that testosterone is the magical cure for that,” says women’s health general practitioner Dr Karina Severin. Patients “will be very, very insistent that that’s what they want”.

As awareness grows of women’s experiences around menopause, and more women in midlife seek out menopausal hormone therapy, testosterone has entered the picture. There’s been an uptick in women seeking out prescriptions in Britain; while in the US, women over 40 taking it in high doses has become a “cultural phenomenon”, reports The New York Times, despite it not being medically approved for them. “Rhapsodic stories of sexual reawakening have spread on social media, where testosterone influencers share their experiences,” writes Susan Dominus, who notes an increasing number of women willing to risk “unpleasant – and possibly irreversible – side effects to pursue a dramatic high.”

In Australia, women’s health researcher Professor Susan Davis began researching the effect of testosterone on women in the 1990s and is considered a world expert. She says many women in midlife are “desperately seeking how to feel better.” “People are making claims and telling women it’s the missing hormone, based on absolutely no data,” she says. The buzz is being driven by various factors, she suggests, including “people of goodwill who have become evangelical” and “people who are being predatory financially”.

Women have led a surge in testosterone use in Australia, with prescriptions rising from just over 1800 in 2016 to nearly 34,000 in 2025. The female product is medically approved only for a specific group: postmenopausal women who are distressed about having low libido, a condition called hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction, which affects between 8 and 33 per cent of women and peaks in their early 40s. Yet women are seeking out testosterone for a host of other reasons as well.

Meanwhile, social media abounds with men and teenage boys “T maxxing” to improve their strength, physique, libido and mood, spurred by influencers such as US podcaster Joe Rogan, fitness influencers and “manosphere” personalities who, as one Australian study puts it, are framing testosterone testing and treatment as “remedies for a perceived masculinity crisis”.

In the US, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has introduced annual testosterone deficiency screening for all service members aged 30 and older (including women) to keep them “on the leading edge of lethality”. The goal, he says, is a “High-T Department of War”. Another key figure in the Trump administration, Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr, takes testosterone as part of an anti-ageing protocol. US nutrition guidelines now include a section on how to support testosterone levels (protein is important, it says, just not too much).

As people find various ways to access testosterone drugs, including by buying it online, we’re in uncharted territory. “It’s a prescription medicine, and rightly so because it’s a very powerful drug,” says Michael Buckley, the chief executive of Lawley Pharmaceutical in Perth, which makes testosterone for both men and women.

The evidence shows if you take too much, the consequences can be serious and permanent: in men, testicular shrinkage, breast development, reduced sperm production or infertility; in women, a permanently deepened voice, changes in menstruation, uncomfortable clitoral enlargement. In both, hair loss, irritability and acne.

What does testosterone do to men and women? Why do people want it? And what does the evidence say about its benefits and risks?

Human bodies produce more than 50 hormones – chemicals that control everything from our metabolism and mood to our sexual function and sleep. Women and men produce the same hormones but in different concentrations. Women’s main sex hormone is mostly oestrogen; men’s is testosterone.

Men produce about 6 milligrams a day (about 10 times more than women), peaking in the morning. From the testes and adrenal glands, it moves through the blood, triggering puberty in boys, producing sperm and sex drive. It helps maintain muscle mass and bone density as well as increasing red blood cell count (the ones that carry oxygen) before it is excreted in urine.

In Australia, testosterone treatment for men is medically approved only in cases where the testes don’t produce enough, a condition known as hypogonadism, which occurs in about one in 200 men, mostly those who are older, obese or have diabetes. A deficiency can also be caused by damage to the testicles or the pituitary gland, infections, tumours and some cancer treatments. One in 600 men has hypogonadism due to Klinefelter syndrome, where an extra X chromosome results in small testes and low testosterone.

A normal level of testosterone for a young man is about 20 to 25 nanomoles per litre of blood, says endocrinologist Associate Professor Carolyn Allan. Levels fall about 1 per cent a year from a man’s late 30s. What constitutes low testosterone in a man is a controversial question, says Michael Buckley, whose company supplies testosterone products to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Britain, with measures varying across different places, including Europe and the United States.

In Australia, to qualify for discounted testosterone via the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS), a man’s levels must be lower than 6 nanomoles per litre, although men can access testosterone products without the subsidy if their levels are higher. In Australia, the medically approved testosterone treatments – creams, gels and injections – are designed to restore levels to within the normal range associated with the patient’s age group, as well as to reduce symptoms.

Prescribed testosterone therapy can ease low mood and boost libido, which is a fillip for confidence, says University of Queensland public health researcher Benjamin Bonenti. ”It’s like night and day when they get that function back in terms of the ability to tackle life,” says Bonenti, who has analysed worldwide surveys of testosterone users (including some who are using it simply for muscle strength and a buff physique).

Brisbane man Nick started buying testosterone from a “contact” about 12 years ago to take his bodybuilding “to the next level”. He knows of some bodybuilders who dose themselves with 10 or 20 times more testosterone than their body would naturally produce. “Some [competitions] test for that stuff,” he says, “and others don’t. And you go to those [that don’t test] because you’re on steroids.”

Over the years, Nick has taken anabolic-androgen steroids, which mimic testosterone (anabolic means “tissue-building”). These have legitimate medical uses, such as treating delayed puberty in males or muscle loss caused by diseases such as cancer, but they’re illegal when used outside medical supervision and are, famously, banned by sporting bodies who class them as performance- and image-enhancing drugs. Their long-term effects include sudden cardiac death and kidney failure.

At other times, Nick has taken lower doses of testosterone products, or none. He now takes a dose prescribed by a doctor. “I’m nearly 40 years old now, and because I put my body through that on-and-off process a few times, and then went to TRT [testosterone replacement therapy] for a little bit, I do actually need it legitimately for replacement,” he says. Improving muscle mass was only part of the benefit for Nick. “You feel better, you’re in a better mood, you’re happier, you’re more driven to do things, more motivated, less lethargic and sluggish.”

The number of PBS-listed testosterone prescriptions for men, including transgender men, has grown from just over 148,000 in 2015 to close to 166,000 in 2025, says the federal Department of Health. However, the total number is higher, as the figures exclude men whose testosterone levels are not low enough to qualify for a PBS discount, or who have bought it offmarket, through websites, gyms or encrypted apps.

A recent University of Sydney analysis of how testosterone is portrayed to men looked at 46 popular TikTok and Instagram accounts and found 72 per cent had financial interests in promoting the hormone while two-thirds included direct links to either a test, promotion codes or a consultation at a testosterone clinic. Themes running through the posts, which were targeted mostly at men aged between 20 and 40, included “needing testosterone treatments to become better men or better versions of themselves”.

The seminal research on the effect of testosterone on muscles dates to 1996, when researchers in Los Angeles found that men given doses of testosterone higher than their body would naturally produce increased their muscle size and strength more than those who didn’t take the hormones. “Our results in no way justify the use of anabolic-androgenic steroids in sports,” the researchers said at the time. (Carolyn Allan notes “scale weight is not changed but muscle is gained and fat is lost with testosterone”.)

Other studies have shown testosterone helps the sex drive and sexual performance of men with low levels, but there’s little improvement once levels reach a certain point (15 nanomoles per litre). A study co-authored by Carolyn Allan also found testosterone treatment prevented the progression of type 2 diabetes among men aged between 50 and 74 who were overweight or obese, helping to regulate blood sugar and decrease body fat.

Allan says men with underlying medical conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome, who can’t produce enough testosterone and are treated under medical supervision, “should be reassured that lifelong testosterone replacement therapy is both safe and necessary for optimal physical and psycho-sexual wellbeing”. However, there are still questions about the long-term benefits and risks of medically prescribed testosterone for men with levels that fall within the normal range but at the lower end, she says. A large US study, the Traverse trial, “did not find concerning heart or prostate cancer effects after five years,” she adds, “but we do not have information beyond this”.

Erratic fluctuations in oestrogen and progesterone during perimenopause (the lead-up to menopause, which is when periods stop) can run for years and create havoc for women. Hot flushes, night sweats, disturbed sleep, joint pain, anxiety, mood swings, weight gain and bone-density loss are just some of the symptoms. Menopausal hormonal therapy, or MHT, typically consists of oestrogen and progesterone, or oestrogen alone for women who’ve had a hysterectomy because progesterone is used to reduce the risk of cancer of the uterus.

Sydney woman Belinda, who is on MHT, added testosterone about 18 months ago to boost her energy, at the suggestion of her GP. Australia was the first country to approve a female-specific testosterone product, a cream called AndroFeme, which is what Belinda takes. “The big thing I noticed was the energy,” she tells us. “I wanted to do more exercise, I’ve been back at the gym three days a week. I’d wake up [before testosterone] feeling kind of achy and old. It’s gone from that to now feeling really good in the morning.”

Testosterone does play a role in women’s sex drive, mood, bone and muscle strength and fertility. In women, levels decline about 25 per cent by the age of 40 and continue to drop until age 60. This means that the fall in testosterone occurs before menopause (unless you’ve gone through “early menopause” as a result of chemotherapy or radiation therapy, or “surgical menopause” due to both ovaries being removed). Testosterone levels actually rise slightly again after about age 60, although the reasons are not yet known.

The drop-off doesn’t bother every woman. But it can lead to low libido and when this is distressing, for postmenopausal women at least, doctors can prescribe testosterone. Markers of success include increased sexual frequency and satisfaction. “The effects are modest – they’re not massive,” says Susan Davis, who heads the Monash University women’s health research program. “And often women will come back, saying, ‘Look, I’m not initiating sex any more, and I’m still not initiating sex’, and you say, ‘Well, yes, but if your partner initiates, what are you like?’ And they respond, ‘Oh yes, I’m more interested.’ So the effects don’t blow you out of the water, but the effects can be real.”

Karina Severin says she prescribes testosterone to women wanting to improve their libido several times a day. The typical patient once had a great sex life, got through menopause and now feels great on MHT – except for a non-existent sex drive. (As with many drugs, testosterone can be prescribed “off label”, including for patient groups for whom it’s not officially approved such as women in perimenopause.)

About 20,000 women use AndroFeme in Australia, says Buckley at Lawley Pharmaceuticals. Davis’s research has also shown the number of midlife women who use the hormone is extremely small – just 28 of 2500 participants in her Australian Women’s Midlife Years Study in 2024. Most of them used AndroFeme while others got a male drug prescribed off label by their GP or in a form compounded by pharmacists.

The bottom line, Davis says, is that any benefits other than for those seen in postmenopausal women with low libido are, for now, unproven. “That’s because either no benefit has been shown in good studies or the studies are inadequate to give us the information we need,” she says.

But what about preventing loss of muscle mass? “An effect is only seen when the dose is high enough to cause male blood levels in women,” says Davis.

And what about as a mood booster? Says Karina Severin: “I think that in general, we see lots of people having mental health issues around menopause, which could well be hormonal.” (Symptoms include anger, sadness, brain fog, low energy, panic attacks, worry and low self-esteem, and are more common in women with a history of depression and premenstrual syndrome, says Beyond Blue.) But she is wary of prescribing testosterone for low mood. “One of the biggest problems we see is there’s such a placebo effect, which means that women feel better just by the fact that they’re coming and talking to you. No-one’s shown in any study that testosterone is better than that.”

Sydneysider Belinda says some of her friends have asked their GPs about taking testosterone for general health and vitality but have been knocked back. “So we all know the hack is: you have to go in and say, ‘Yes, I want it because I want it for my libido’, and then they will prescribe it to you. Which is interesting because why isn’t our health as important as our libido?”

Severin agrees women are using libido as a pretext. “The criteria to prescribe it for low libido are subjective,” she explains. “The questions are: did you previously have a good sex drive, has it decreased, does that bother you, and do you want to do something about it? The fifth question is exploring for other reasons why they might have less sex drive. But anyone can come and say that.”

Sydney sexual health physician Dr Terri Foran says about half of her female patients who take testosterone discontinue it after a trial. When this happens, doctors and patients can look at other reasons for low libido, such as the state of their relationship.

Despite feeling better, Belinda says she’s experienced some judgement about taking testosterone, including from men who argue the hormone is not important to women. “I think if a woman wants to take it, she should have the choice to take it for a health and vitality reason,” she says. “It should be dispensed easily, and it should be on the PBS.”

The women’s product is not discounted via the PBS, unlike the 14 PBS-listed testosterone medicines for men. This means women pay about $100 for three months while men pay $25 under the PBS subsidy (and as little as $7.70 for concession cardholders). “Yes, it’s $30 a month,” Belinda tells us, “but then there’s also the oestrogen and the progesterone, and then this GP who specialises in this, she’s more than a normal GP, she’s $240 a visit, so if you start adding up all the costs of doing this, some people are just like, ‘I can’t afford all of that.’” (Buckley’s company is appealing the decision of the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee not to list his product on the PBS.)

The experts we spoke with were divided on whether the women’s product should be subsidised. Says Severin: “I think that a lot of these people in this stage are like, you know, if that’s what I gotta pay to get my sex life back then that’s what I’m gonna pay, it’s not that much.” Foran has a different perspective. “It’s not cheap, and that puts it beyond the range of women who should have medical access to it. However, if it was PBS listed, I suspect this thing would just go nuts, it would be almost an imprimatur to use it.”

Davis thinks while there should be some discount for women by listing it on the PBS, the treatment should remain tightly prescribed. She stresses that women must use the female-specific treatment, even though it’s more expensive, as they risk overdosing on a male-specific product. “Overseas, women are getting just crazy doses [of the male product],” she says. Buckley agrees. “Testosterone in women: more is not better,” he says. (The New York Times has reported rapturous reviews from women on high doses of the male version – “It’s changed my marriage” – but tells of another whose hair fell out in chunks through overdosing and another whose voice became “very raspy” and remained so after she stopped taking the drug.)

Too much testosterone can make women irritable and hot-headed, too. “I had a patient once,” Foran tells us, “who had been advised to take significantly higher doses than would be recommended, and she said she knew she was in trouble when she started getting really angry at the people around her … and she said, ‘Look, this isn’t me’. And when she stopped it, that went away.” Belinda says the cream is tricky to measure. One of her friends used “too much” and stopped “because it had such a strong effect on her mood.”

Even at medically prescribed levels, taking the hormone is not “no risk”, says Severin. “And the risk is that you’re going to have permanent voice changes and hair loss.” Adds Davis: “We know from clinical trials, even when you use a dose within the female range, that there’s an increased likelihood of acne and excess body hair growth and some weight gain [possibly due to fluid retention or increased appetite].”

Belinda grew hair she didn’t want. “The testosterone gel is very easily transferable, so you have to really rub it in. You need to vary the place when you do it, which I didn’t know at first. Because I kept doing it in the same spot, I grew hair there.” Buckley says users should apply the cream only to the upper outer thigh and buttock where there are fewer hair follicles.

Belinda is also frustrated at what she sees as a lack of research. “We know 50 per cent of the population will go through menopause, so that’s a guarantee, and we know that the other 50 per cent will be impacted by that woman going through menopause. Why is that not a benefit to everybody that we actually throw some medical research into it?”

Pharma executive Michael Buckley says there’s so much research on testosterone for women in relation to libido because the emergence of erectile dysfunction drug Viagra in the 1990s created huge momentum for a female equivalent. For her part, Davis urges women to speed up research by signing up for trials. She says it was a “nightmare” trying to recruit women to recent studies looking at testosterone’s effects on bone and muscle.

Researcher Benjamin Bonenti warns that people who source testosterone through illicit channels – those apps and “contacts” we mentioned earlier – will not always get what they expect. “The product may contain a different compound to what they expected, the dose may not match the label, or there may be contamination.”

He says many testosterone users, especially the younger ones who fear they have low levels, don’t feel comfortable talking to their GP or endocrinologist about it. “Now, that might sound trivial,” he says, “but it could be argued that that is one of the main reasons we’re seeing things being sourced from informal sources, people using doses beyond medical guidance, and people using products where the contents, dose or safety profile may be uncertain.”

Carolyn Allan notes that men actually have a lot more agency in maintaining testosterone levels as they get older than women. She knows men in their 80s whose testosterone levels are “very well-preserved – maybe not quite equivalent to their 20s but they still have very good tests. So it’s not an inevitable part of ageing for men that they will lose testosterone.” On the other hand, “all women will go through menopause – and have a [roughly] 95 per cent drop in their oestrogen levels that year that they go through the menopause transition”.

Managing stress, appropriate sleep, losing weight, exercising – for men, says Allan, “all of those things are going to help in terms of optimising your body’s ability to make its own testosterone.” Studies of patients on very low-calorie diets or who had bariatric surgery for obesity have found improved testosterone. There’s a flurry of research now on whether weight loss via Ozempic is having a similar effect.

While diet and lifestyle can’t help women boost their hormones, it may help their libido, says Terri Foran. “The fitter and the healthier you are, the more energy you have, the more likely that your libido will increase. But the problem with that is it takes time and commitment, and women are time-poor.”

Michael Buckley believes that testosterone will one day – after more research and regulator approval – be added to oestrogen and progesterone in menopausal hormone therapy. “Hormone replacement therapy, as we know it now, will become a triple therapy. We are playing catch-up science.” Davis is more cautious: “We don’t have evidence to support this belief presently.” Buckley also suggests testosterone could be prescribed to help offset the lean-muscle loss experienced by people using Ozempic and other similar weight-loss drugs, although Davis notes the evidence isn’t in to support such a move.

Meantime, there’s still a lot of work to do to make sure that women in midlife, whether peri- or postmenopausal, get the support they need. “We have everything going on right now,” says Davis. “We have women who are being treated who don’t need to be treated, we have women who are being treated but with inappropriate therapy, and women who are missing out on treatment and who need it. And then women who are getting appropriate therapy with good symptomatic relief.”

Her team is studying whether testosterone also boosts the sex drive of women in early and late perimenopause. “And we hope to have the support of women,” she says, “to get these studies done so they can make informed choices.”

‘It took its toll’: The price Sherry-Lee Watson paid for her shot at acting success

Sydney Morning Herald August 02, 2026

The 27-year-old, who grew up on an outstation near Alice Springs before attending boarding school in Victoria, talks about starring in an Australian classic.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Take a look at Sherry-Lee Watson’s screen work to date: all different expressions of young, powerful, energetic women on the precipice of adult life and everything that might mean. The 27-year-old actor has a short but powerful list of credits to her name. Deliberate choice? Happy accident? It probably doesn’t matter.

Her first on-screen acting job was playing high school student Missy on the Netflix reboot of Heartbreak High – a quick-paced, high-energy ensemble project Watson describes as “unapologetically Aussie”.

In the 2024 Stan eight-part miniseries Thou Shalt Not Steal, she played Robyn, a juvenile delinquent making her way across the outback in a stolen taxi in a role that garnered her an AACTA Award nomination for Best Lead Actress in a Drama.

Sherry-Lee Watson on My Brilliant Career

The Heartbreak High actor is starring in a reboot of the Australian classic

Her latest role is young drover and horse wrangler Nell on Netflix’s big-budget miniseries My Brilliant Career, the most recent interpretation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 novel. Filmed around Adelaide on the traditional land of the Kaurna people, it’s the most expensive television show ever made in South Australia, with a budget of roughly $17 million.

It’s also a real smorgasbord of luscious costuming, perfect lighting and broad South Australian vistas, set in a time of buttoned-up Victorian primness, but with just a hint of wild bohemian fancy creeping in. It’s deeply evocative and deliciously escapist.

Watson describes the story arc of her character as working in parallel to the main character of Sybylla, played by Philippa Northeast (The Family Next Door, The Newsreader, Paper Dolls). “They’re both women who are very modern and they don’t want to be defined by the boundaries of their time.”

She says the process of working on such a large-scale production taught her to stay humble, open and curious. “I feel like this industry [requires] so many different types of vulnerability,” she says, referencing how easy it can be to shut down and go into self-protection mode when it feels the world is closing in.

“You have to keep your heart really open to act, or to share things with people, or to be on a red carpet or in a photo studio capturing parts of you that perhaps you don’t necessarily love about yourself,” she adds. “But I think being around other actors like that has [made me feel] safe and passionately creative.”

A proud Arrernte woman, born and raised in Alice Springs, Watson trained in music theatre at Victorian College of the Arts. Having worked on back-to-back screen performances for the last few years, she’s excited to be returning to the stage on August 7 in Break of Day at Malthouse Theatre in Melbourne, co-starring with Kat Stewart (Underbelly, Tangle, Offspring).

“Screen is amazing, and I’m so grateful for everything I’ve gotten out of it, but I’m not satisfying that hunger to interrogate text and to go deep into characters,” she says. “I’m really grateful for all the screen work I’ve had, and the people I’ve gotten to meet, but I want to come home to the stage for a little while.”

The play focuses on an intense mother-daughter relationship and is set over the course of a single night shift at the world’s largest online retail warehouse. “It’s a really heavy one,” says Watson, “but it’s beautiful.”

Shaping that relationship with Stewart, she says, required a lot of trust. “Theatre’s so different from film. You’ve really got to go so deeply into the text, and you need to be able to go there every night. I love negotiating the boundary between what’s safe enough and what sells the story as much as possible.”

Watson describes her own upbringing – she was raised by a single mother on an outstation – as working class. But, thanks to a scholarship from the Smith Family, she left the Northern Territory to attend The Geelong College for years 10, 11 and 12. Moving from family and friends and the red sands of Alice Springs to an elite boarding school with its green, manicured grounds was a massive culture shock.

“It’s hard if you’re not brought up in the same environment,” she says. “I wasn’t prepared for how different it was. I wasn’t ready for it. It took its toll, but ultimately it had an amazing outcome.”

She says it’s where the idea of pursuing a career in acting first seemed feasible. “I’ve always wanted to be a performer, but it never became something attainable until I’d gotten into a space like that, where I actually could see it becoming a realistic thing. My confidence, even my ability to articulate myself, grew so much just by going there.”

The other reason acting seemed unattainable as a career was the lack of theatre in Alice Springs. “There’s one play a year, and it’s for one night,” she says. “You know, you can’t do something that you don’t see as possible. I can’t describe to you a colour I’ve never seen before.”

For Watson, who often gets homesick, there’s a split between who she is in Melbourne and who she is when she goes home to the Northern Territory. “It’s two different worlds, a big culture change,” she says. “Different ways of speaking, different ways of being and doing, different values. Different cultures value different things, and adjusting from one to the other takes a toll on your body sometimes.”

Working on Thou Shalt Not Steal, which was filmed in the NT, gave Watson the rare opportunity of experiencing a meeting of her two worlds, even if it did bring some mixed feelings.

“It’s always going to feel a little bit more secure and a little bit more relaxed – I know this place, this place knows me,” she says. She adds, though, that she felt a little too relaxed at times. “I’m used to the certain tension at work, I guess. A certain way that I hold myself. It was a bit confusing to be honest.”

Looking into the future, Watson would like to return home to teach. “I just want to be happy telling my stories, doing my plays, and showing a lot of younger mob that we’re allowed to be happy, and that we’re allowed to like to reach for things we might not think we deserve, but we do. And it’s OK.”

It’s a positive message she wants to convey to that younger mob: “You know, it might not feel like it, but we are loved. The more you get out there, the more you meet people and the more you realise, maybe we’re gonna be OK.”

Of all the women in her life, Watson draws the most inspiration from her mother. “Her strength and her resolve is just incredible. She shows me that you can just handle so many things with so much class and grace.

“There are a lot of women in the industry who really hold me down, and Shari Sebbens is one of them,” says Watson, referring to the actor whose credits include The Sapphires, Redfern Now, The Office and Top End Bub.

“I had the privilege of working with her on My Brilliant Career – she was an associate producer on it – and learnt so much from her as someone who comes from the Territory and has gone into performing arts. Knowing that cultural shock, knowing what it’s like to exist in two worlds – she’s been a really amazing mentor to me.”

Getting back to Country as often as possible is vital for Watson. “Sometimes I’m just like, ‘What am I giving up for this? What’s the exchange that’s happening here?’ I’m remembering to be grateful for things. It makes you grow up very quickly.”

After Break of Day finishes its run, Watson will enjoy a long spell at home with her mother. “It’s been over 10 years of being away,” she reflects. “I haven’t sat down there for a long time. I need to go back and ground myself and be with my family on Country, and see what comes out of that.”

My Brilliant Career is on Netflix from August 13.
