Gianni Infantino ‘has lost Uefa’s confidence’ after Fifa chief scraps World Cup sell-off plan

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 10:08:33 GMT

Infantino ditched proposals after widespread backlash

Uefa adds: ‘We cannot keep going on with secret schemes’

Uefa has warned Gianni Infantino that his style of leadership cannot continue in demanding a thorough and fundamental review of Fifa’s governance.

In a strongly worded statement that referred to “secret schemes”, “shabby backroom deals” and “faceless individuals”, the Uefa leadership made clear it wants change at the top of Fifa, despite the world governing body’s overnight U-turn in abandoning Infantino’s plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions.

While stopping short of calling for Infantino to resign, Uefa’s leadership is understood to be determined that he should not be permitted to survive a crisis of his own making, a view that is shared by many of the biggest football governing bodies across the world. Leading European officials are already understood to have begun the process of identifying a candidate to stand against Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election, which will continue over the next few days.

Uefa’s statement made clear that under the leadership of president Aleksander Ceferin, who succeeded in getting all 55 member associations to support a World Cup boycott last Thursday, it will continue to push for change. “We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game,” the statement read. “We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

“It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, Uefa will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again. That review should be thorough and fundamental. No option should be off the table. The current Fifa leadership has not only lost Uefa’s confidence, but also that of many other members of the football family.”

Uefa went on to criticise Infantino directly, saying he has failed to deliver on pledges he made to be transparent and accountable before he was first elected president in 2016.

The Football Association backed Uefa and, in a statement, said: “We fully support Uefa’s position. It is time for a full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently, for the benefit of all 211 member nations and with the long-term stewardship of football at its heart!”

Speaking in Manchester on Saturday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was the “right decision” for Fifa to back down. It comes after he previously called the plans “outrageous” and said bringing them forward made it clear that Infantino was “the wrong man to lead the organisation”.

Elsewhere in Europe, the Dutch FA said the withdrawal of Infantino’s proposal was not the end of the issue, adding: “The matter is ⁠not settled for the KNVB. The way this process has unfolded has led to a fundamental breach of trust in the leadership of Fifa president Gianni Infantino. The KNVB no longer has ⁠confidence in his leadership.”

Bernd Neuendorf, president of Germany’s DFB said: “The events surrounding this project initiated by Gianni Infantino must now be fully investigated. The Fifa president acted unilaterally, opaquely and ultimately irresponsibly in the best interests ⁠of football.”

Infantino had been expected to be re-elected unopposed for a third full term at next March’s Fifa Congress in Rabat, but while he is determined to stay on the 56-year-old could now face a challenger. While he has already secured more than 200 letters of support from member associations endorsing his re-election campaign they can be withdrawn, and the deadline for other candidates to announce an intention to stand is not until 18 November.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

The Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi is favoured by many in Europe, but appears reluctant to stand and is also chair of powerful lobby group, European Football Clubs. Other potential candidates include Victor Montagliani, the Canadian who is the president of North American confederation Concacaf, and the Asian Football Confederation president Salman al-Khalifa, who lost narrowly to Infantino in the 2016 Fifa election.

Uefa’s statement used Infantino’s own words from his initial election campaign 10 years ago against him. “When Gianni Infantino asked for the trust and the votes of Fifa’s Member Associations to elect him as their president in 2016, he said, ‘Of course we have to be transparent. I have been this in the last 15 years of my life in Uefa. You will have to play a part every day in the life of Fifa,’ before telling the assembled stakeholders, ‘The money of Fifa is your money. It’s not the money of the Fifa president. It’s your money. You are the national associations, and the money of Fifa has to serve for the development of football and not for anything else.’ On both these promises, he has failed to deliver. The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent. And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations’ money for the benefit of the game.”

Uefa also called for an immediate overhaul of Fifa’s system of financial distribution, the Fifa Forward programme in which all 211 member associations receive the same central payment from Fifa over each four-year cycle. Infantino had claimed that selling 20% of a new commercial company – Fifa Forward Enterprise – to private investors would enable them to increase the Fifa Forward payments from $8m over the next four-year cycle to $20m, as well as a one-off $20m bonus for signing up to the scheme.

Handing out millions of dollars to tiny nations has been widely criticised as a system of patronage designed to keep Infantino in office, while the $20m bonus on offer for associations who signed up by a deadline of 19 September was condemned.

“Uefa will begin work immediately with partners and stakeholders all over the world and right across the game to propose a new way of distributing resources through the existing Fifa Forward programme,” its statement continued. “We must start to use some of that money that is sat idle in Fifa’s bank account to deliver the kick start that the grassroots and the wider game need in each of the 211 countries of Fifa. But we don’t need to sell off the family silver to pay for it.

“This is a victory for the whole game. But it must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in Fifa has only just begun.”

Concacaf later echoed Uefa’s call for a review of Fifa’s leadership in a similarly powerful statement.

“A proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident,” Concacaf said. “It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place. “This concern is not Concacaf’s alone. It is shared across many confederations, Member Associations and those who serve and love the game. When people entrusted with protecting the game conclude they can no longer do so from within, the football family is entitled to ask how such a proposal was allowed to proceed, and who bears responsibility for it.

“Fifa is not a private enterprise. It is a body held in trust for the game and its members. Those appointed to serve it carry a fiduciary duty, a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional. “The unity demonstrated by our Member Associations this week has reaffirmed that when guided by courage, integrity, and sound governance the game will remain where it belongs: in the hands of football - not a single individual.”

There was one positive for Infantino, though, as the Qatar FA issued a statement supporting his leadership. Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: “We welcome Fifa President Gianni Infantino’s decision to withdraw the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community. While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations.

“The Qatar Football Association fully supports President Infantino’s efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally.”

Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a bout

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 10:07:05 GMT

Tarona Taafaki makes history in women’s 75kg category

All boxers eliminated in semis receive bronze medals

A boxer has made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the tiny Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight.

Twenty-year-old Tarona Taafaki, ⁠one of five entrants in the women’s 75kg category, received a bye to the semi-finals where she lost on an unanimous points decision to India’s Lovlina Borgohain on Friday. At Commonwealth Games, all boxers eliminated in the semis receive bronze medals.

“I’m very proud and very glad to be able to represent my country on this big stage,” said Taafaki, one of only eight athletes and paraathletes from her country in Glasgow. “Probably 95% of the audience don’t know where my country is, so I feel very privileged to represent Tuvalu.”

Badi Taafaki, her coach and father, said the medal would be celebrated by the 10,000 population of the 10 sq mile nation – the world’s fourth smallest – and serve to highlight a climate emergency.

“For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything,” he said. “We’re one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it’s a stepping stone.”

Athletes often train on the island’s airport runway as it is its most stable land mass. However, with sea levels rising, climate experts predict half of the nation’s capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050. “Yes, we train on the runway,” said Taafaki. “When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.”

However, Tarona and her brother Pasoni, who also boxed in the Commonwealth Games, are based in New Zealand where the facilities are better. “When I was growing up, boxing barely existed in Tuvalu,” said Badi. “We didn’t have gloves, so we were forced to fight bare-knuckle, and hit bags filled with sand. My children are very fortunate. They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline. It’s where our genealogy comes from.

“If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change. It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades.

after newsletter promotion

“Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can’t sleep if there’s a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes.”

Taafaki is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia’s Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women’s flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her first bout to England’s Lisa Whiteside.

The US war on Iran is spinning out of control

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 09:00:49 GMT

Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow

The US war against Iran is spiraling out of control. Over the past week, the conflict has expanded across the Middle East, with attacks and counterattacks in at least five other countries. Instead of a quick war that sought to topple Iran’s regime, Donald Trump has started a regional conflict that risks severely disrupting energy supplies and prices – and triggering a global recession.

After a few days of relative calm, the conflict resumed with the Pentagon carrying out almost nightly strikes against Iran, and Tehran retaliating against US military bases in the region. The conflict also extended to attacks in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan and Egypt. And there’s little sign that peace negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being brokered by Pakistan and Qatar, are making much progress.

The most serious escalation took place on Wednesday, when Saudi Arabia announced it had joined the US in carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq, against the Iranian-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters. Saudi officials had blamed the Iraqi-based militias for launching drone attacks against Saudi oil facilities on 27 July, and warned that the kingdom would retaliate if the Iraqi government did not restrain the groups. The PMF is a network of mostly Shia Muslim militias that was created, with Tehran’s support, in 2014 to fight the Islamic State terror group that had taken control of large parts of Iraq.

Trump said the US and Saudi militaries coordinated with the Iraqi government before carrying out airstrikes, but Iraqi leaders quickly denied having any prior knowledge. That denial highlighted the fact that many regional leaders don’t want to be associated with Trump’s expanding regional war. And the attacks threatened to undermine a fragile power balance within Iraq, which has struggled to stop the US-Iran war from spilling over its borders and to maintain a good relationship with both sides.

After the US invaded Iraq in 2003, it ousted Tehran’s enemy, Saddam Hussein, and his Sunni-dominated regime from power. Washington then helped install a Shia-led government for the first time in Iraq’s modern history, opening the door for Iran to extend its influence over its neighbor and cultivate powerful Shia militias. Iran’s efforts were largely overseen by Qassem Suleimani, a general who headed the foreign operations wing of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimani was assassinated by a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020, on Trump’s orders – an attack that helped set the stage for the current war and fueled further animosity between the US and Iraq’s PMF coalition, whose deputy chief, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was killed alongside Suleimani.

Beyond drawing Iraq’s Shia militias further into the regional conflict, the US and Saudi Arabia risk expanding the war in even more dangerous directions. The kingdom is reportedly planning for a major military offensive against the Houthi militia, another Iranian ally, which controls large areas of Yemen.

After Trump launched his war in late February, Iran effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies passed each day. As a result, some oil producers, especially Saudi Arabia, shifted their exports to the Red Sea. But the Houthis are able to disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea, as they did after Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023, when the Yemeni militia began firing missiles and drones at ships near the Bab el-Mandab strait. That caused insurance premiums to soar and forced companies to reroute vessels around Africa, adding weeks to a typical journey and increasing the cost of goods in Europe and elsewhere.

So far, the Houthis have not tried to disrupt ships passing through the Red Sea on a large scale, via the Bab el-Mandab chokepoint, which comes closest to Yemeni territory. But on 20 July, the militia declared a blockade on Saudi vessels transiting the Red Sea, claiming it was in retaliation for an air and naval blockade that the kingdom had imposed years ago against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The Houthis have since attacked several ships in the Red Sea, forcing Saudi Arabia to reroute nearly half of its oil exports through a longer and more expensive journey around the southern tip of Africa. On 25 July, the Houthis claimed to have struck “sensitive” oil infrastructure sites inside Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones, disrupting the kingdom’s Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. The Saudis have retaliated with air strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.

Like Iran’s other neighbors in the Persian Gulf, the Saudi economy has been hit hard by the war, especially Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz and its attacks against energy infrastructure in the Gulf. Saudi Arabia’s GDP decreased by nearly 5% in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year.

Saudi leaders are blaming Iran for the latest Houthi escalation, and they’ve vowed to establish an international maritime coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea. On Thursday, the Saudi defense ministry announced that 14 states – including Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Sudan – had agreed so far to join the coalition. But it’s unclear how this new Saudi-led effort would differ from an existing naval protection mission, organized by the European Union and known as Operation Aspides, which is focused on the Red Sea.

While Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, has tried to steer clear of a direct confrontation with Iran, his latest conflict with the Houthis risks reopening a painful chapter in recent Saudi history. In 2015, Saudi Arabia, with US weapons and political support, led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in Yemen’s long-running civil war. The Saudis tried to dislodge the Houthis from Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, and restore the country’s internationally recognized government to power. By the end of 2021, the United Nations estimated that the conflict had killed 377,000 people in Yemen, nearly 60% of whom did not die from direct warfare. Rather, they died from food shortages, cholera outbreaks and destruction of Yemen’s healthcare system.

Despite thousands of airstrikes over seven years, the Houthis remained in control of the capital and the two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022. But negotiations over a permanent peace deal, which would recognize Houthi control over parts of Yemen and provide some form of Saudi reparations, stalled after the militia started attacking ships in the Red Sea in 2023.

Today, Saudi Arabia’s tenuous ceasefire with the Houthis is in danger of collapsing – yet another casualty of Trump’s disastrous war against Iran.

Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York University

Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless underwear isn’t as outrageous as it seems

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 08:00:47 GMT

Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say

The news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to “S & M”.

But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used by women who wear stomas. The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.

Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.”

Shuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023.

Shuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?”

This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.”

There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’”

M&S has sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947. It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, which reached the apex of popularity in the mid-00s.

In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021, thongs were back, thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs.

Lorraine Topper, a researcher at The Underpinnings Museum, argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics.

“M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.”

She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.”

​What makes a good comic novel? Andrew Sean Greer on the joy of funny writing

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 08:00:46 GMT

The Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laugh

In March 2020, when the mayor of San Francisco instructed all citizens to remain in their houses due to a pandemic, the first thing I did was order all the books of Agatha Christie. I was not alone; I think many of us immersed ourselves in reliable narratives to drown out the chaos. It did not matter if it ended in marriage or murder; the reliability was what mattered. Later when I realised I would need to hole up for some time, my reading shifted to a different kind of novel. And because, like Christie, our world has an endless supply of new terrors, it is the comic novel that still fills my reading hours.

Nobody knows what a comic novel is. And once you start discussing it, all the fun runs out. EB White compared it to dissecting a frog (you’re left with innards and a dead frog) but I would compare it to turning all the lights on at a party: everyone looks terrible and you’ve ruined the party. Most would agree, of course, that Wodehouse wrote comic novels, but I turn to books hardly anybody would classify that way – Moby-Dick by Herman Melville, for instance – that yet seem to me to be a hoot. I think they are books that decide something is funny, as Jerry Seinfeld once defined comedy. In Moby-Dick, it’s a coin nailed to a masthead. In Vladimir Nabokov’s Pale Fire, it’s the worst best poem you’ve ever read. And yet we feel we’re getting at something the most solemn narratives aim for: an understanding of the human condition, of grief, of love, of death. All the big stuff. The comic novels I love are books that could just as easily have been tragedies. It is simply that the author has decided it’s funny.

It’s something I learned from a wise friend of mine who once, after I angrily related a publishing story of mine, responded: “That’s not a very funny story.” I was shocked. And then I understood that I had not processed the story at all, and was serving this dish to her raw. I had to learn to turn an old outrage into a funny story. And then she would be willing to listen. I did learn to do this. And I have put the very scene I have described to you into my latest novel. A comic novel, if you like.

I have written both comic novels and novels where you would not crack a smile – serious novels, I suppose. And I can relate that, for me, writing the comic ones is a much more pleasant, though very different, kind of work. But the plots are no funnier than the serious ones. See if you can guess which one is comic and which is serious:

A young woman in 1952 San Francisco joins with her husband’s gay lover to remove obstacles to her liberation and gain a small fortune.

A middle-aged writer travels across a troubled United States while struggling to maintain his recently renewed relationship with a younger man.

Even if you guessed, you see my point: I have to decide it’s funny. And that takes double-processing. Like blond hair at the salon. First, I work out the hardships and frustrations of the characters as realistically, even tragically, as possible. People die in comic novels. Sometimes the world ends, or sometimes just the world we thought we knew, and I have to consider the real reactions of my characters because, after all, they don’t know it’s a comedy. Second, I begin to write it as if it’s all just a funny story. That takes a great deal of struggle and sometimes feels impossible.

In my last novel, Less Is Lost (that’s the one about the middle-aged writer), I found myself sitting with my notes on visiting three forced labour plantations in the American south. There was nothing humorous about them, yet I didn’t want to cut them; I knew my protagonist had to confront that part of American history. But then I read over the notes of my final visit and realised that I was the comedy: myself and the other white visitors, showcasing our guilt and anxiety through statements that were utterly absurd. In fact, I ended up portraying the visit almost exactly as I had it in my notes … but with a different emphasis. Is it “funny”? No. Is it “comic”? Definitely. Why? I don’t know. I don’t know. I can’t explain it any better for fear of turning on the party lights.

In writing my latest novel, Villa Coco, I had a much easier time, since I was working off notes in my diaries from my time living in Tuscany, and those notes were already blond hair in a salon; I made a promise to myself that I would turn each day’s events into a “funny story”. And yet, in a way, I found myself sifting through these stories for the other thing: the real feeling. Because there was the death, in those days, of a dear friend. A turn of seasons. A broken heart. All the things I would have previously put down in my diary now had been expunged, and though I had processed them into lovely stories, the job (as a novelist now and not a diarist) was to get to the hardships and frustrations of my characters. Because, to me, comedy is only great fun if it is about something hard and true.

“I don’t think of you as writing a comic novel,” a writer friend told me. “I think of you as working through something in whatever way you have to.” He meant that my books are not “about” women in 1952 or middle-aged writers or olive harvests in Tuscany. They are about marriage and growing old and the terror of death. It is just that, in a comic novel, those issues are temporarily resolved, often in a flagrantly artificial fashion. As if to say: life is a vale of tears, and there’s no fixing it, but just for fun let’s fix this one small piece. Let’s decide, briefly, to lift the weight of being. You can’t successfully do that, I think, without being honest about it first.

And yet – what a lovely time I have working on these books. Because everything has to be processed in this way, each awful moment of the day becomes more material for comedy. Thus I become, somehow, more resilient; a trip on the sidewalk is no less embarrassing than before but, instead of trying to play it off, I laugh with anyone who notices (and people do notice). What would normally be a dull wait at a bus stop (or a mind‑numbing trip through the internet) becomes a delightful experience with my notebook. “Cheese rolling contest May 20,” I might copy down from a poster, “Prize is the wheel of cheese.” Or “lady in black sequined dress yelling at a mailbox at nine in the morning. I think she mailed her purse by mistake.” I am not a person who particularly lives in the present tense, but comedy forces me there. A good place to be.

Language also achieves a new richness. People assume writers think about plot or characters, in the way they assume painters or photographers think about their subjects. But painters think about paint. Photographers think about light. And writers think about words. There is something so utterly delicious about being able to make use of words that are otherwise forbidden to touch. I don’t mean curse words; I mean fancy ones. Take for instance something like “noise”. In a serious novel, you would have to say “down the street came a noise”. Anything more elaborate would be a red flag of pretentiousness. So you settle for the austerity of “noise” and move on. But when writing comedy, suddenly a whole feast of words is spread before you: hullabaloo and brouhaha and hubbub and chivaree. Chivaree! Banging pots and pans together to publicly shame a citizen or tease a newly married couple! What a word! My language has not become simpler by writing comedy; it has become zestier. And if, like me, words are your favourite medium, it is akin to tomatoes finally coming into season after months of cabbage and kale.

No wonder what some consider the very first “novel” was one of the most rip-roaring, slapstick comedies around: Don Quixote. Chaucer himself was not above a fart joke, and Shakespeare could never resist a pun. There is a grand tradition, in fact, of great writers dabbling in comedy – Philip Roth, Saul Bellow, Thornton Wilder – and I think there is something about having seen the darkness that pulls so many to laughter. Certainly, in these difficult times, with endless apocalyptic films and novels appearing, many of us find ourselves picking up Stella Gibbons’ Cold Comfort Farm instead.

There is something dear and beautiful about the comic novel, something to love. A friend to hold your hand when the lights flicker out and tell you a story until they come back on again. And, for those of us who write them, a way to feel our way forward down the tunnel into the light. I know that it was a solace to imagine a much younger American man, finding himself delivered to a rural Tuscan train station that he says is “so fanciful one might unwrap it and find it was chocolate”. And to be seated next to a princess who cannot understand him because she has not mastered “the American dialect”. And throw a wild animal into his window at night. And make the septic tank overflow. All to get at a simple truth: the world is trouble, and full of sorrows, and we will not get out alive.

But look closely: it is, in fact, made of chocolate.

Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer is published by Sceptre. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Cold Comfort Farm by Stella Gibbons This is a satire of a genre that no longer even exists (the rural English romance) because it erased it with its perfect sense of humour.

Pomp and Circumstance by Noël Coward The queen is coming to visit a far-flung island nation and everyone is aquiver.

Pnin by Vladimir Nabokov The poignancy of Nabokov’s tortured Russian academic makes one fall in love with poor Pnin.

Bech: A Book by John Updike The first of a series of books about a Philip Roth-like novelist adrift in the world. Like Nabokov, a wordsmith having great fun with the English language.

The Sellout by Paul Beatty A brilliant example of taking the most serious of subjects – slavery in America – and turning it completely on its head.

I Capture the Castle by Dodie Smith I reread this book annually and both laugh and shed tears over the fate of our teenage narrator, Cassandra, whose diary this is.

Our Man in Havana by Graham Greene Personally, I prefer Greene’s “entertainments” to his serious fiction, from Travels With My Aunt to this wonderful case of mistaken identity.

Little Me: The Intimate Memoirs of That Great Star of Stage, Screen and Television, Belle Poitrine by Patrick Dennis From the writer of Auntie Mame, a deliciously deluded memoir of an absolute nobody, complete with photographs!

The Pursuit of Love/Love in a Cold Climate by Nancy Mitford Eccentricity and delight mix with heartache in this classic fictionalised version of her famous family.

Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes Hilarious from beginning to end, and the sequel is even better, because suddenly Don Quixote and Sancho Panza are famous because everyone has read the first.

‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 07:00:47 GMT

Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds

Parliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, a report has revealed.

Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed.

Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events.

Those are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcher allegedly having had her drink spiked in Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one time drinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week – the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar.

The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces.

“Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.”

Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.”

The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue.

Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.”

A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.”

A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”.

Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture “unprofessional and worrying” and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”.

The IAS report also found that:

42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily.

22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking.

Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking.

The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.”

Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one?

“If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.”

Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol.

She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking.

“That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.”

Katherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added.

The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking.

In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme said alcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigations into alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”.

In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review.

A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said.

“Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.”

Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated.

The hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 07:00:46 GMT

Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine

The other day, I met a friend at the park for a catch-up. After 45 minutes of blissful note-swapping – my new tabi shoes, his new boyfriend – he pulled out a pair of ping-pong paddles and indicated a nearby table. “Fancy a quick game?” We are no longer speaking.

I’m joking, but only sort of. As far as I’m concerned, games of any sort ought to be illegal once everyone present is over the age of 12. I will make grudging exceptions for professional athletes, because apparently they’re earning a living, and realistically there is very little chance of me being asked to join in with, say, the Wimbledon final. But when it comes to anything less formal, the risk of being corralled is just too high: bat those balls, pucks, packs of cards, spinning bottles and Scrabble boards away from me, please.

Truly, there is no social situation made better by adding a game. In a setting with people I know and love, it feels like a cruel and unusual punishment to have organic conversation curtailed by something ghastly like Articulate! And although structured activities are often wheeled out for groups of strangers, that’s even worse – because now not only am I playing a game, but doing so with a bunch of people I don’t know, and I want to die.

Let’s go round the office and introduce ourselves with two truths and a lie! Let’s get each of the hens to write down their favourite thing about Milly and she can guess who wrote what! Let’s stick pins in our eyes!

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In axing games, I’m not advocating for anything to replace them. On the contrary, all I want is space to be together, ideally while clutching either a coffee or a glass of wine, depending on the time of day. Don’t start thinking that activities that bridge that divide – pub quizzes, for instance – are an exception to my furious veto, either; they’re actually the most dire of all, the Uncanny Valley of organised fun. All the cues – friends, booze – are there for a lovely time, then suddenly, shhhhhh!, it’s the music round and Ollie takes this one very seriously.

Speaking of which, I’m fully aware that there exists a whole cohort who feel just as strongly as I, only in the opposite direction. I have encountered them in the wild – frothing at the mouth as they chastise you for putting your card on the left instead of the right or whatever – and frankly, they frighten me. Maybe I envy their strength of feeling. I’m not sure I’ve ever felt that righteous about anything, but it looks energising.

Am I pathologically uncompetitive? Has my lack of interest in games birthed a unique ineptitude at almost every single one? Yes and yes! Nonetheless, my years on the sidelines have made one thing abundantly clear: the real fun begins as soon as the games stop. As I said to my friend at the park: put the paddles down and get me a glass of pinot, please.

Emily Watkins is a freelance writer based in London

The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UK

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 06:00:44 GMT

Nigel Farage’s £5m gift, the Cottrell family’s links and donations, and Richard Tice’s business dealings form part of an increasingly clear nexus of relationships

It has been three months since the Guardian revealed that Nigel Farage had accepted a £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a billionaire donor to Reform UK.

This was not the first story in our continuing investigation. But it has proved the most significant, and the consequences of the disclosure are still being played out.

Little by little, a picture is emerging – one that shows how Reform UK has been funded and by whom. Each new detail raises more questions for Farage and the coterie around him.

Aside from the “gift”, the Guardian has revealed details of secret donations, a behind-the-scenes loan from a donor and how the Metropolitan police have interviewed two people under caution.

Sources have described how staff at several different banks were so concerned about a range of transactions, some of which are referenced above and involved senior figures at the party, that they reported them to the National Crime Agency.

Sources have now told us that George Cottrell, a convicted fraudster based in Montenegro, transferred a total of more than $2m to his mother, Fiona, in 2024, with each sum arriving shortly before she made substantial donations to the party.

The stories have given voters a much clearer idea of the people and the financial transactions that underpin Reform.

It is a financially and politically incestuous set of relationships.

Farage is friends with George Cottrell, who is said to be an unpaid adviser to Reform. Cottrell is friends with Harborne, the billionaire who has given millions to the party, and to Farage himself.

Farage’s deputy, Richard Tice, has known the Cottrell family, he says, for 50 years. Fiona is also a significant donor to the party. George has also lent money to Tice.

These five people are at the heart of a party that believes it can form the next government.

Without them and their money, Reform would not exist in its current form.

Scrutiny has provoked Farage into an array of explanations for why he accepted the £5m gift, and broad declarations there is an establishment plot to undermine him.

Rather than answering questions posed by the Guardian, he and other senior Reform figures have sent threatening legal letters, or attempted to “spoil” the Guardian’s stories with pre-emptive interviews with the Daily Telegraph, which reported what they said uncritically.

Farage has also made unsubstantiated claims about the Guardian’s reporting – citing, without any evidence, illegal hacks involving Russia, or talking about state-orchestrated leaks.

Throwing sand in the air is one way of distracting attention, but when it settles, certain facts remain unchanged, and certain questions remain unanswered.

Several relate to George Cottrell, who is known as “Posh George”, and has been at Farage’s side for at least a decade.

Many of those questions pertain to his wealth and business activity.

In January, the Guardian reported on his alleged role as a frontman for the betting syndicate of the megastar gambler and football proprietor Tony Bloom.

Court documents claimed that Cottrell, as well as raking in millions by allowing Bloom’s syndicate to place bets using accounts in his name, also had a financial interest in the offshore gambling outfit Tether. bet.

The claims went further still: that he had approached gamblers in the UK to use Tether. bet, despite that outfit not holding a UK gambling licence.

Lawyers for Cottrell repeatedly said he was not a director or shareholder of Tether. bet and had not commented on the court proceedings, as he was not party to them. The case relates to a former employee of Bloom’s gambling syndicate who claims he introduced Cottrell to Bloom.

Cottrell, who was unable to pay for legal representation when he was initially arrested in the US in 2016, and then had to rely on family assistance, has seen a rapid reversal in his fortunes since his release from US prison in 2017.

In recent years he has pursued a costly, jet-set lifestyle, often using Montenegro as a base.

Then there are the questions around Farage, who said he was “skint” in 2017.

Not any more. He now owns a number of houses, and has shown flashes of anger when asked about this, and what he has done with the £5m given to him by Harborne.

“Literally none of your business,” he said to the BBC.

The £5m came via a deed of gift in April 2024, just as Farage, who was the main shareholder of Reform UK, weighed his political future.

In fact, the Guardian would later report our sources’ claims that some of the £5m was not transferred to Farage until just before he declared he would stand in the 2024 general election.

Lawyers for Harborne have said their client’s gift was unconditional and that, when it was made, Harborne did not foresee Farage returning to politics.

The Guardian has since been able to shed more light on the tangled web of overlapping personal financial activity and donations to the party.

Cottrell, whom the Guardian revealed is sometimes called Farage’s chief of staff (Reform has said he has never held an official position in the party), was also providing financial support to Tice behind the scenes.

He lent Tice’s company £78,100 in late 2024 when he was already a sitting MP. Tice says this money was then repaid, but only after he made a donation of £613,000 via the same company – Tisun Investments – to Reform. Tice has called it a “bridging loan”, a type of short-term loan.

But the benefits and support Cottrell gave to Farage, and the £78,100 loan to Tice, were a drop in the ocean compared with the apparent largesse Cottrell may have extended to the party.

As the Guardian revealed, his mother, a woman with aristocratic roots but who is understood to be of relatively modest means, had secretly given Britain Means Business – a fundraising vehicle for Reform solely controlled by Tice – £1m on 10 June 2024, just weeks before the July general election.

Half the sum, £500,000, was almost immediately transferred into the party, despite queries from bankers to Tice about the origin of the funds. This was in addition to two more donations of £250,000 made in her own name in May of the same year.

The Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.

If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.

To send a message to Anna Isaac please choose the ‘Business (UK and Global)’ team.

If you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email: anna. isaac@theguardian. com

You can message Anna using the Signal Messenger app: 07341998403

If you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via our SecureDrop platform.

Finally, our guide at theguardian. com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.

On Wednesday, the Guardian revealed that sums totalling more than $2m were transferred to Fiona by her son, according to financial industry sources.

The pair have now been interviewed under caution as part of a police investigation into the 2024 donations from Fiona to the party and Britain Means Business.

Fiona has not responded to multiple efforts by this newspaper to contact her. George has not denied giving his mother large sums of money. Instead, his lawyers said any political donations his mother had made had been entirely her decision and were a matter for her.

Two parliamentary standards investigations are due to be concluded in the autumn, one into the £5m gift Farage received from Harborne; another into his benefits from Cottrell.

There is an ongoing Metropolitan police investigation.

Reform is learning that with great success comes ever greater scrutiny.

CatsRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, to 19 September With Jesus Christ Superstar and Starlight Express staged in London, Andrew Lloyd Webber is having another moment. The idealism of the Esperanto movement, a plague of flies and a clinic in a deep salt mine

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 05:00:45 GMT

Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days

double quotation markWho would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.

Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. Jenny Kleeman wrote a remarkable story about how a chatbot brought them together.

Read more

For a satirist or a cynic, Esperantists are easy fodder. Many of its enthusiasts are undeniably eccentric. But Esperanto was once a force in global politics. Before facing heavy persecution during the second world war, it gained serious traction in international labour, anticolonial and anarchist movements. Katie Thornton wrote an illuminating long read about the idealistic movement and the vibrancy of its annual congress. She explored why today’s adherents – many of whom are no strangers to global conflict – still believe that the widespread adoption of a century-and-a-half-old invented language may yet overpower the world’s divisions.

Read more

If just one fly buzzing around your head is annoying, imagine what it’s like to be surrounded by clouds of them, week after week. Lucy Knight visited one of Britain’s most insect-plagued neighbourhoods for this fascinating story, which also poses the question: although flies are regarded as disgusting, could they be due a rebrand?

Read more

double quotation markFor most people, spending hours deep underground in darkness would seem an odd prescription for better health. Yet every morning, a handful of Armenians descend 250 metres beneath the earth into an active salt mine where they spend six hours in cavernous chambers carved from rock salt, hoping the air below ground will help them breathe more easily.

Pjotr Sauer visited one of the world’s only hospitals in a deep salt mine. The underground clinic’s fate now hangs in the balance after Armenia withdrew state funding, raising broader questions about its role in supporting alternative medicine.

Read more

On that fateful day in 1945, Kondo was just a baby in her mother’s arms. She talked to Simon Hattenstone about her father’s newly discovered eye-witness account of the aftermath, and why she decided to continue his work as a peace campaigner determined that Hiroshima and Nagasaki will never be repeated. “I don’t want to see any child go through that. That’s why I do not want to see any war in this world. This beautiful world.”

Read more

Shark thrillers are often positioned as something akin to an all-natural slasher: horror movies that expand just slightly beyond the bounds of the world we know and into heightened but not completely outlandish territory. They’re the water equivalent of the masked killer stalking around the woods.

Jesse Hassenger wrote about Shark Week, which arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre – even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all.

Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 05:00:44 GMT

With a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our country

Like Andy Burnham, I was once an enthusiastic altar boy, although I don’t recall competing to be at the front with the communion plate as the prime minister apparently did. Much of my motivation had little to do with piety. The tips received for serving at weddings were often very generous and I got on well with Father Jerome, an engagingly worldly monk from Ampleforth who shared my passion for Manchester United.

I’m five years older than Burnham, but the atmosphere of the small-town northern Catholicism we grew up with will have been much the same. The second Vatican council’s reforms, responding to the social changes under way since the 1960s, were “democratising” the tone and style of worship, and traditionalists were mourning the sidelining of the old Latin mass. The huge success of Pope John Paul II’s groundbreaking visit to Britain in 1982 – the first by a reigning pontiff – had made the faith seem more mainstream and less rarefied. Politically, most Catholics voted Labour, and the large number of Celtic surnames in parish registers testified to a demographic significantly different from Anglican congregations, which were both more English and more Tory.

Burnham is the first British prime minister to have been raised in this kind of environment, and he has been explicit about its influence upon him. To which the response of many secular well-wishers may well be polite indifference. Catholicism gets a better press among progressives these days, as Rome takes a stand against the cruelties and excesses of Maga-style xenophobia and nationalism. But most liberals would be wary of any Catholic proselytising in areas beyond migration and human rights.

They should look deeper. Like Burnham, I lapsed – in my case when I went to university and started looking for different kinds of truths in western Marxism and leftwing social theory. But unlike Burnham, I went back to the church in my 30s. So I have watched with some fascination as the significance of the new prime minister’s cradle Catholicism has been pondered beyond the confines of the religious press.

Two weeks into Burnham’s premiership, it is already clear that something important is at stake here that meshes with Burnham’s conventionally political critique of “40 years of neoliberalism”. He himself talks of “a direct read-across between what I was learning at … church and Labour values”, which might sound a bit broad brush and a bit obvious, in a “be kind” type of way. In fact it is anything but, and it matters that the church was a Catholic one.

During the 1980s – the decade Burnham has pledged to “roll back” – Margaret Thatcher did not attempt to disguise the theological roots of a political vision that emphasised self-reliance and the Protestant work ethic as primary virtues. The Methodist worldview she inherited from her lay-preacher father translated into a strident individualism, and a contempt for the collectivist institutions and ethos of the postwar welfare society. As Thatcher asserted in the first phase of her premiership: “Economics are the method; the object is to change the soul.”

As she evangelised, the surplice-clad Burnham was immersed in the Catholic resistance to this harsh new social doctrine, digesting and disseminating the sermons of the archbishop of Liverpool, Derek Worlock. Based on the social teaching of papal encyclicals, Worlock’s politics (and those of his Anglican counterpart, David Sheppard) emphasised fraternity, solidarity and mutual obligation. “I am my brother’s keeper,” he observed in 1990. “And he’s sleeping pretty rough these days.”

Cut to Burnham’s first big policy announcement , when he vowed to use his premiership to end rough sleeping across the country. Commentary, understandably enough, has focused on the practical difficulties he encountered in delivering a similar pledge in Greater Manchester as mayor. But just as important is the message it sent about priorities: in the early morning of his first day in the country’s highest office of state, Burnham made a point of going to talk to homeless people on the streets of central London.

The Catholic church would call this the “preferential option for the poor”, a way of systematising the gospel idea that the last should be first. In the ethical architecture of Catholic social teaching, it is accompanied by other pillars designed to protect people from both an overmighty technocratic state and the moral indifference of the market. Subsidiarity, the idea that power should not be hoarded at the top but devolved downwards, is clearly at the heart of nascent Burnhamism. The dignity of work, elaborated upon in papal encyclicals such as John Paul II’s Laborem Exercens, has been at the core of our angst-ridden debates about the legacy of deindustrialisation and the future of AI.

The clue is in the word “social”. Thatcher’s assertion that “there is no such thing” as society channelled a Protestant emphasis on individual responsibility. It revealed a perspective with a lineage going back to post-Reformation distrust of a Catholicism that, with its smells, bells and rituals, inserted its clerics between the believer and their Bible. Burnham’s much-quoted naming of his chief influences as “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church” indicates a quite different sensibility; one which finds meaning and truth in relationships and social institutions, and is at heart convivial. His determination to present the crisis in social care as an issue to be collectively faced and resolved comes from the same source.

One could go on. Burnham’s love of Philip Larkin, a (self-described “agnostic”) poet who captured the pathos and sadness – but also the beauty – in ordinary lives, is of a piece with an understanding of the world that is not obsessed with individual achievement and material wealth. It was Labour’s grievous error in the 90s and 00s to succumb to the meritocratic, aspirational creed, alienating vast swathes of its traditional support that looked to the party for different, associational values.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Burnham’s Catholic upbringing appears to have provided him with convictions that allowed him to emerge relatively intact from that heretical turn. The intriguing possibility is that as a result, the country finally has a prime minister able to understand the deeper origins of the anomie gripping a country in which former sources of social solidarity are under threat, or have already disappeared. The nation’s discontents are of course eminently practical, with the cost of living and the degradation of public services taking their place at the top of the list. But they can also be attributed to a sense that the common good – another concept of Catholic social teaching – has been chronically neglected in many ways, in an unbalanced, unequal society.

That is a moral issue about the way we live now, as much as it is a technical policy challenge. If Burnham’s stint as an ambitious altar boy can help him resolve it, it will be good news for a largely secular nation.

Julian Coman is a Guardian associate editor

‘Pretty much the downfall of society’: Adam Ramsay-Peaty on press intrusion, forgiveness and going all in for LA 2028

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 05:00:44 GMT

After a rollercoaster week at the Commonwealth Games, the double Olympic champion says he will never stop believing what he can achieve

“I couldn’t switch off because it’s been a real rollercoaster of a week,” Adam Ramsay-Peaty says with a weary smile on a quiet Thursday morning in Glasgow. He has just endured a rough night in which, after winning his third medal of the Commonwealth Games, he managed less than three hours of sleep. The medals consist of bronze in the 100m and 50m breaststroke and a silver in the men’s 4x100m medley. For most swimmers this would constitute success and satisfaction, but Ramsay-Peaty is different.

The fact that none of his three medals are gold, or attached to anything remotely like the kind of supreme performance that Ramsay-Peaty churned out with an aura of invincibility for eight years, has taken a chunk out of the double Olympic champion. There have been tears of frustration and an admission that “nothing makes sense this week”.

Ramsay-Peaty also sent out a fiery message to his tormentors in the tabloid press, and on social media, to stress that “you can’t hurt me” before urging an end to the excessive intrusion into his private life: “It has to stop. How many athletes have to go through this until the media learn their lesson?”

Now, in a small room on the outskirts of the city, Ramsay-Peaty admits that “decompressing last night was hard”. The European championships, which begin in Paris on 10 August, will see him gather himself for the next chapter in a tumultuous career, which he hopes will peak at the LA Olympics in 2028.

“I’ve experienced a lot in this sport,” Ramsay-Peaty, now 31 years old, says intently. “I’m never going to stop believing what I can do. I just need to get to that peak once more.”

Ramsay‑Peaty did not lose a single race in the 100m breaststroke from 2014 to 2022. Apart from winning three Olympic golds and eight world titles, by 2021 he had swum the 20 fastest times in the history of the discipline – and the 10 fastest in the history of the 50m.

After finally losing a 100m race, in the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Ramsay-Peaty suffered a breakdown a year later, quit swimming and lost himself in a haze of drink and depression. It was an epic feat to drag himself back from the brink and, in the 2024 Olympic final, miss gold by two-hundredths of a second while swimming with an undiagnosed case of Covid.

“After those Commonwealths in Birmingham,” Ramsay-Peaty says of his shock defeat four years ago, “I went on the attack and turned myself into scorched earth. I gave too much and that led to the burnout zone in 2023. I know not to do that now. I’ve got to find that peace and consolidation and realise we couldn’t have done anything more.

“We’ve trained extremely hard. I’ve only been 12 weeks in London with a new coach and a new programme. That takes time to reach fruition. Once you prune the tree, you grow more fruit in the end.”

After losing the 100m last Saturday, having swum almost three seconds slower than his world record, Ramsay-Peaty said: “I’m not crying because it’s a bronze instead of a gold. I’m crying because I know that the swim could have been better, and I worked way better than that.”

Another bronze in the 50m was accepted more philosophically by Ramsay-Peaty: “When I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human. Now it’s human first.”

This is a healthy alternative to the raging obsession that once consumed him. “It’s a natural progression from putting absolutely everything into the sport, which came at a huge cost,” he says. “You realise now that if you’re second you’re not going to die. You just have to learn from it. So there is a new approach because to do what I did you have to go to a place of anger, almost a place of hate, and I don’t want to be in that place. It’s a huge emotional cost that isn’t sustainable. I know I can win with a newer mindset and without the dark stuff.”

Ramsay-Peaty remains a fierce competitor and, looking ahead to the Europeans, the old fire crackles: “I’ve still got to burn the boats. I’ve still got to go all in, and believe I can win. If I don’t have that mentality I’m never going to get close. I know the Europeans are going to be fast in the heats. But I’m going to be good.”

After a dozen years at the summit, it sounds as if the more human side of Ramsay-Peaty is winning: “Every athlete has their own version of success. Of course, mine is still tied to quantifiable things like medals and times. But if I enjoy this journey and know I’ve given my best, and I touch that scoreboard in LA, that’s already success. That’s not defeatist. I’m still going to be a warrior. I’m still going to fight and give my absolute best.”

I tell Ramsay-Peaty about a column in which my colleague Barney Ronay compared him and his monumental achievements to other ageing sporting greats such as Lionel Messi. Ramsay-Peaty grins; he watched the 39-year‑old Messi stroll around so many World Cup pitches this summer before bursting into flaming genius when his grinding teammates needed him.

“Team sports have the benefit of being able to carry special players. But as a swimmer, when you’re older, it’s harder to race in the heats, and then the semis and finals. There’s nowhere to hide. When I’m going through that last 25 metres, it’s not like I can pass the ball and say: ‘You take this bit for me.’ Believe me, I probably would. But on the other side, with the success I had when I was younger, I wouldn’t have wanted to be in a team sport because my values and work ethic are so high I don’t think anyone could have kept up.”

Has he made sense yet of what went wrong in Glasgow especially as, a few months ago, he won the nationals in a time that would have clinched gold in the 100m Commonwealth final? “I was probably in a better block of work then, as we have to constantly balance our aerobic and anaerobic capacities. Maybe this past week was one of adaptation and, with a week of rest going into the Euros, I’ll be stronger. I worked the hardest I’ve worked in a very long time these last 12 weeks but maybe it wasn’t enough time for me to adapt. You also have to be race‑fit, and that’s a very different skill set. It still doesn’t make sense but tomorrow we have a debrief with my coach, Lisa Bates.”

Ramsay-Peaty adds: “We overthink a lot in this sport and we can look at all the data variables and rip up what is actually a lot of good work. Sometimes we just have a bad day, and that’s OK. But it’s not OK if it keeps happening.”

Bates replaced the great Mel Marshall, who had coached Ramsay-Peaty for his entire career until the 2024 Olympics. Marshall now works in Australia. “I’ve known Lisa for a long time,” Ramsay-Peaty says, “and Mel’s very close friends with her. It came with the decision to move to London because my wife [Holly] is pregnant so we needed her family. We’re having a little girl in December.”

Holly’s father is Gordon Ramsay, and the combination of a celebrity chef’s family in London and an Olympic champion’s working-class family from Uttoxeter has been catnip for the tabloids. Personal problems between the swimmer and his parents have been the source of feverish gossip and adding his wife’s name since their marriage has fuelled wild speculation.

Has it had a serious impact on him? “I wouldn’t say on me because I’ve got a thick skin. But I care about my wife, I care about my son [from his previous relationship]. I care about the relationships that people think I have with my son, and my own family, but that’s my private life. I have incredible relationships with some people in the media, like the one with you, which is built on trust over time. The ones that don’t go well are with the tabloids selling these stories for advertising. It’s pretty much the downfall of society when we’re exploiting people’s private lives to sell. Will it get better? Probably not. Will the truth come out one day? Absolutely.”

His mother, Caroline, posted a statement on social media this week about the rift. Is he hopeful there can be a reconciliation? “For me, as a Christian, there has to be forgiveness. It doesn’t mean you have to forget, but forgiveness takes time. I’m not saying that it won’t get better but it has to come from a place where I feel like they’ve improved as people, in a sense, and opened that communication up. I haven’t told one thing to the media. I haven’t done one story over the last eight months and more.”

We return to the sense of invincibility that Ramsay-Peaty carried for so many years. I read him a quote that he gave me in 2015, after he had won three gold medals at the world championships. Aged 20, he sounded remarkably mature as he said: “I feel no pressure. I enjoy racing. What’s the worst that could happen? You’re going to come second or lose? It’s not like someone has got a gun to your head.”

Eleven years on, he says : “There’s a part of me which screams that you want that risk [of hating defeat]. That’s the athlete. The human knows that isn’t the right path. That isn’t going to make me the best husband, the best father, the best friend. That athlete is incredibly selfish, and will ruin any form of relationship. I guarantee that because I’ve been there. But I still haven’t found that healthy medium.

“In training I don’t struggle one bit with that [athlete’s] mentality. I can switch it off when I leave training. It’s more about the exhaustion of training twice a day, going for it every single day. It’s now about finding what is optimal and sustainable in LA.”

If Ramsay-Peaty is preparing for the 100m he needs to swim around 9,000m on a training day. But if he concentrates purely on the 50m it would be “way less, probably 3,000m a day. You’d only have to do 12k a week, but I’m doing 40k for an extra 50 metres.”

Is he thinking of giving up the 100m and aiming only for the 50? “Not yet, no. I know I can be so strong in the 100. We’ve got to keep it in perspective. This is my first championships in two years. It’s been a bad week and we need to be better.”

Does he believe he will finally unearth the elusive balance of compulsion and decency and, in 2028, complete his journey in the most meaningful way, whatever the colour of any medals he might win?

Ramsay-Peaty pauses and then his face cracks open in a big, gleaming smile: “Yes. I’ve got a good armoury. I’ve just to get the polishing cloth out now.”
