The final hit: Is Glasgow’s 25-year gruesome gangland feud finally over?

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 05:00:44 GMT

The double murder of two Scots in the Costa del Sol may have ended the war between the Lyons and the Daniels – but the crimes haven’t gone away

It was a warm evening in Fuengirola on the Costa del Sol last year when two Scottish men met a violent end.

The punters of Monaghans seafront bar had barely finished watching the Champions League final on 31 May when a car pulled up outside. A masked gunman emerged and headed to the table of 46-year-old Eddie Lyons Jr, shooting him at point-blank range. The assassin turned the gun on Lyons’ friend, the bar’s owner Ross Monaghan, 43, but it jammed.

Grainy CCTV captured Monaghan racing inside the bar, pursued by the gunman, and falling to the ground, where he was shot three times while crawling on his hands and knees. The shooter fled the scene and, allegedly, the country too.

This double murder in a public place was the apex of 25 bloody years of feuding between two Glasgow families and their allies in organised crime: the most untouchable gang in Scotland, the Lyons, and their bitter rivals, the Daniels.

Earlier this month, police said they had noticed a lull in violence coming out of the criminal underworld. Could Scotland’s most deadly criminal war be over?

After a particularly unpleasant six-month spell of attacks and firebombings across “the length and breadth” of Scotland, there had been “a clear and obvious downturn of activity”, Police Scotland said.

“The cause of that downturn was without question multi-factorial, including the resolution of differences within the serious and organised crime community,” the force wrote in an update to the Scottish Police Authority.

Police Scotland will not comment on whether they intervened to mediate, though this is a known police tactic in other forces.

Karyn McCluskey, the pioneer behind Scotland’s Violence Reduction Unit, said in this case it was more probable that the gangs had changed their approach in response to heat from the police. “If you’re a good organised crime group, you don’t commit violence, because that’s just what brings the police down on you,” she said.

A total of 64 people were arrested in less than a year, the Police Scotland report said, after 84 incidents of violence. Search and arrest warrants recovered seven firearms and “assorted weapons” and more than 90 safeguarding plans were put in place to protect vulnerable members of the public caught up in the feud.

Police were also given a boost when – between March and June 2020 – officers in 13 European countries infiltrated an encrypted communications service called EncroChat used by crime bosses and their subordinates all over the world. The breach allowed police to investigate figures at the very top of the underworld, watching them ordering drugs, weapons or assassinations in real time.

As of 2023, the hack was responsible for 6,558 arrests worldwide, including more than 3,000 in the UK. Defendants are still appearing in front of judges month after month based on evidence gathered from EncroChat.

The beginning of this very specific feud can be traced back 25 years and has been compared to the plot of a gangster movie, somewhere between The Godfather and Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels. In 2001, a £20,000 stash of drugs belonging to the Daniel clan was stolen by associates of the Lyons family, and, it is suspected, the teenage Monaghan and Eddie Lyons Jr.

This did not go down well with the Daniels’ patriarch, Jamie Daniel, a highly territorial scrap-metal dealer who turned a hand to dealing heroin, eventually building a criminal empire. He was a man people knew not to cross. He was linked to beatings and a sniper murder of a rival drug dealer, a crime that is still technically unsolved.

“He had the reputation of being one or two steps ahead of the police and pretty much untouchable,” said a former detective inspector, David Moran, in a 2018 documentary.

It was Kevin “Gerbil” Carroll who did a lot of the dirty work and his increasing hubris began to pour jet fuel on an already roaring fire. Around 2005, amid a spate of gangland killings, Glasgow was labelled the murder capital of the UK. Police were handing out dozens of threat-to-life warnings, known as Osman warnings, to gang members and their families every year.

Gerbil, Jamie Daniel’s son-in-law and chief enforcer, was volatile and notorious for his “alien abduction” kidnap and torture routine, where his victims were often found at night injured and in their underwear claiming to have no memory of what happened to them.

In 2006, in revenge for being shot, he desecrated the grave of the eight-year-old son of Eddie Lyons Sr, which appeared to cross a line.

Only weeks later, two Daniel hitmen wearing “old man” rubber masks carried out a daylight ambush at a garage, killing an innocent member of the Lyons family, 21-year-old Michael Lyons.

A judge described the attack as a “cold-blooded, premeditated execution”, before handing out the longest jail terms in Scottish legal history to the men responsible – 32 and 35 years in prison.

Fearing for his life, Eddie Lyons Sr’s son Steven Lyons fled abroad, conducting business from Spain and slowly taking over the job of running the business from his father.

Next came a murder so audacious it would cause reverberations across the Scottish criminal underworld that are still felt to this day. In January 2010, the Daniels’ enforcer Gerbil was shot dead by two masked men in a busy Asda car park in Robroyston. He was in the back of a three-door Audi, and his associates in the front seats ran, leaving him a sitting duck, to be shot 13 times in the head and chest.

William “Buff” Paterson became the key suspect and during the trial his defence read out a list of 99 people who had reasons to want Gerbil dead. Despite this, he was convicted of the murder.

When the patriarch Jamie Daniel died of cancer in 2016 without leaving an obvious successor, the role of mob boss fell – somewhat uneasily, some people say – on the shoulders of Jamie’s nephew, Steven “Bonzo” Daniel, who became a primary target for the Lyons family.

Bonzo is known for distinctive scarring across his face, caused by a 2017 machete and meat cleaver attack so severe his jaw detached, his nose was nearly severed and his tongue shredded. It is said that he survived only because the attack happened close to a hospital.

He was taking over at a time of great change in organised crime. Gangs began to enter uncharted territory, moving operations on to the dark web and finding new partnerships overseas. Unlike previous generations who lived relatively modestly and conducted their business semi-privately, these TikTok-friendly gangsters were living outwardly glamorous lifestyles in exotic locations, photographed with Botox, filler and Turkey dental work.

Steven Lyons was expanding the family’s business from Spain and later Dubai, forging links with Ireland’s largest gang, the Kinahans, through his associate, Ross “Miami” McGill. McGill was formerly the head of the Rangers’ “Union Bears” ultra fans and now leads a young Scottish enforcer gang called Tamo Junto (Portuguese slang meaning “we are together”). He is currently on the run.

Members of Tamo Junto and a Daniels-aligned group calling themselves the A-Team have posted anonymous TikTok videos each ridiculing the deaths of gangland figures such as Gerbil, Monaghan and Eddie Jr. They have taunted one another with threats in the style of memes as they meted out violence on the ground, filming attacks and firebombings and posting them online.

Steven Lyons’s links to the Kinahan cartel would be his undoing. Detectives working on information gathered during the EncroChat breach targeted the Kinahans’ money manager, Johnny Morrissey, and as a result gathered enough evidence on Steven Lyons to arrest him, his wife and more than a dozen other key figures earlier this year.

Steven Lyons’s arrest and the assassination in Spain of his brother and Monaghan was a “decapitation” of the powerful Lyons gang, the former Police Scotland superintendent Martin Gallagher said. The downturn in violence observed by police represents a shift in thinking among those who are left.

“Things are just falling into place with what the new normal will be,” Gallagher said. “Although that doesn’t look like crime occurring to the general public – so nobody’s house is being set on fire, no lorry is being driven through somebody’s front door, as has occurred – that means they’re focusing on what they want to do to make money – which is import drugs.”

He added: “There’s still crime happening, it’s just not as obvious and they’re not trying to bump each other off.”

Last week, police found a cocaine stash worth £1.7m in Moodiesburn, a village on the outskirts of Glasgow. A 34-year-old man has been charged.

Graeme Pearson, a former police officer and Labour MSP, said: “The business is too lucrative to suddenly die overnight. It’s like running a seam of gold. If you know the gold’s there, you’ll keep going back to it.”

This article was amended on 1 August 2026. The double murder happened on 31 May 2025, the night of the Champions League final, not 8 June 2025, the night of the Nations League final as stated in an earlier version.

‘Who could have done this?’ Mystery over Briton found dead in a suitcase in Athens

The Guardian Sat, 01 Aug 2026 04:00:42 GMT

Greek police throw entire homicide division at trying to explain fate of 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane Ross

Two worlds separated by sheets of corrugated iron: one, a tree-lined road, bordered by a park and the home of Greece’s oldest sports club; the other a wasteland of derelict buildings and graffiti-covered walls in what was once a car park.

It is here, on the wrong side of the divide, in Kypseli, a neighbourhood in central Athens, that the body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross was found, inside a suitcase last month.

The 38-year-old who had longtime connections to the country – she reportedly worked in the charity sector – had arrived in the Greek capital on holiday almost three weeks earlier. “She was an angel,” a friend in her native Edinburgh told the Guardian. “Wherever she went, she did good. Who could possibly have done this?”

The homeless man who made the grim discovery was among the few who ventured into the abandoned lot, located between an apartment block and design school on Evelpidon Street. It was midday on 18 July.

What he did next – alerting authorities to the find – would shake up police forces in Greece and Scotland. “We’ve had the entire homicide division of the Greek FBI working night and day on the case,” said the police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou. “We’re in contact with other police forces. We’re going to solve this.”

But four days after Ross was publicly identified, with Greek authorities announcing the body was that of a Briton based on fingerprints that matched biometric data in the US, mystery continues to shroud the case.

Initial examination of her remains proved inconclusive although pathologists deemed she had probably been dead for several days before the discovery. There were no evident injuries or sign of struggle on her body, raising further questions as to how she had died.

On Friday, as local people left flowers at the site, police said investigators were intensifying their search of CCTV footage after it emerged that DNA analysis of the suitcase had not produced any evidence that could be linked to a suspect.

“Whenever I pass by I think of that poor woman,” said Manos Andreou, a fashion designer who walks his dog each day along Evelpidon. “Until the area was closed off, I used to go in there and let her run around it, so it’s all been a bit of a shock. They say they’re looking at camera footage, they say they’re making progress, but can you see any cameras anywhere on this street?”

The daughter of a lawyer, Ross, who had lived and worked in the US, flew into Athens from Edinburgh on 26 June. Until 15 July she had stayed with the son of a Greek friend in Keratsini, a working-class suburb close to the port of Piraeus. Before moving on, she had told him she would be spending a few days with friends from the US in Kypseli.

Detectives, now desperately trying to reconstruct her movements, have expressed frustration at their inability to trace the Americans. Other members of the Briton’s social network in Athens have been interviewed at length, giving testimony that has been described as “incredibly helpful”. None are considered suspects.

“July 15 was the last day she had contact with any of her friends,” said the police spokesperson. “Our investigations are focused on the intervening days and whom she may have met and where she stayed. The Americans have not been identified or found.”

Police remain confident the suitcase was not at the crime scene more than 48 hours before its discovery on 18 July. They are also convinced that Ross died nearby in Kypseli although have stopped short of describing her death as a murder.

“There is always the possibility that she died and then for some reason was hidden,” added Dimoglidou. “Our priority is to get to the bottom of who left the suitcase. Whoever they were was careful not to leave any fingerprints or DNA.”

Adding to the mystery, it emerged that the Briton’s mobile phone was in operation and being used days after her death. Ross’s distraught father is reported to have told police he received text messages from his daughter, believing she was alive and well, until her body was identified, publicly, on Wednesday.

Messages spoke of her “need to be alone”. Authorities, who have yet to retrieve the device, believe they were deliberately sent so that she would not be declared missing and “to buy time”. Investigators have located the phone’s digital footprint to Athens.

One source said: “We have to presume that the person who had her phone and then sent these messages, days after pathologists believe she probably died, is connected to the crime and we cannot rule out that they knew Ms Ross.”

More than 60 people in the Greek police department’s homicide division have been assigned to the case. Urgency is such that investigators have also requested that laboratory tests be fast-tracked to determine the cause of death.

“At such times, when there is advanced decay because of heat or the conditions in which a body is kept, only toxicological tests and in-depth examination of [vital organ] tissues can determine, exactly, how a person died,” said Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine.

There would be answers, he said, that would unearth the truth.

“I have no doubt they will come but it won’t be easy and it will take time.”

Andy Burnham’s first step towards fairer social care for all

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:11:18 GMT

Readers respond to the prime minister’s pledge to spend his ‘political capital’ and find cross-party consensus on reforming social care

I write as someone whose disabilities mean that I will be in receipt of social care support my whole life (Andy Burnham seeks cross-party agreement on future of social care, 27 July). For too long, people like me have been cannon fodder for politicians who routinely forget that their highest duty in providing social care is to protect those less able, or unable, to care for themselves. Investing in the right support for us unlocks our often-forgotten abilities. When we are successful, it is often because we have had opportunity to be because of that support, and when we aren’t, as so often happens, it is because society writes us off.

Andy Burnham’s intervention is welcome news as it shows that he considers us a priority. Reform of the social care system has to be taken hand in hand with disability groups and people with lived experience of being disabled. Too often the system traps people into dependency on temporary accommodation rather than providing them with the means to receive support in their own home.

Six years ago, this was the case for me, but not any more. I am now studying at university and have settled into a life that is light years better than what I had before.

The prime minister’s own experience of dealing with this issue is also helpful in this. In his first five years as the mayor of Greater Manchester, rough sleeping was reduced by two-thirds. If he wants to be bold, he only needs to look north and to his prior success in delivering this for Manchester. Robbie BentleyBristol

Despite economists saying that it is too hard to tax wealth rather than income, there is already a wealth tax in place paying for social care in this country. The trouble is that it’s only levied on those who have the misfortune to need it. As your explainer points out, disabled and elderly people in England with assets over £23,250 have to pay the full cost of their social care.

Why shouldn’t the super-rich be taxed on a similar basis – all assets over a threshold – and then they can pay for a functional and decent social care system for all the people who they made their money from by charging extortionate profits and paying sub-living wages?

If the working class isn’t allowed to pass down generational wealth, why should anyone else be?Rachel Powild Manchester

Rightwing politicians and newspapers screaming about inheritance grabs and new taxes to fund social care are missing the point, probably deliberately. Socialising the cost of social care does not increase the cost, but spreads it more fairly. At present it is a lottery: if you get a losing ticket and you or a family member needs long-term care for dementia, all your savings, and the capital tied up in your house, could disappear. If you are lucky and die quickly, your children get a windfall.

It is clearly fairer that everyone gives up a share of their wealth rather than some all and some none. Not only that, it removes the stress about whether a lifetime’s savings will suffice. A properly designed national care service will share risk, which is what a civilised society should value. Mike Cushman London

Any attempt to pay for the broken social care system should start with the abolition of the triple lock on pensions. I welcome the moves towards achieving a cross-party consensus, but fear that political point-scoring and manoeuvring will defeat them, as they have done in the past. Michael LeeStockton on Tees, County Durham

In the debate on how to fund care costs, can all parties drop “no one should have to sell their home” mantra? If you are the sole occupant and need residential care, why shouldn’t you sell it to pay the costs? After all, you’re not using it. Is it fair to receive financial support and still be able to pass your biggest asset on to your children?John TraynerLondon

We are shocked that Palestine Action barrister faces contempt proceedings

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 17:09:31 GMT

Former clients of Rajiv Menon KC, including Tariq Ali and Hillsborough family members Margaret Aspinall and Sue Roberts, say the charges against him must be dropped. Plus a letter from Andrew Smith

The fight for truth and justice can too often be a hard and long struggle. Navigating the law is complex, and justice depends on lawyers who we can trust – lawyers who listen to our voices, stand up for us, and pursue the truth on our behalf.

Rajiv Menon KC is an experienced and highly respected barrister who has spent his career representing people like us. At some of the most traumatic times in our lives he has represented us with professionalism, integrity and compassion, ensuring that our voices were heard in inquests, inquiries and criminal trials.

We are all deeply shocked that Rajiv is facing contempt proceedings (Palestine Action barrister’s prosecution criticised as ‘chilling’, 23 July). As clients we must have confidence that our lawyers can represent us fearlessly and independently. This case risks undermining the fundamental relationship of trust and confidence between clients and their lawyers without which meaningful participation in the justice system is impossible.

We stand with Rajiv and believe that these proceedings must be dropped immediately. Tariq Ali Witness, undercover police inquiry; Margaret Aspinall Mother of James Aspinall, who died in the Hillsborough disaster; Sue Roberts Sister of Graham Roberts, who died in the Hillsborough disaster; Marieha Hussain Protester acquitted over “coconut” placard; Tippa Naphtali Cousin of Mikey Powell, who died in police custody; Selma Taha, Divina Riggon, Danae Thomas (King’s Cross Three)

Imran Khan makes a valid case against the charge of contempt against Rajiv Menon KC (One day, your life and future may depend on a jury. The integrity of that legal process is in peril right now, theguardian. com, 23 July). I wonder how this charge would stand up to the Hillsborough law, where state actors are required to tell the whole truth when giving evidence.

The disparity of justice meted out to Palestine Action seems to point to inevitable fines or prison when the above law should be giving everyone the opportunity of a fair trial. Apart from that, no advocate should be concerned for their own freedom when defending another citizen, no matter what they have done. Andrew SmithBolton

The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:32:06 GMT

Devolution should finance transport, skills and industry, not become a rightwing contest to promise the largest tax giveaway

That England is among the rich world’s most centralised countries underpins Andy Burnham’s critique of the economic history of the past 40 years. Only post-communist Europe deindustrialised as rapidly as Yorkshire and the Midlands did in the 1980s. Centralisation did not close every factory or pit, but left regions without the powers, finance or institutions to cushion the shock or build a resilient, replacement economy. Hence Mr Burnham’s radical and welcome plan to unbundle English government.

There are three facets to his devolution programme. The first are the detailed and concrete proposals contained in a cabinet paper Mr Burnham released on Friday. This appears to be a blueprint to create a decentralised state organised around mayors as the key regional economic actors, while jointly governed pan-regional agencies could emerge, say for transport, energy, investment and industrial systems, that cross mayoral boundaries. Regions without mayors will get a chance to have one – or limit themselves to weaker powers.

The second, outlined in the Guardian and later confirmed by No 10, is that mayors will be able to keep income-tax and business-rate revenues, with the forthcoming budget and spending review deciding on how much. Before entering No 10, Mr Burnham proposed a third pillar: a duty, modelled on Germany’s Basic Law, requiring English regions to pursue equivalent living conditions nationwide.

Following this logic, a mayoral authority would receive a share of tax revenues and benefit when its economy and tax base grow. But the national government would continue redistributing resources so that poorer places can provide comparable services and possess meaningful investment capacity. Without such an equalisation measure, disparities would widen. One thinktank pointed out that if mayors received 2.5% of the 20p basic rate of income tax, London would get £2.3bn in 2026-27 while Hull and East Yorkshire would get £135m.

Ben Houchen, the Tory mayor of Tees Valley, wants to turn devolved income-tax revenues into new powers to offer tax rebates. That mistakes a regional investment settlement for a tax-cutting competition: poorer places would forfeit the cash needed to rebuild transport links as well as skills and industrial capacity. What some rightwingers seek is to turn regional elections into tax-cutting auctions over who can return the most public money. But cash giveaways now would just mean the bill of the underinvestment would land later.

England’s devolution map remains incomplete, but Mr Burnham wants to finish it. New mayors are due in Cumbria, and Cheshire and Warrington, in 2027, followed by ones in southern and eastern regions in 2028. The rest of the country will be asked to choose between mayoral strategic authorities with stronger powers or non-mayoral “foundation” bodies operating with more limited controls.

A new Harvard Kennedy School and King’s College London paper, co-authored by the former Labour minister Ed Balls, argues that Britain’s weak productivity stems from persistent regional divides, with the gap between south-east England and the rest of the nation wider than that separating east and west Germany today. One reason this has not been tackled is that Britain has never had both No 10 and the Treasury committed to regional growth. Now it does. The country may finally discover what happens when the centre pulls in the same direction.

The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:32:01 GMT

Funders have picked a damaging fight with scientists and the public. They should reconsider their plans

The iconic Lovell telescope, housed at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire, has always expanded our view of the universe – from tracking the Sputnik launch in 1957 to its current contributions to the study of dark matter. It is now threatened with closure after it was announced that government funding will not continue past March 2028. The projected savings are just £2.8m a year.

This is just the latest in a rolling package of cuts from the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) – which disperses government funding to particle, astro and nuclear physics, among other disciplines – aimed at saving about £160m over the next four years. The STFC has insisted that the measures are a result of cost overruns. That may be true, but it is hard not to see this as part of a larger shift in what kind of science the government funds and prioritises, and what areas it allows to wither.

There is no doubt that physics is expensive. From telescopes to synchrotron beams, its instruments are increasingly large-scale and power-hungry. And scientists are not immune to the cost of living crisis. If households are feeling the pinch of electricity costs, just imagine getting the monthly bill for a particle accelerator. However, UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), of which the STFC is a subsidiary, has just gone through a revamp of its funding model, one that clearly prioritises economic growth and measureable outcomes. Looking across the programmes cut, which include international collaborations with other telescope arrays and the Cern facility in Switzerland, many scientists believe that long-term, fundamental research is under specific threat.

The UKRI and STFC have not helped the situation by badly misreading the politics. In a session at the House of Lords earlier this month, the UKRI chief, Ian Chapman, seemed surprised by the scientists’ “hyperbolic” reaction, and noted that they “feel that they have been cut” when, in fact, overall physics funding has increased. But scientists have reason to feel slighted when valued ongoing projects and collaborations – rather than future plans – are axed, and when what appear to be relatively small cost savings (the UKRI budget will be £10bn by 2030) fall on their shoulders. There are shades of the departed Starmer government in this saga: the UKRI wants to tell a big story about science funding going up, but instead is mired in a row over a fairly minor sum that has angered scientists and sections of the public. One does not have to be an astronomer to know that optics matter.

The UKRI and STFC are technically arm’s‑length bodies, but it hasn’t escaped notice that the ministers who set its funding priorities, Liz Kendall and Patrick Vallance, are no longer in office, while Andy Burnham has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. It would seem a good time for the current course to be reconsidered, whether by the funding councils or the new government itself.

There is a conversation to be had about what research we fund with limited resources, and the balance between so-called blue sky projects and those expected to yield commercial returns. But when physicists warn that the UK could lose a “generation of scientists” to these cuts – in one of the few fields in which we can credibly claim to be world-leading – they should be heeded. It’s time to refocus, and look again.

Don’t let Jodrell Bank Observatory become another industrial museum

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:30:45 GMT

Readers respond to reports that the world-famous big dish is facing closure due to spending cuts by UK Research and Innovation

Throughout my long life, Jodrell Bank Observatory has been a source of wonder and pride (Jodrell Bank Observatory facing closure after major funder cuts support, 27 July). Sir Bernard Lovell’s inspirational creation never ceases to awe with its combination of cutting-edge space exploration and heroic engineering structure. A tour of its welcoming visitor centre with my grandchildren confirmed that this sense of awe is being passed on to future generations.

Yes, it would make another fine museum. But here in the north we have quite a few museums of our glorious industrial past. We have only one Jodrell Bank, probing the mysteries of the universe right now. So I’m afraid it is over to my fellow English graduate Andy Burnham to reverse the philistine decision of UK Research and Innovation, reminding him of his poetic hero Philip Larkin’s fear for the possible future of the UK: “Our children will not know it is a different country./ All we can hope to leave them now is money”. Dr Ken SmithMacclesfield, Cheshire

The one thing that Britain can still claim to be a top-division power in is science and technology. From numbers of Nobel laureates, to startups being funded then absorbed by global enterprises, and our universities and research establishments attracting the best minds from all over the world, the evidence is there. When trade delegations travel the world, the selling point is our science and technology. So it seems odd that there is a squeeze of government investment in this area of soft power.

One of the symbols of Britain’s scientific prowess is the big dish at Jodrell Bank. Generations in Britain and around the world have grown up seeing it as the backdrop to space travel and astronomical discoveries. Reducing its funding will draw attention to the reduced circumstances of Britain’s scientific endeavour and a lack of ambition to keep Britain as a world leader. If the government wants to quietly cut spending on scientific research, reducing Jodrell Bank to a museum is not the best route. £2.8m a year seems a small price to pay for keeping an international symbol of Britain’s prowess going. John SommerSaltford, Somerset

I’m dismayed at the news that Jodrell Bank Observatory is under threat. I enjoyed an enlightening day at the visitor centre recently, and was planning a return visit. Could I suggest that the relevant funding body dig out their own telescopes and take a long hard look at the future of British science and those young people looking forward to careers in science, engineering and technology?Peter Baddeley Painswick, Gloucestershire

Commonwealth Games builds to finale and the Tour de France Femmes – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 31 Jul 2026 16:05:43 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The penultimate day of action in Glasgow features a twist in the tale of the track as the mile returns for the first time since 1966, replacing the middle-distance blue-riband 1500m. Expectations are high in the men’s race as the Scottish duo of Jake Wightman and Josh Kerr vie for glory. Kerr has just lowered the world record for the event and said after his midweek heat: “How many times in my career am I going to be running to the line in front of a world-class pack feeling as good as I am in front of a home crowd?” Elsewhere, the boxing concludes today, with 14 gold medals up for grabs, plus action in track cycling. The netball competition reaches the semi-final stage. England, who beat South Africa in a comeback thriller on Thursday, will face New Zealand at 9am. In the later semi, Australia – four-time Commonwealth Games winners and reigning champions – meet Jamaica. John Ashdown, Billy Munday and Rob Smyth will keep the updates flowing. Sean Ingle reports from Glasgow.

Goodwood has certainly lived up to its glorious billing this past week and the final day of the high-summer meeting on the rolling South Downs has plenty of interest for racing’s cognoscenti. Consent can gain the upper hand once again during her continuing tussle with Santorini Star in the Qatar Lillie Langtry Stakes (3pm). Sir Mark Prescott’s star filly returns to the distance of her Prix de Royallieu victory at Longchamp in October. In the preceding contest over a mile and a half, William Haggas’s Al Aasy is seeking a third successive Glorious Stakes victory (2.25pm). There could be another successful title defence with Richard Spencer’s Two Tribes in the Stewards’ Cup (3.35pm). The Phil Cunningham-owned five-year-old is treading the same path as last year which yielded glory in the International Handicap at Ascot, too, where this year he came second. Greg Wood is at the track to liveblog all the action.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot begins the Tour de France Femmes determined to repeat last year’s triumph, but the Frenchwoman faces a tough challenge in a field headed by her in-form Dutch rival Demi Vollering. Ferrand-Prévot, the Olympic mountain bike champion, returned to road racing two years ago with the Tour as her primary target, and rewarded that decision by becoming the first home winner of the race since 1989. She has carefully tailored her schedule to repeat the feat, finishing second at the Tour of Flanders and third at Paris-Roubaix before stepping away from competition after the Vuelta Femenina in May, where she finished 35th overall. Her Team Visma-Lease a Bike squad has been built around another bid for yellow and includes the triple stage winner Marianne Vos. However, Vollering is viewed as the pre-race favourite. The Dutchwoman has enjoyed a stellar season, winning the Giro d’Italia as well as several marquee one-day races, and arrives with perhaps the strongest form in the women’s peloton. Luke McLaughlin helms the stage one liveblog, with Jeremy Whittle reporting from Lausanne.

The final day of the 2026 Games sees 15 gold medals on offer and features the contest for netball gold, plus a compelling day of action at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome. In the women’s event, Great Britain’s Olympic medal-winning trio of Katy Marchant, Sophie Capewell (both England) and Emma Finucane (Wales) go head-to-head in the keirin. But the one to beat is New Zealand’s reigning Olympic and Commonwealth champion, Ellesse Andrews. The sprinter has been the dominant force over recent years, and became world champion in the event in 2023 in Glasgow. England’s Kadeena Cox has a strong chance of success in the Women’s C4-C5 4,000m individual pursuit, her signature event, which she won gold medals in at Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020. In the bowling, Scotland’s Paul Foster and Alex Marshall are targeting a repeat of the pairs gold they claimed on home grass at Glasgow 2014. Rob Smyth and Daniel Gallan host the rolling blog, all the way to the closing ceremony.

The nine-stage route features nearly 19,000m of climbing, an individual time trial in Dijon and a potentially decisive summit finish on Mont Ventoux. It is the first time the legendary climb features in the women’s race. If that doesn’t decide the battle for the yellow, it could come down to the demanding final stage around Nice. Among those in contention are the Swiss rider Marlen Reusser, the Vuelta winner, Paula Blasi, and the former Tour champion Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney, while the veterans Elisa Longo Borghini and Anna van der Breggen cannot be ruled out. Sunday’s second stage from Aigle via the Vaudois vineyards ends with back-to-back ascents before the finale: a bunch sprint on Quai du Mont-Blanc. Alex Reid saddles up for our liveblog.

Spain Installs Floating Barrier in Ceuta After Influx of Migrants

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Migrant Surge Into Spanish Territory

Advertisement

Supported by

Most of those who came to the territory, a Spanish exclave in Africa, have returned across the border to Morocco. At least 67 people died trying to enter, the authorities said.

By Carlos Barragán and Lynsey Chutel

Carlos Barragán reported from Ceuta, Spain.

The Spanish authorities said on Saturday that they were installing a floating barrier near a sea wall between Morocco and the autonomous city of Ceuta, after a surge of tens of thousands of migrants into the territory two days earlier raised questions across Europe about Spain’s ability to control its borders.

The announcement, from Spain’s Interior Ministry, came as a vast majority of those migrants appeared to have left Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa. For those who have stayed, and who have tried to evade the police and angry crowds of locals, the next steps remained unclear.

At least 48,300 of the roughly 50,000 to 60,000 people who entered from Morocco had returned there by late Friday afternoon, according to Spain’s Interior Ministry, while hundreds more continued to leave throughout the night. A press officer for Spain’s government in Ceuta said at least 67 people died trying to enter the city in recent days.

The crisis in Ceuta prompted over 20 European Union countries to pen a letter to the European Commission asking for an emergency meeting of interior ministers. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain wrote his own letter to the commission that defended his government’s migration policies and accused those who had called to suspend Spain from the bloc’s free movement zone of being “selfish.”

Most of the migrants who entered Ceuta were young Moroccan men seeking work. On Saturday, a few hundred migrants from elsewhere in Africa rested on a beach in the city’s northwest. Many said that they believed Spain could not return them to Morocco because they were from other countries and that they had not eaten since Thursday.

“I don’t want to go to Morocco,” said Kamal Omar, 24, who said he left his home in Sudan in 2023 because of the civil war there and arrived in Morocco last year. “Please give us protection.”

The Spanish government appeared focused so far on bolstering Ceuta’s border with Morocco. On Friday, Mr. Sánchez said Spain would install buoys to “create a containment barrier, a physical barrier, if only a visual one.”

The buoys will also comply with a recent ruling from Spain’s Supreme Court that may have prompted the influx of migrants this week, Mr. Sánchez said.

Mr. Sánchez blamed human traffickers for spreading misinterpretations about the ruling, which said that migrants intercepted at sea could not be immediately sent back unless they had bypassed a barrier while trying to reach Spanish territory.

Note: Satellite image from March 30, 2026. Sources: Spanish government; Reuters (photo); Airbus (satellite image). Samuel Granados / The New York Times

The new structure is an inflatable barrier 500 meters (about 1,600 feet) long that extends as much as one meter below the surface, the Interior Ministry said in a statement. It will be reinforced by an outer line of anchored buoys provided by the Spanish Navy, the ministry said.

Judith Sunderland, of Human Rights Watch’s refugee and migrant rights division, said that Spain’s plans were “raising red flags.”

“It is hard to imagine how the authorities would intercept people trying to swim around the barrier,” Ms. Sunderland said. She recalled a 2014 episode in which Spain’s Civil Guard fired rubber bullets at a group of migrants trying to reach Ceuta from the sea. At least 15 people died in that attempt.

Mr. Sánchez’s critics on the right, who have seized on the crisis to portray him as too lax on immigration, called the new measure inadequate.

“You don’t secure a border by putting buoys in the sea,” Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative Popular Party, the main opposition group, said on Friday.

Mr. Sánchez hit back on Saturday at the many anti-immigrant leaders and right-wing politicians in Europe who had blamed his government’s migrant-friendly policies for the crisis.

In a letter to the European Commission, Mr. Sánchez said some “have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area,” which allows for freedom of movement among European countries.

“Such an attitude — driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest — is not only contrary to European law, humanitarian law and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” Mr. Sánchez wrote in the letter, which his office shared on Saturday.

“It is also contrary to Europe’s long-term interests and to the most basic common sense,” he added, noting that Spain has one of the least porous external borders in the E. U.

Twenty-two European leaders wrote their own letter to the European Commission on Saturday, calling for an urgent meeting of interior ministers and a coordinated response to the crossings in Ceuta.

The letter, signed by Prime Ministers Giorgia Meloni of Italy and Mette Frederiksen of Denmark and Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany, among others, said the E. U. could not allow mass crossings to create the impression “that a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into a legal stay.”

That “would encourage further attempts, undermine confidence in our common migration policy and have repercussions for all member states,” the leaders wrote.

Ceuta has been governed by Spain for centuries, along with Melilla, another autonomous Spanish city farther east along the same coast. The territories, which have the E. U.’s only land borders with Africa, have long been a source of tensions between Spain and Morocco. While Ceuta is part of the bloc and the Schengen Area, it operates under special rules that require additional border controls before people can travel onward to mainland Spain and the rest of the bloc.

On Saturday, young Moroccans were still wandering the outskirts of Ceuta, looking for food or sheltering under trees’ shade, then rushing into the hills or hiding in the brush when police officers or soldiers approached.

“There is still a sense of unease among the population,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the president of Ceuta, said at a news conference on Saturday.

But most of the migrants were returning to Morocco by foot or by hitching rides.

Clashes also erupted overnight in Beni Ensar, a Moroccan border town close to Melilla, as Morocco’s security forces pushed back people trying to cross the border.

“It was all night yesterday,” said Omar Naji, who works for the local Moroccan Association for Human Rights. “This morning it is calm.”

Aida Alami contributed reporting from Morocco, and Jeanna Smialek from Brussels.

Lynsey Chutel is a Times reporter based in London who covers breaking news in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.

In Dropping Reflecting Pool Case, Pirro Draws Trump’s Wrath

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Jeanine Pirro, the U. S. attorney in Washington, blamed shoddy construction, contradicting President Trump’s pet theory. Mr. Trump said he disagreed “100%” with her.

By Glenn Thrush

Reporting from Washington

Jeanine Pirro faced the cameras on July 2 with characteristic self-assurance to announce the indictment of the 67-year-old ex-Olympian David Hearn for trashing “sacred” government property, President Trump’s highly prized but shoddily renovated Reflecting Pool.

“This is not only a priority for the president, but for myself,” said Ms. Pirro, the U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia, disclosing felony vandalism charges against Mr. Hearn for touching the lining of the pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial. She added: “We will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hearn willfully destroyed property.”

This was not the case.

Ms. Pirro’s office dramatically reversed course on Friday, not only withdrawing the charge against Mr. Hearn but blasting the Interior Department for the rushed and “botched” renovation, along with U. S. Park Police officials who fed bad information that led her to publicly cite “tremendous evidence” against Mr. Hearn. In the process, intentionally or not, she skated perilously close to contradicting Mr. Trump — and he noticed.

Ms. Pirro’s 20-page filing did not refer to, much less rebuke, Mr. Trump for claiming the damage was caused by left-wing vandals rather than his administration’s missteps. But it raised innate doubts about his assertion that criminals had slashed the pool’s lining with a “knife or blade.”

That Ms. Pirro, a former Westchester, N. Y., district attorney and Fox News personality was aiming much of her criticism not at Mr. Trump, but his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, who oversaw the issuance of a no-bid contract to renovate the pool, did not appear to matter much.

On Saturday morning, Mr. Trump dashed off a post on Truth Social that made clear he was unhappy with Ms. Pirro, a friend and ally since the 1980s.

“I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro,” Mr. Trump wrote.

“I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM,” he wrote, adding, “There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!”

In his own social media post on Saturday, Mr. Burgum said that his department had “provided the U. S. Attorney’s office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool.”

Ms. Pirro’s U-turn was a rare instance in which a Trump-appointed U. S. attorney publicly acknowledged that a prosecution once embraced was fatally compromised, in an administration in which admitting fault is seen as weakness and in which taking actions that contradict the boss is seen as self-destruction.

“Trump is mad at Pirro because she finally admitted what we made clear in our legal filings all along: Trump’s botched renovation was responsible for the damage, not Davey Hearn,” said Norman L. Eisen a member of Mr. Hearn’s defense team and a co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, which has represented people targeted by the Trump administration.

“Her claim that she and her office were previously duped by Interior is nonsense,” he added. “Starting immediately after the arraignment, our motions repeatedly proved that the administration was to blame, not Davey.”

Tim Lauer, a spokesman for the U. S. attorney’s office, declined to comment. “The filing speaks for itself,” he wrote in an email.

The about-face also underscored a recurrent pattern that has diminished the Justice Department’s once-sterling standing with federal judges and juries — the rush by Trump- appointed U. S. attorneys across the country to take quick action against those accused by the president of transgressions, even petty ones.

It is now much more common for grand juries around the country, particularly in Washington, to reject indictments brought by the department. In years past, this almost never happened.

Last December, grand jurors in Virginia rejected the department’s effort to indict Letitia James, the New York attorney general, on mortgage-related charges for the second time in a one-week period. Earlier, a jury in the district halted an attempt by Ms. Pirro’s office to prosecute a Justice Department employee who tossed a sandwich at federal officers. Around the same time, she thrice tried and failed to indict a woman who pushed an F. B. I. agent during a protest.

Ms. Pirro’s filing is, in a sense, an effort to replace the case against Mr. Hearn in federal court with a case in the court of public opinion against Mr. Burgum; the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings; and Park Police officials.

In the filing, she said that her staff relied almost exclusively on claims by Interior Department officials that the extensive damage to the lining of the pool was caused by Mr. Hearn and other vandals who were observed tugging at or removing pieces of material from the wall.

That information, coupled with police testimony about Mr. Hearn’s movements, convinced prosecutors to bring the case before the grand jury on July 2. They opted for a felony, which carried a potential 10-year prison sentence, rather than a misdemeanor, because the damage exceeded the legal threshold of $1,000.

At the time, Ms. Pirro wrote, her office “was not in possession of any information from D. O. I. indicating that any damage to the Reflecting Pool was caused by anything other than the actions of the defendant and other vandals who damaged the pool’s lining.”

It all began to unravel, however, after prosecutors followed up by asking for “everything” — government reports, police and witness statements, photographs, body camera footage and, critically, internal assessments of the high-profile renovation project.

By late July, Ms. Pirro’s office obtained 695 megabytes of documents that led Ms. Pirro to conclude the damage observed was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor,” coupled with “the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America250 celebration.”

But Ms. Pirro’s critics, including Mr. Eisen, said her account ignored the fact that problems with the renovation of the algae-choked pool had been widely known and reported in the press and in their own court filings.

Mr. Hearn’s team maintained that he had merely “touched a piece of coating that had already detached, released it when asked to do so by a park employee, and left the pool in no worse condition in which he found it.”

Photos and testimony introduced in the case had indicated that substantial cracks had already appeared, and water started leaking from the pool, before Mr. Hearn’s visit. Mr. Hearn’s lawyers questioned whether that information had been made clear to grand jurors, complaining of “irregularities that reflect a misleading presentation.”

His legal team was “evaluating all legal remedies,” Mr. Eisen said.

Zach Montague contributed reporting.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

As Cease-Fire Teetered, Iran Plotted a Wider War With Aid of Its Proxies

The New York Times August 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

During a fleeting truce, Iranians covertly devised a plan to raise the war’s costs for President Trump if U. S. forces attacked anew.

By Farnaz Fassihi and Neil MacFarquhar

A drone attack sent smoke billowing from a giant Saudi oil facility, the largest such plant in the world. Two gas tankers burst into flames at an Egyptian port near the Suez Canal, a crucial choke point in global trade. Fireballs erupted over Jordan as missiles flew toward a base housing U. S. personnel.

War has enveloped a widening circle of targets across the Middle East in recent days, as Iran and its phalanx of proxy militias have sought to strike at U. S. allies, roil global markets and push the United States to halt its campaign against the Islamic Republic.

The attacks are part of what two senior Iranian officials depicted as a step-by-step plan, devised in secret during a fleeting cease-fire this spring, that would use Iran’s allies to escalate attacks if the United States intensified its assaults. The goal, the officials said, was to make the war as costly as possible for President Trump.

Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator, even crowed on social media about the strategy with the proxy forces, which are known in the region as the “Axis of Resistance.”

“The rules of the conflict are changing and being rewritten, we are creating new conditions and platforms in the war,” Mr. Mohammadi said. “The fronts are multiplying from different directions in the region; they are of course coordinated but act independently. A new axis of resistance is emerging with new players.”

Iran and its allies have taken powerful blows since 2023, when the militant group Hamas attacked Israel. Recent events, however, have shown their capacity to regroup, stir chaos and gain Iran leverage.

Still, analysts do not consider the proxy forces — each with its own agenda — mere puppets of Tehran, though Iran’s level of coordination and control varies among them.

The Houthis in Yemen, for instance, are seen as the most autonomous of the groups that make up the alliance. Hezbollah coordinates the most closely with Iran, while Shiite militias in Iraq are somewhere in the middle in the degree of their willingness to act as a direct arm of Iran.

But the groups still find common cause against the United States and Israel. During the short-lived cease-fire, Iranian generals covertly strategized with proxy militia commanders on how to expand the war and raise its cost for Washington, according to the two officials, both familiar with the planning as members of the Guards, and both speaking anonymously to discuss sensitive internal deliberations.

Senior commanders from the Quds Force, the external arm of the Guards that fosters proxy militias, held virtual conference calls with commanders from Hezbollah, the Houthis and Shiite armed groups in Iraq, the officials said.

Quds Force commanders and advisers have also been working closely with the militias on the ground, according to the two officials. The Guards have tried to fill the void in Hezbollah’s ranks, which have been decimated by war with Israel, while also serving in Iraq on bases operated by Shiite militias.

A wave of U. S.-Saudi airstrikes targeted militias in Iraq early Wednesday, and Iranian media published photographs of four men killed in the attacks, all wearing the distinctive olive uniforms of the Quds Force, their coffins draped with Iran’s flag.

“We are playing a grand game of chess; the militias are Iran’s chess pieces to be moved wisely at the right time and place, for maximum impact,” Mehdi Rahmati, an analyst in Iran and an expert on the regional militias, said in a phone interview.

Aside from lobbing missiles and drones at military bases housing U. S. troops, the attacks have been calibrated to avoid direct confrontations with American or Israeli forces, which could lead to harsh retaliation against Iran, analysts said. Igniting a fire at the Saudi oil facility drew the kingdom into the war, but the Saudi response targeted Iraqi militias accused of the attack rather than Iran.

Iran mobilized its proxy forces for a variety of reasons, analysts said. First and foremost, the strategy aims to limit oil exports from the region, driving up gas prices in the United States ahead of the U. S. midterm elections and reducing revenue for Washington’s Arab allies.

Tehran senses that severe economic damage might make its neighbors more amenable to Iran’s ambition to control all traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, analysts said. About 20 percent of the world’s oil supply transited the strait before the war.

“Iran thinks that its neighbors are vulnerable,” said Afshon Ostovar, the author of a history of the Middle East in the 21st century. “They are basically just trying to twist the arm of the Saudis and gain some concessions.”

With its oil exports largely blocked in the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has been shipping much of its oil through a pipeline across the kingdom. It is then exported out of a Red Sea port and through the Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait separating Yemen from Africa.

The Houthis, who had largely sat on the sidelines after the United States and Israel attacked Iran, announced a naval blockade against Saudi shipping on July 20 and began missile and drone attacks to enforce it.

Then another, far longer route to Asia, through the Suez Canal and the Mediterranean, came under threat on Wednesday as unidentified drones hit tankers in Egypt — opening a new front. Iran rejected accusations that it was responsible.

The Houthis have their own reasons for putting pressure on their neighbor, Saudi Arabia, especially finding an end to Yemen’s long-running civil war, in which the kingdom had played a devastating role.

“They are coordinating with Iran, but they are not necessarily acting on behalf of Iran,” said Firas Maksad, the managing director for the Middle East and North Africa at Eurasia Group, a risk consultancy. “It’s a calibrated escalation and it’s part of this negotiation by fire that is ongoing between the Houthis and the Saudis.”

Another reason that Iran’s allies are attacking is more ideological, analysts said. Iran developed its proxy network with two primary goals: to help drive the United States military out of the region and inflict harm on Israel, and to use the militias as a shield against attacks on Iran itself.

Neither strategy fully worked, especially after the fall of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria, the linchpin of the axis. Hamas, too, is a mere shadow of its former self.

“Iran’s proxies are participating in the war because they, alongside Iran, are desperately trying to hold onto their claimed status as revolutionary forces against the U. S. and Israel,” said Lina Khatib, an associate fellow at Chatham House, a London research group. Absent their original intent, the militias have instead become “a force for disruption,” she said.

Hezbollah, once Iran’s powerful partner on Israel’s doorstep, feels newly threatened by an Israeli-Lebanese peace deal, brokered by Washington in June, that includes the unlikely goal of disarming the militia.

The group has been attempting to rebuild after war with Israel, which assassinated the militia’s longtime leader and killed dozens of top commanders and thousands of foot soldiers.

Iran has tried to buttress those efforts, deploying Revolutionary Guards commanders to serve directly on Hezbollah’s leadership council, according to both Lebanese government officials and analysts. Senior Lebanese officials have expressed surprise that Iranian commanders turned out to be longstanding residents of buildings that Israel attacked far from traditional Hezbollah strongholds.

“One of the unintended consequences of destroying or degrading Hezbollah’s leadership is that the I. R. G. C. is now even more effectively in control of Hezbollah and its actions,” Mr. Maksad said.

Similar conditions hold true for Iraq, where a dizzying patchwork of militias emerged after the American invasion in 2003. At the urging of Washington, Iraq has been incorporating militias into its armed forces, but some smaller groups are resisting.

Unleashing Hezbollah and the Iraqi militias is an effort by Iran to thwart such American efforts. “They see that their footprint is diminishing, and they want to reaffirm their presence in the region and their regional role,” said Randa Slim, the head of the Middle East program for the Stimson Center in Washington.

Although the various militias have their own reasons for attacking, there is a unity of purpose, analysts said — and a shared sense that Mr. Trump and his Arab allies are reluctant to pursue war, leaving Tehran and its proxies with an opportunity.

“They see a moment,” Mr. Ostovar said. “They smell blood in the water, and they are pushing their advantage.”

Hwaida Saad contributed reporting.

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.

Neil MacFarquhar has been a Times reporter since 1995, writing about a range of topics from war to politics to the arts, both internationally and in the United States.

The New York Times August 01, 2026

The president vowed to push for the payout fund if Senate Republicans fail to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general, reigniting a dispute over the settlement.

By Mark Walker

President Trump said on Saturday that he would revive a proposal for a $1.8 billion so-called anti-weaponization fund that would compensate his supporters if the Senate does not confirm his nominee for attorney general.

The administration had backed off plans to establish such a fund in June as it was criticized as a scheme to reward political allies with taxpayers’ dollars.

But in a social media post, Mr. Trump reacted to skepticism about his nomination of Todd Blanche, his former defense lawyer, to be attorney general, saying that he would keep Mr. Blanche as the acting attorney general if the Senate failed to confirm him, and added that he would “push hard” to pass legislation creating the fund.

“Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media.

Senators have delayed an important vote on Mr. Blanche’s nomination, partly because of the anti-weaponization fund proposal, which embodies the president’s claims that his supporters, including those who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, have been unfairly prosecuted.

Senators Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, and John Cornyn, Republican of Texas, have stalled the nomination of Mr. Blanche from advancing.

The lawmakers — who are both leaving office at the end of their terms — are withholding their support until the White House agrees in writing to shelve a tax provision tied to a settlement that Mr. Blanche brokered to resolve Mr. Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Mr. Trump’s suit faulted the I. R. S. for a leak of his tax returns in 2019.

Senator Cornyn, who lost his Republican primary to the Trump-backed candidate Ken Paxton earlier this year, had not publicly commented about Mr. Trump’s post. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Responding to Mr. Trump’s comments on Saturday, Senator Tillis, who is retiring, said that the president “clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against.”

“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal,” Mr. Tillis wrote on social media.

The White House did not immediately respond on Saturday to a request for comment elaborating on any plans behind Mr. Trump’s post.

The Justice Department announced the settlement in May in the case over the disclosure of Mr. Trump’s tax returns.

The agreement proposed creating the compensation fund for his aggrieved supporters. It also included a tax provision shielding Mr. Trump and his relatives from audits over past tax years.

Mr. Blanche said in June that he would abandon the compensation fund but would leave the tax provision in place. That provision has remained one of the chief points of disagreement in his confirmation.

Senator Cornyn has said that he has not received written assurances that the tax provision would not apply to future tax liabilities or be expanded to cover more people.

On Wednesday, Senator Charles E. Grassley, the Iowa Republican who leads the committee considering Mr. Blanche’s nomination, postponed a vote to allow negotiations to continue and to try to secure enough support for the confirmation.

His office had not issued comment on the latest development.

Mark Walker is a Times reporter who covers breaking news and culture.

Israel Says It Killed Several Hezbollah Members on Key Lebanon Hilltop

The New York Times August 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The confrontation, over a strategic ridge in southern Lebanon, challenged a fragile cease-fire between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group.

By Pranav Baskar

The Israeli military said on Saturday that it had killed several Hezbollah members overnight on a strategic ridge in southern Lebanon, challenging a fragile cease-fire between Israel and the Iran-backed militant group.

The encounter happened in the area of the Ali al-Taher ridge, a hilltop about six miles from the Israeli border where violence has flared in recent days. The Israeli military said it had “struck” Hezbollah fighters in an Israeli-occupied area where its soldiers were operating, and that an Israeli soldier was wounded.

Hezbollah did not immediately address Israel’s claim.

A cease-fire between Israel and Hezbollah has barely held in recent weeks, just as Israel and Lebanon have worked to implement a separate, U. S.-brokered agreement to end months of fighting. That deal calls for Israel to gradually withdraw from territory in southern Lebanon.

Hezbollah has rejected the deal, saying it effectively allowed Israel’s continued presence in southern Lebanon and that the group would not give up its weapons without an Israeli withdrawal.

Clashes have persisted in southern Lebanon, with daily reports of airstrikes, artillery shelling, demolitions and sonic grenades, according to the United Nations. But Saturday was the first time Israel announced deaths from the fighting since July 15, raising fears of a renewed escalation.

The latest conflict between Hezbollah and Israel erupted on March 2, after the group attacked Israel in solidarity with Iran following the U. S.-Israeli strikes that began the war with Iran. The fighting has killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon, and Israel now occupies large swaths of the country’s south. Israeli officials say at least four Israeli civilians and more than 30 soldiers have been killed.

In recent months, the Ali al-Taher ridge has become one of the most strategically significant areas in the conflict. Lebanese and Israeli officials say they believe Hezbollah has established one of its largest underground installations beneath the ridge. Israel says the complex has for years served as a crucial command center for planning and launching attacks against its territory.

This week, the Israeli military said, Hezbollah launched an explosive drone at one of its vehicles on the ridge. A Hezbollah spokesman said the group did not claim responsibility for an operation in the area, and accused Israel of using “false pretexts” to continue attacks in Lebanon.

The area is about three miles north of Beaufort, a Crusader castle that Israel said it captured on May 31. On Friday, Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, and Israel Katz, the defense minister, said in a joint statement that the military had destroyed what it called Hezbollah’s “terrorist tunnels” in the area, which they claimed formed a key part of the group’s plan to infiltrate communities in northern Israel.

As recently as May, the ridge was beyond the area that Israel had occupied several miles inside southern Lebanon. Israel marks the boundary of this zone with a yellow line on its maps and views anyone within it as a legitimate military target. In June, however, Israel redrew those boundaries, extending the yellow line to include the ridge.

The U. S.-brokered agreement between Israel and Lebanon calls for the Lebanese Armed Forces to move in and secure the areas as Israel slowly withdraws, and to facilitate the return of displaced residents. Officials are expected to discuss more details in Rome this week.

The first areas slated for implementation, described as “pilot zones,” are intended to test the broader agreement reached last month. Three villages have been designated in the first phase of the withdrawal plan.

But the framework has been criticized in Lebanon because it sets no fixed timetable for Israel’s withdrawal, and is tied to the Lebanese government’s tentative efforts to disarm Hezbollah, a goal it has so far pursued in vain.

Abdi Latif Dahir and Hwaida Saad contributed reporting.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

Scope of Hacks on U. S. Water Supply Widens as Evidence Points to Iran

The New York Times August 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Michigan and Minnesota are among at least seven states coping with cyberattacks aimed at disrupting water systems nationwide.

By Dustin Volz and Ernesto Londoño

Dustin Volz covers cybersecurity and intelligence in Washington. Ernesto Londoño is a national correspondent based in St. Paul, Minn.

The scope of cyberattacks on U. S. water systems has grown to include at least seven states and may be far wider, officials and experts warned, as the authorities raced to safeguard the nation’s water supply against an assault that increasingly appeared to be the work of Iran.

While there were no indications that any water supply had been altered or made unsafe to drink, state and local officials throughout the country were on high alert for potential problems in vulnerable computers that are commonly used to monitor and adjust water quality, including chemical-treatment levels and water pressure. Minnesota first publicly reported the attacks, and now Michigan says its systems have also been targeted.

The attack has little precedent, experts said, but has long been the stuff of nightmares and sensationalized Hollywood thrillers: an apparent cyberattack by a foreign power during a time of war that could, at least in theory, jeopardize the health and safety of Americans.

Officials cautioned that they had not definitively determined that Iran was responsible for the attack and that the investigation was still preliminary. But they said Iran had stepped up cyberattacks since the U. S. and Israel launched a war against the country five months ago, and had previously targeted similar water systems and other critical infrastructure in the U. S. There seemed no financial motive, making a criminal attack less likely.

Despite growing concerns, President Trump sought to downplay the matter on Friday by blaming Minnesota — which was early to spot and report the recent surge in malicious hacking activity, helping to prompt other states to probe their own water systems — for suffering intrusions his own intelligence agencies believe were highly likely carried out by Iran, officials familiar with the assessment said.

“I think Minnesota is behind it,” Mr. Trump said on Friday in response to a reporter’s question about Iran’s possible involvement, which The New York Times earlier reported. “I don’t think there was an Iranian cyberattack.”

The state’s Democratic governor, Tim Walz, dismissed the accusation, warning in a social media post that this “is what modern warfare looks like.”

After Mr. Trump’s remarks, federal officials privately said Iran remains the top suspect but that the assessment remained preliminary and had not yet established definitive forensic proof. That is not unusual in complex cyber-investigations, which can often take months to reach authoritative conclusions, if at all.

Nate George, the mayor of Braham, a small city north of Minneapolis that was among those affected by the cyberattack, said federal and local officials had little doubt about the likely culprit.

“We’re getting bits and pieces of information from the state of Minnesota and the F. B. I.,” he said in an interview on Friday afternoon. “They are pretty sure it’s Iranian actors” but are reluctant to say so publicly, he added. A memo sent by an industry group that shares cyberthreat information among water utilities that was obtained by Wired magazine said the attacks aligned with hacking activity being conducted by Iran-affiliated actors.

Mr. George, a Republican who is running for state auditor, said he had heard the president’s remarks casting doubt on Iranian culpability. He said that the president was “entitled to his opinion,” but that it is incumbent on state officials to help cities harden their defenses against cyberattacks.

Minnesota was not the only state to suffer intrusions. In a public advisory published late Thursday, after the Times report, the F. B. I. and the Environmental Protection Agency said that since Monday “at least seven states have reported incidents to the F. B. I., and some of that activity degraded water operations.”

Officials have declined to say which states have been affected, but a spokesman for the Michigan state government confirmed that his state’s system was attacked.

“We received a small number of reports from Michigan communities indicating activity consistent with what federal agencies described,” Dale George, the spokesman, said in an email. He added that all systems affected continued to operate safely, and that there were “no known impacts that posed a public health concern.”

Mr. George later said that nine municipal water systems in Michigan had reported issues. Earlier in the week, Minnesota reported hackers were spotted targeting roughly three dozen municipalities.

Alex Orleans, a former U. S. government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, said Tehran had been engaging in a wide variety of hacking operations against U. S., Israeli and Middle Eastern targets since the start of the war in February. But the intrusions into the U. S. water systems appeared to be a significant escalation.

“What’s unprecedented here is that we’re seeing direct, tangible effects to live industrial control systems inside U. S. critical infrastructure,” said Mr. Orleans, who is now the chief of threat intelligence at Sublime Security, an email protection company.

The U. S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, in an advisory issued Thursday, said the hackers were “targeting water entities of all sizes” and recommended facilities unplug vulnerable controllers from the internet. The hacking activity, it added, had “resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations.”

The agency has for months been warning the public that Iran may seek to compromise water utilities and other critical infrastructure.

Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said the hackers were likely engaging in opportunistic behavior rather than selecting specific cities and towns to infiltrate. That means that potentially any facility using the vulnerable internet-connected operational systems was at risk.

Iran, Mr. Orleans said, was likely looking to infiltrate as many victims networks as possible throughout the states before they can protect against “the opportunistic tradecraft that the U. S. government has offered multiple, explicit warnings about.”

Mr. George, the mayor in Minnesota, said city officials had received guidance on how to patch water systems that had been affected and how to bolster defenses against attacks Iranian hackers are capable of carrying out.

While manual workarounds are keeping water flowing for now, he said the attack highlighted the rudimentary nature of critical infrastructure in many small cities.

“I think the troubling thing on the horizon is how do we move forward to a more secure system,” Mr. George said.

“IT infrastructure upgrades are very costly and we are a very small municipality.”

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Ernesto Londoño is a Times reporter based in Minnesota, covering news in the Midwest and drug use and counternarcotics policy. He welcomes tips and can be reached at elondono.81 on Signal.
