Timeline of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool Saga

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump vowed to restore the Reflecting Pool, a defining feature of Washington. Months later, it is empty and closed to the public.

By Pooja Salhotra

In the months since President Trump vowed to restore the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, the century-old landmark has been plagued with problems, from bright green algae to peeling paint.

The saga began when the administration awarded no-bid contracts for the multimillion dollar project in an effort to complete renovations by the country’s 250th birthday celebrations on July 4. When problems surfaced, President Trump and his administration — without evidence — blamed “vandals,” accusing individuals of slashing the pool with a knife or razors “in the dead of night” and dumping fertilizer into the shallow water to promote algae growth.

Federal prosecutors charged at least four people with damaging the pool, including a former Olympian who faced a felony charge punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Then, in a stunning reversal, prosecutors dismissed that charge and said the damage was the result of a “botched” installation by federal contractors.

The pool remains empty. Here is how we got here.

On April 3, a Virginia firm called Atlantic Industrial Coatings was hired to repair leaking joints between the pool’s concrete slabs, waterproof the pool’s bottom and paint it a color that Mr. Trump called “American flag blue.” The firm was awarded a no-bid contract, bypassing the requirement to seek competing offers through a mechanism that contracting experts called highly unusual and typically reserved for desperate cases where work must start immediately to protect lives.

Mr. Trump at first said he chose the firm, which had never previously held a federal contract, because it had repaired a pool at one of his golf clubs. He later reversed himself and said he did not know the firm. The company added a 20 percent profit margin to the its bill, which has totaled $14.7 million so far.

Greenwater Services of Brookfield, Ohio, was awarded a $1.7 million no-bid contract to install a water purification system meant to combat algae. The owner of that firm is a donor to Mr. Trump and a neighbor to Mar-a-Lago, the president’s private club in Florida.

Mr. Trump’s motorcade drove over the drained, coated reflecting pool as he surveyed the state of the renovations.

Mr. Trump showed reporters the reflecting pool being filled with water.

Days after the project to coat the base of the pool blue was completed, clumps of algae appeared on the surface, giving it a green hue. Initially, a spokeswoman for the Interior Department said the algae was “residual” and came from supply lines that sat dormant during the renovations.

But contributing to the algae bloom was the removal of temporary water-purification devices called nanobubblers, enormous machines that were brought in to clear the pool. These devices, which infused the water with tiny bubbles of ozone gas to kill algae and bacteria, were removed during the time that a promotional event connected to an Ultimate Fighting Championship event at the White House was planned at the Lincoln Memorial on June 12.

Once the algae began growing, it proved difficult to eliminate, even with the nanobubblers back online. Park Service workers tried dumping jugs of hydrogen peroxide into the water to clear the algae more quickly. But the peroxide largely dissolved before it could reach the large clumps in the middle of the basin. The algae remained for about a week before the water became clear again.

A more discreet water purification system is now being used.

On June 9, Park Service workers discovered holes, cracks and peeling caulking in parts of the pool, along with cuts in sections of foam, according to government documents. A few days later, they also noticed that chunks of blue sealant that covered the bottom of the pool were peeling and floating to the surface.

David Carter Hearn, a three-time Olympian who said he stopped at the pool on June 19 to take a look, was arrested after he reached down to touch a strip of the peeling blue paint. Mr. Hearn was charged with “destruction of property $1,000 or more.” His lawyers called the charges “outrageous” and said, “This indictment reflects the administration’s effort to shift blame for their own failures.”

Three other people were charged with misdemeanors in connection with destroying the pool. According to court records, the defendants were observed peeling and removing pieces of paint from the Reflecting Pool.

The cause of the cuts was unclear, but on June 23, Mr. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that six people had been arrested for damaging the pool. He said there was a “350 foot gash, made by a very sharp knife or razors.” He also blamed the algae blooms on “vandals,” who he said had dumped fertilizer into the pool to fuel their growth.

While Mr. Trump squarely pointed blame on vandals, he provided no evidence to support the assertion, and experts said that the problems could have been caused by the pool’s quick overhaul.

On July 10, crews were observed draining the pool again to complete more renovations. Officials said firework debris from July 4 celebrations would be cleared and the peeling coating would be addressed.

On Friday, the U. S. attorney in Washington, Jeanine Pirro, said she was seeking to dismiss the charge against Mr. Hearn because prosecutors had been misled by the Interior Department about the source of the damage to the pool.

Ms. Pirro said that the pool’s blue coating had in fact started to peel within two days of the project’s completion, and that the Interior Department kept that information from prosecutors and instead told them that “nearly all of the damage” was done by vandals. Ms. Pirro blamed the damage on a “flawed installation” and “the rush to complete the project” by July 4.

After Ms. Pirro moved to drop the charge, Mr. Trump doubled down, saying in a Truth Social post that most of the damage was caused by vandals. “I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro,” he wrote. “I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM.”

Recently, the pool was fenced off and drained so the lining could be inspected and repaired. It will remain closed until Aug. 10, according to a court filing from the Interior Department.

Pooja Salhotra covers breaking news across the United States.

Justice Dept. Subpoenas Times Freelancer in Effort to Identify Sources

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A previously undisclosed subpoena, involving reporting on a failed SEAL Team 6 mission in North Korea, reflects the government’s expanding campaign to investigate leaks of secrets.

By Devlin Barrett

Reporting from Washington

A freelance reporter has been fighting a subpoena from the Trump administration seeking to force him to reveal his sources for a New York Times article about a failed top secret mission in North Korea, according to people familiar with the matter.

The subpoena, which has not been previously disclosed, reflects the administration’s intensifying campaign to investigate leaks of government secrets by pressuring reporters to divulge their sources. Until President Trump began his second term, federal subpoenas to reporters were exceedingly rare.

In February, F. B. I. agents showed up at the New York home of the reporter, Matthew Cole, to deliver the grand jury subpoena, which was issued by prosecutors in Newport News, Va., according to the people familiar with the matter, who described the private conversations on the condition of anonymity.

The investigators are seeking his testimony about two years’ worth of information about Mr. Cole’s contacts and conversations, as they try to identify his sources for the article about the operation in North Korea, the people familiar with the matter said. It is unclear if the administration has also sought Mr. Cole’s phone and email data, as it has done in other cases.

Mr. Cole’s lawyer, David A. O’Neil, who has also represented The Times in a separate fight with the administration over subpoenas about its coverage of Air Force One, said in a statement that Mr. Cole “has dedicated his professional life to bringing official misconduct to light and informing the public about the workings of its government.” His client, he added, “will not be intimidated from continuing that important work. He will defend press freedom and the First Amendment from this administration’s brazen attacks on journalists, and he will honor his commitment to his sources.”

The Times is providing a legal defense to Mr. Cole.

The Justice Department declined to comment on the specific investigation, but said in a statement that it would use all available legal tools to “uncover those who unlawfully disclose national defense information.”

In the months since Mr. Cole’s subpoena, The Times, The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post have faced similar subpoenas seeking information about their reporting. The news organizations have resisted, and judges have voiced skepticism about the government’s efforts, prompting the administration to back down in those cases.

However, the Justice Department has so far refused to withdraw its subpoena of Mr. Cole, despite his efforts to challenge it.

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesman for The Times, said in a statement that the subpoena to Mr. Cole was “part of the government’s escalating attacks on journalists, which should concern all Americans.” He added that the demand to disclose Mr. Cole’s sources “is another brazen and illegal attack from the administration designed to deny the public information of vital importance.”

Last fall, Mr. Cole, along with a staff reporter for The Times, Dave Philipps, revealed the details of a Navy SEAL Team 6 mission in 2019 that went awry. The article described how the SEAL members killed two or three unarmed North Koreans who appeared to have stumbled upon the mission, a classified operation to plant a secret eavesdropping device near the country’s coastline. The Times’s account, published in September, drew on interviews with two dozen people.

The article also noted that the Trump administration did not notify key members of Congress who oversee intelligence operations, before or after the mission, an omission that may have violated the law.

The Justice Department has not subpoenaed Mr. Philipps, according to people familiar with the matter. He declined to comment.

Mr. Cole disclosed more details of his reporting on his Substack newsletter, stating that despite learning about the mission in 2023, he waited for months before making calls to find out more given the sensitive nature of the reporting.

Mr. Cole is also the author of “Princes and Thieves,” a coming book about the finances and global entanglements of President Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and “Code Over Country: The Tragedy and Corruption of SEAL Team Six,” a 2022 book about the elite Navy unit.

When F. B. I. agents tried to serve Mr. Cole with a subpoena at his New York City apartment in February, he was not home at the time, according to the people familiar with the matter. The subpoena was eventually delivered to his lawyer.

The Justice Department’s policies on leak investigations can change between administrations, and in 2025, it loosened restraints on such inquiries. The new guidance, however, still labels subpoenas to reporters a “last resort.” But in Mr. Trump’s second term, the department has rushed to issue such demands, sometimes just days after the articles in question were published.

In March, the Trump administration demanded records from reporters at The Wall Street Journal, seeking to identify their sources for an article published Feb. 23 that described internal discussions in the administration about the risks of a war with Iran.

The Justice Department also subpoenaed a Washington Post reporter over coverage of U. S. military operations in Venezuela, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The Post and Journal challenged the subpoenas under seal, leading to monthslong court battles in Virginia. In June, the administration withdrew the subpoenas after the federal judge overseeing the dispute indicated she was likely to quash them, according to people familiar with the matter.

In January, federal agents executed a search warrant at the home of another Post reporter, seizing her phone, computers and a smartwatch, as part of a separate, continuing leak investigation and prosecution.

In early July, the administration sought to determine the sources behind The Times’s reporting about the new Air Force One, a 747 jet that was a gift from Qatar.

Two days after The Times reported that Mr. Trump did not fly out of Turkey on the plane as a security precaution and that it did not have all the features of the older jet, F. B. I. agents delivered subpoenas to three of the reporters who wrote the articles.

The administration also demanded phone companies turn over the reporters’ phone records, as well as the phone records of two of the reporters’ wives and of one reporter’s mother.

The Times sought to quash the subpoenas, arguing that they were a dangerous attack on press freedom.

At a hearing last week in federal court in Manhattan, a judge sharply criticized prosecutors at the U. S. attorney’s office for apparently failing to follow the law and the department’s internal rules for conducting leak investigations.

Prosecutors denied intentionally flouting the law or regulations, but admitted making mistakes, which they attributed to not knowing the relevant case law before they demanded the reporters’ data. The judge in that case, Arun Subramanian, has ordered the Justice Department to turn over internal emails leading up to those actions.

Under pressure from the judge, the Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas of the Times journalists involved in the Air Force One reporting, but said it would continue to investigate, leaving open the possibility that it might revisit the subpoenas.

Devlin Barrett covers the Justice Department and the F. B. I. for The Times.

She Voted for a Justice Who Overturned Roe. Now it Haunts Her on the Trail.

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Senator Susan Collins, who supports abortion rights, endorsed Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination for the Supreme Court. It has emerged as a major issue in her campaign for re-election.

Senator Susan Collins, who supports abortion rights, endorsed Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination for the Supreme Court. It has emerged as a major issue in her campaign for re-election.

Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

Supported by

By Lisa Lerer and Beth Reinhard

Of the more than 10,000 votes cast by Senator Susan Collins of Maine, there is one that has shadowed her like no other as she runs for a sixth term.

On Oct. 6, 2018, Ms. Collins, one of only two Senate Republicans who support abortion rights, cast a deciding vote to confirm Brett M. Kavanaugh to the U. S. Supreme Court. Four years later, Justice Kavanaugh voted with the conservative majority to overturn Roe v. Wade, which had guaranteed a constitutional right to abortion for nearly half a century.

The vote cut against her well-cultivated reputation as a moderate Republican who is unafraid to break ranks. It also put her at odds with abortion rights activists, who had previously backed her campaigns, and with advocates for victims of sexual violence, who rallied behind a woman who accused Mr. Kavanaugh of sexual assault, an allegation he denied.

Now, Ms. Collins’s support for Justice Kavanaugh has become a major issue in her first re-election campaign since Roe was overturned, a race that could swing control of the Senate. The 2018 vote has emerged as a character test of Ms. Collins for Maine voters: Some consider her a principled lawmaker taking tough votes, while others see a calculating politician determined to keep her job.

Publicly, Ms. Collins appears unbowed. “I do not regret that vote,” she told reporters in Portland in June. She went even further after an event at a fire station in Randolph, Maine, this month.

“I would vote for him again, yes,” she said, according to audio acquired by an operative for American Bridge, a major Democratic super PAC.

But people who interacted with her during the Kavanaugh hearings say Ms. Collins still harbors frustrations about the continued backlash after a confirmation process she described in 2018 as “more like a caricature of a gutter-level political campaign.”

Even as she was accused of capitulating to the demands of her party and President Trump, Ms. Collins believed she took the more politically difficult vote while representing a Democratic-leaning state, she told a confidant at the time. And in the years since, she has appeared to hold grudges against people who criticized her vote.

“She takes all of it very personally,” said Dana Singiser, a former Planned Parenthood vice president, who raised concerns about Judge Kavanaugh with Ms. Collins during his confirmation process. “For us, it’s not really personal, it’s just about our mission. That was an abortion-defining vote.”

This account is based on interviews with more than two dozen former aides, Senate colleagues, activists and others involved in the confirmation process. Some spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

Ms. Collins declined an interview request from The New York Times. Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins, dismissed criticism of the senator’s vote as driven by “hyperpartisan voices.”

“Senator Collins fully and honestly explained her decision in the days before and the years that followed Justice Kavanaugh’s nomination,” she said.

Ms. Kernen also drew a contrast between the senator, who she said “has always been pro-choice,” and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, who opposed abortion as a state lawmaker until about a decade ago. He later helped enact a Maine law that allows abortion at any stage of pregnancy, as long as a doctor deems it necessary — one of the most permissive in the country.

Ms. Collins’s allies say she made a principled decision to back Judge Kavanaugh after extensive research, including hours of conversations with him, scrutiny of his work and feedback from thousands of constituents. In the end, they say, her vote came down to a simple calculation: She believed Judge Kavanaugh when he said he would respect precedent, which she interpreted to mean that he would leave Roe v. Wade largely intact. And she did not believe Christine Blasey Ford, the California professor who said he sexually assaulted her when they were in high school.

“She did her job,” said Mike Davis, who helped spearhead Justice Kavanaugh’s confirmation as chief nominations counsel for the Senate Judiciary Committee’s chairman. “She did her homework.”

But what she saw as a conscientious vote provoked years of protests from Capitol Hill to her home in Maine. As the years progressed, she grew irritated by liberals continuing to vilify her support for Justice Kavanaugh while failing to acknowledge her support for the three justices nominated by Democratic presidents, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

“It is a major source of frustration for Senator Collins that while there seems to be an endless discussion of the Kavanaugh confirmation, there is never any mention that she is the only Republican senator to have voted to confirm all three,” said Stephen Diamond, a Maine attorney who helped her prepare for the Kavanaugh confirmation hearing.

Ms. Kernen defended Ms. Collins’s record on abortion rights, noting that a Maine affiliate of Planned Parenthood commended her in 2025 for opposing Republican efforts to defund the organization. And she pointed to legislation that Ms. Collins introduced in 2022 that she said would codify abortion rights into federal law. But the senator voted against a broader Democratic measure preferred by advocates for abortion rights, saying it was championed by “far-left activists.”

Kay Rand, who served as chief of staff for Senator Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the vote shifted views of Ms. Collins in Maine, even as she handily won re-election in 2020.

“It’s just never been the same for her since the Kavanaugh vote,” said Ms. Rand, who worked for Mr. King during the Kavanaugh hearings. “It was a lightning rod, a galvanizing issue.”

Even before President Trump unveiled his pick to replace retiring Justice Anthony Kennedy on the Supreme Court, Ms. Collins issued a clear litmus test: She would not support any judge who demonstrated “hostility” to Roe v. Wade.

With Judge Kavanaugh, who sat on a federal appeals court and had worked in the George W. Bush White House, the Trump administration believed it had found a nominee who could satisfy Ms. Collins, a pivotal swing vote at a time when Republicans held a single-seat majority.

The nomination was announced in July 2018, and Ms. Collins began preparing for a fraught confirmation process. Her approach, she has said, is to defer to the White House on judicial selections as long as the nominees are qualified and within the legal mainstream.

She put together a team of five lawyers to help her learn all she could about the nominee, recalled Mr. Diamond, who had previously served as Ms. Collins’s legislative director and joined the team. The nonpartisan Congressional Research Service offered 10 hours of briefings covering Judge Kavanaugh’s significant opinions, speeches and articles. Ms. Collins attended all the sessions, Mr. Diamond said.

She also had a two-hour meeting in her Capitol Hill office with the nominee himself. When she emerged, Ms. Collins told reporters they had discussed abortion cases “at length,” and that Mr. Kavanaugh said he agreed with Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who said during his 2005 confirmation hearings that he regarded Roe as “settled law.”

Mr. Diamond left the meeting with a similar impression.

“I am pro-choice and I came away with the conclusion that there was a reasonable possibility that he would not overturn Roe, though maybe modify it around the edges,” he said.

Abortion rights advocates viewed the senator’s statements as naïve or willfully ignorant. A year earlier, Judge Kavanaugh had dissented from a high-profile decision that allowed a 17-year-old detainee in an immigration facility to receive an abortion, a notable position given his limited record on the issue. He argued that the decision created a new right for “immediate abortion on demand,” adopting the political language of the anti-abortion movement.

The day after her meeting with Judge Kavanaugh, Ms. Collins reassured Julia McDonald, a Maine physician who performed abortions, that she had asked the nominee “hard questions” about his view of Roe and she believed his commitment to stare decisis, the legal doctrine that directs courts to follow precedent-setting cases.

“Those of us in that meeting pushed back hard, asking how she could believe that from a man with his record,” said Dr. McDonald, who met with Ms. Collins in her office alongside two patients, another doctor and a Planned Parenthood representative. “She was not interested in hearing our concerns. It seemed very clear that she had made up her mind.”

At times, Ms. Collins seemed focused on smaller issues. In two meetings with Planned Parenthood leaders, she complained that Colby College students had distracted from her May commencement address — before Judge Kavanaugh was even nominated — by wearing “I stand with Planned Parenthood” stickers, according to people present in the meetings.

The activists were taken aback by the senator’s remarks, given the stakes of the confirmation fight. To the Planned Parenthood leaders, the stickers were not antagonistic: Less than a year earlier, the organization had honored Ms. Collins.

By early September 2018, Ms. Collins was feeling the brunt of the escalating pressure on the few undecided senators. Agitated and sometimes crude callers besieged her offices. About 3,000 coat hangers arrived by mail, stark reminders of the time before Roe. v. Wade, when desperate women used hangers to try to end unwanted pregnancies. Protesters stood outside her home, wearing red robes and white bonnets like the characters in Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel, “The Handmaid’s Tale.”

There were also violent threats, including a fax from someone promising to slit her throat and sever her limbs if she voted for Judge Kavanaugh. One man ambushed her outside her home in Washington in the rain after she arrived from work late at night.

The Trump administration was mounting its own pressure campaign. Mr. Davis, a lawyer for the Senate Judiciary Committee, recalled warning Ms. Collins about one scenario that he said did give her pause: Judge Amy Coney Barrett, who had been promoted by abortion opponents, was likely next on the president’s shortlist.

“Judge Kavanaugh was seen as our best hope of preserving Roe,” Mr. Diamond, the former Collins staffer, said.

Then on Sept. 16, the confirmation process took a dramatic turn. The Washington Post reported that Dr. Ford had accused Judge Kavanaugh of pinning her down on a bed, groping her, and attempting to pull off her bathing suit at a high school party in the 1980s. She said he covered her mouth with his hand to muffle her screams.

Judge Kavanaugh denied what he called “false accusations.”

Ms. Collins immediately pushed for both Dr. Ford and Justice Kavanaugh to testify under oath. She told reporters she was “appalled” when the president attempted to undermine Dr. Ford on social media.

Hours after Dr. Ford’s testimony, Tamara Field, a freelance journalist from Camden, Maine, traveled with about 20 other women on an overnight bus to Washington, D. C., hoping to urge Ms. Collins in person to reject the nomination.

Sitting in Ms. Collins’s office, Ms. Field recounted being sexually assaulted on a first date just a few months earlier. Ms. Collins hugged her and thanked her for sharing her story, she said, but Ms. Field felt in her gut that the senator was leaning toward supporting Judge Kavanaugh.

Years later, she still feels betrayed.

“Susan Collins can look somebody in the eye and tell them how sorry she is that they were attacked and then vote for a man that probably in my opinion committed sexual assault,” Ms. Field said. “There’s a duplicity to her.”

As Judge Kavanaugh’s nomination advanced through the Senate Judiciary Committee, Ms. Collins joined calls from Jeff Flake, then a Republican senator of Arizona, for an F. B. I. investigation of Dr. Ford’s allegations — and a one-week delay in the confirmation process.

Mr. Flake recalled eating dinner with Senator Collins that evening, along with Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a moderate Republican from Alaska. The mood was tense.

“I know the vote was weighing on her,” said Mr. Flake, who described “massive” pressure from both sides of the political spectrum. “There were obviously death threats to me and my family and to her. This was a tough time.”

Ms. Collins continued her research, spending time in the secure room where the F. B. I.’s investigative materials into the case were stored. She contacted friends of the judge to ask if they could imagine him doing anything like this, speaking to former colleagues including former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice. George W. Bush called twice to lobby her personally.

“She put the Senate judiciary staff through the wringer,” Mr. Davis recalled. “She was in a league of her own in terms of the level of scrutiny and attention to detail.”

By the time Ms. Collins was ready to announce her decision on Oct. 5, few knew for certain what she would say. Ms. Murkowski, the only other Senate Republican who favored abortion rights, had announced she would vote against Judge Kavanaugh. So had Senator Heidi Heitkamp, a Democrat from the red state of North Dakota. The three women had kept in close contact during the process, discussing the claims, testimony and evidence.

Ms. Collins stepped behind the lectern on the Senate floor and launched into a point-by-point defense of Judge Kavanaugh.

She described the future justice as “more of a centrist.” She was confident he would uphold the Affordable Care Act’s health insurance protections for pre-existing medical conditions and the federal right to an abortion. And she was convinced he would serve as a check on presidential power.

“My fervent hope is that Brett Kavanaugh will work to lessen the divisions in the Supreme Court so that we have far fewer 5-4 decisions and so that public confidence in our judiciary and our highest court is restored,” she said.

Though Ms. Collins described Dr. Ford’s testimony as “sincere, painful and compelling,” the senator said her allegation did not meet a “more likely than not” standard.

Twenty-four hours later, she cast her vote for Justice Kavanaugh.

“I do not believe that Brett Kavanaugh was her assailant,” she said in a CNN interview that aired shortly after the vote. “I do believe that she was assaulted. I don’t know by whom. I’m not certain when.”

Lisa Banks, one of the attorneys who represented Dr. Ford, called the notion that she had misidentified her attacker “preposterous,” in a recent interview. She added, “If Senator Collins had questions or wanted to speak directly with Dr. Ford about her experience and allegations, Dr. Ford would have gladly done so.”

Ms. Collins’s fellow Republicans hailed her as a hero. Mr. Trump praised her effusively and dubbed her a “star.” Leonard Leo, the conservative megadonor credited with helping Mr. Trump build the court’s conservative majority, held a fund-raiser for Ms. Collins at his Maine home the following year.

The event drew picketers, which Ms. Collins called “just ridiculous, absolutely ridiculous,” according to a Bloomberg reporter.

Three years later, in the hours after Roe fell, protests exploded across the nation. Ms. Collins felt compelled to defend her decision-making process.

She took the unusual step of releasing private notes from her meeting with Judge Kavanaugh in which he talked about his respect for court precedent. “I feel misled,” Ms. Collins said then. Lance Dutson, a Maine Republican and a former campaign aide to Ms. Collins, said the senator should not be blamed for Justice Kavanaugh’s decision. She did her research, was transparent with her constituents and made the best decision she could at the time, he said.

“She took a Supreme Court nominee’s word,” he said. “From the information she got, she felt comfortable voting for him, and things went the other way after the fact.”

The senator’s unease over criticism of her vote lingered. In a 2021 phone conversation, she confronted a Biden administration nominee who had criticized her support for Judge Kavanaugh on social media. Ms. Collins described those posts as “nasty” and implied that the remarks disqualified the candidate for the position, according to a person familiar with the confirmation process. The nominee was later confirmed, without Ms. Collins’s vote.

The senator’s support for Justice Kavanaugh effectively ended her relationship with Planned Parenthood, the country’s largest provider of reproductive health care. In 2017, the organization had honored Ms. Collins for opposing Republican efforts to cut its funding. Three years later, it endorsed her Democratic opponent.

In 2021, as Ms. Singiser was cleaning out her desk at Planned Parenthood, she discovered an artifact of the old relationship: Posters printed before the Kavanaugh confirmation that read, “I stand with Susan Collins.”

“I thought, ‘If she does something really great we’re going to use them,’” said Ms. Singiser, who now advises reproductive rights organizations. “And then, she never did anything great for us.”

Hi, I spent weeks digging into how Susan Collins made her decision on whether to support Brett Kavanaugh for the Supreme Court with my colleague Beth Reinhard. The vote has become a Rorschach test for how some voters view Sen. Collins's character. What do you all think?

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

Beth Reinhard is an investigative reporter for The Times covering politics.

It Is Banal, Bland, Thin and Didactic. We Can’t Stop Talking About It.

The New York Times August 01, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ross Douthat

By Ross Douthat

Opinion Columnist

Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is the blockbuster that launched a million takes. The interpretations crowd my social media feed like Agamemnon’s assembled ships at Aulis. They keen in my ears like the Sirens’ seductive voices. They … OK, look, I’m just saying people have a lot of opinions about the biggest movie of the year.

And for good reason, because Nolan’s film is perfectly calibrated for the contemporary culture war. First, because its source material is a story that everybody wants to claim: woke and anti-woke, masculinists and feminists, film bros and classicists, professional defenders of Western civilization and its would-be revisers and subverters. Other classics are similarly claimed and counterclaimed, but not everyone wants ownership of “The Iliad” (too male), Jane Austen (too female), the Greek tragedies (too depressing), the New Testament (too Christian) or the plays of Shakespeare (too hard to follow the dialogue). But in life as in Homer’s epic, everyone wants a piece of Odysseus.

Then, having plucked the ripest fruit, Nolan proceeded to serve it in the blandest form. Gone is the sex and sensuality, the warring deities, the hero’s outsize ego and charisma. In their place is a story that’s very American, with tropes familiar from war movies and westerns, dialogue that belongs in a contemporary Y. A. novel and a moralism that’s at once extremely didactic and extremely general. “Civilization collapses when you violate Zeus’ law” is the teaching of Nolan’s story, and while you could imagine that Zeus’ law is some arcane instruction requiring the castration of a black heifer on the highest peak on the darkest night, it turns out to just be the golden rule applied to houseguests, dogs and Trojans.

This is a critique, but it’s also a key to the film’s cultural cachet. If you just want to like “The Odyssey,” if you just want to have a good time at the movie, the bland version still has all the good stuff — the Trojan horse! the Cyclops! a bloody homecoming! — stitched together by a director with a gift for propulsion and spectacle. If you have a great enough story, you can reduce the spice level and still satisfy millions of customers with the meal.

Then if you want to claim “The Odyssey” for your own worldview, to insist that the dominant movie of the summer is speaking directly to your concerns, the banal didacticism of Nolan’s script is unusually amenable to personalized interpretations.

I can give you a plausible reading of the movie in which its portrayal of the Bronze Age collapse is an allegory for the crisis of the liberal international order (Nolan the multicultural liberal, lamenting the cruelty of Trumpism). Or a reading in which Odysseus’ guilt over the sack of Troy is fundamentally Christian and the monsters belong to a world that awaits us if Christianity fails (Nolan the lapsed Catholic, unable to shake his religious upbringing). Or, for that matter, a populist reading in which Odysseus returns home from a hubristic Middle Eastern war to find guests abusing his hospitality who need to be cleared out (Nolan the British Burkean offering an allegory of a Europe unable to cope with immigration).

I assume the first reading is closest to the directorial intentions. But the material is thin and therefore supple, ready to be shaped by ideological desire.

Finally, if you want to critique and hate the movie (and under algorithmically driven conditions, haters are hype artists, too), the same rule applies: The banality can be interpreted for maximal dislike. Part of the fun of the “Odyssey” wars is seeing that happen in all kinds of different ways, with an original anti-woke critique of the movie, fixated on colorblind casting, giving way to left-tilting academic takedowns and then bespoke right-wing critiques riding in their wake. (Four thousand-plus words from the best-selling translator Emily Wilson in the London Review of Books on a movie she dismisses as “an entertaining way to hide from the high temperatures for a few hours,” then the pseudonymous online reactionary Bronze Age Pervert responding with 6,000-odd words on a movie he calls “undeserving of a serious intellectual, ideological or aesthetic review.”)

And here I am doing much the same thing, accusing Nolan of banality and then devoting all my column inches to his cultural achievement. So let’s give the man his due: He grasped that what this moment demanded was an adaptation of one of Western civilization’s foundational texts, reworked around the widely shared assumption that Western civilization might be finished or foredoomed, in a style that allowed everyone, fans and haters alike, to blame whatever crime or curse or group of malefactors (including Hollywood directors!) they held responsible for the doom already.

His reward will be a billion dollars in box office, a blank check for next time, and the absolute power to determine what we’ll all be arguing about in the summer of 2029.

Fair enough, but the takeaway is: Homer's is a complex story onto which all interpreters can project their concerns; Nolan's is a simplified story (plus visuals) onto which all interpreters can project their concerns. Isn't that always more or less the way the movie compares to the book?

I saw a man (Matt Damon as Odysseus) struggling with the horrors of what he had done in war. Setting that struggle in the Odyssey made perfect sense to me— a decades long war much like the ones we Americans chronically find ourselves waging but in which only a few families from our warrior caste participate. I loved it.

Nolan's Oddysey might indeed be a sanitized version of the epic, adapted for modern Western sensibilities. Or it may be one of the finest achievements of one of the few film directors who can still appeal to the monoculture. In any case, i'll take the arguing over this movie than whatever the discourse is about the latest movie based on a toy.

Ross Douthat has been an Opinion columnist for The Times since 2009. He is also the host of the Opinion podcast “Interesting Times.” He is the author, most recently, of “Believe: Why Everyone Should Be Religious.” @DouthatNYT • Facebook

Visuals Suggest U. S. Dropped 2,000-Pound Bomb on Home in Iran, Killing 3

The New York Times August 01, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

VISUAL INVESTIGATIONS

The weapon, one of the largest in the U. S.’s arsenal, struck a house in a heavily populated area, according to a Times analysis.

Crater

Image via Payam-e Ma.

The New York Times

By Christiaan TriebertSanjana Varghese and Christoph Koettl

The United States struck a family home on Iran’s Qeshm Island overnight on Thursday with a large-scale bomb, according to an analysis of videos, photos and satellite imagery by weapons experts and The New York Times. Iranian officials said the strike had killed a husband and wife and their 2-year-old son. The couple’s two other children were pulled from the rubble alive, they said.

The size of the crater and munition fragments appear to show the weapon used was a 2,000-pound bomb called a Mark-84, one of the largest conventional bombs used by the U. S. military. The location and time of the strikes are consistent with where and when the United States was operating. The evidence raises questions about what the United States was targeting and why such a large munition was used.

The strike hit a densely populated neighborhood on the island, which sits in the Strait of Hormuz in southern Iran, and appears to have been part of a flurry of attacks the United States said it had launched to retaliate against earlier strikes by Iran on a base used by American forces in Jordan.

The Times found no indication of a military site near the family’s home or any reports of military casualties from the strike, which the Iranian authorities typically announce.

Crater seen in video

Approximate

location of crater

Qeshm City

Iran

Qeshm

City

North

Still image taken from Instagram video by asin_zinlzadh_/tibin. ir. Satellite image by Airbus captured Feb. 21, 2026.

The New York Times

Roughly 20 neighboring households were displaced by the strike, Iranian officials said, and footage shows debris and damaged vehicles over 200 feet away. Additional strikes also destroyed two warehouses outside the city in the same wave of attacks, according to the visual analysis.

U. S. Central Command, which announced it had struck targets in southern Iran on Thursday morning, said it was looking into the reports of civilian casualties but did not respond to questions about the intended target, the munition used or what precautions had been taken to protect civilians.

“We are aware of the reports and looking into them,” said Capt. Tim Hawkins, a Central Command spokesman. “The U. S. military never targets civilians.”

The Times corroborated details in bystander and news footage with satellite imagery to pinpoint the location of the strike and determine the size of the crater. The strike, which occurred in the Chah-Tangu neighborhood of Qeshm City, an area of tightly clustered homes, also destroyed several structures, leaving a crater at least 30 feet wide.

“The large crater and structure damage is consistent with a Mark-84 2,000-pound bomb, which can be equipped with JDAM guidance kits,” said Trevor Ball, a former U. S. Army explosive ordnance disposal technician and an analyst at Armament Research Services, referring to kits that convert unguided bombs into GPS-guided munitions. Photos published by the Iranian media, he said, showed parts of these guidance kits, though The Times could not confirm where the fragments were recovered.

Frederic Gras, a French munitions consultant who reviewed the same imagery, also said the crater dimensions matched an air-dropped Mark-84 2,000-pound bomb. He said the bomb appeared to have detonated below the surface rather than on impact, and that the sandy ground absorbed part of the blast, directing the force downward, which limited damage in the surrounding area.

Mr. Gras also identified the metal remnant as the tail section of a JDAM guidance kit.

Weapons of this size are typically used for “buildings, rail yards and lines of communication,” according to a U. S. Army office that manages ammunition for the Pentagon. Experts say they can cause serious harm to civilians when used in heavily populated areas.

Though it remains unclear who or what the intended target in the strike may have been, international humanitarian law requires combatants to weigh the expected harm to civilians against the military advantage of a strike.

“The attacking force must take all feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm, including in its selection of munitions, times of attack and, whenever circumstances allow, by issuing effective advance warnings,” said Tom Dannenbaum, a professor of law at Stanford University.

The choice of a 2,000-pound munition in a densely populated area, he added, “is very difficult to reconcile with” that obligation.

Ahmad Nafisi, a deputy governor of Hormozgan Province, cited by Fars News, a semiofficial Iranian news agency, identified the dead as Zahra Jafari; her husband, Qeysar Jafari, a taxi driver; and their son Sina.

In a video report from Mehr News, another semiofficial Iranian news agency, a clock on a wall inside one of the ruined houses had stopped just before 3:40 a. m. local time, minutes after Central Command said it had started striking Iran that night.

The Jafaris’ two surviving children, Mohammad Reza and Mehdi, remained hospitalized but were in stable condition, Iranian officials said.

Reporting was contributed by Yeganeh Torbati. Graphics by Lazaro Gamio and Zach Levitt.

Christiaan Triebert is a Times reporter working on the Visual Investigations team, a group that combines traditional reporting with digital sleuthing and analysis of visual evidence to verify and source facts from around the world.

Sanjana Varghese is a reporter on The Times’s Visual Investigations team, specializing in the use of advanced digital techniques to analyze visual evidence.

Christoph Koettl is a Times reporter on the Visual Investigations team.

As a new film evokes his coming-of-age in this bohemian Cape Cod town, Pete Wells goes looking for the people and restaurants that shaped him.

After finding his calling in Provincetown, Mass., in the mid-1970s, Mr. Bourdain embarked on a career as a chef in New York City. Credit... Courtesy of Nancy Bourdain

Supported by

By Pete Wells

Reporting from Provincetown, Mass.

One summer day in the mid-1970s when Anthony Bourdain was a teenage dishwasher at the Flagship in Provincetown, Mass., he and the rest of the kitchen crew gathered around a window to watch their boss have a very intimate encounter with a female customer outside in the trash-bin corral. Dressed in a bridal gown, the customer had just been married and was about to have dinner with the rest of her wedding party. First, though, she was getting a little something from the chef.

History does not record whether the marriage prospered. We do know, though, what witnessing that primal scene did to Mr. Bourdain’s adolescent brain, already buzzing from the swaggering misbehavior he’d seen inside the kitchen. In that moment, he said later without elaborating, he knew he wanted to become a chef.

Mr. Bourdain came to Cape Cod that summer with no job and few ambitions other than hanging out and getting high. By the end of the season he had found, possibly for the first time, something he wanted to aspire to.

This discovery is the theme of “Tony,” a feature film directed by Matt Johnson that opens in theaters on Aug. 7. The movie, set in Provincetown, takes liberties with what really happened, as biopics do. Its focus is squarely on the kitchen rather than the ways his three summers there shaped the sensibility he expressed in the 2000 memoir that made him a media star, “Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly,” and the television shows that followed.

To get a clearer picture, I went to Provincetown this month, following the Bourdain trail as many fans have done during his life and after his death by suicide, in 2018, at 61.

No doubt there are Asian and African villages where Mr. Bourdain, traveling with his camera crew, stayed for less time but is remembered in more detail by more people. But I still found people who knew him in Provincetown, and it was still possible to see the place where his first career began and his next one may have started to percolate.

Michael Cunningham, the novelist and a part-time local, recently called Provincetown “one of relatively few places in America that not only tolerates eccentricity but prefers it.”

This was even more true in the 1970s, when the town floated on cultural tides far from mainstream American currents. Except the Portuguese-speaking Azorean fishermen, who were there for the fish, almost everybody came for what the town didn’t have: rules, malls, two-car garages, stringent morality and a cost of living likely to interfere with personal desires.

Provincetown’s patchwork social fabric came together at places like Piggy’s, where Norman Mailer and Robert Motherwell shared the dance floor with local characters. Apartments and cottages all over town could be rented on the cheap.

Living a marginal existence was easy. In a sense, the town was nothing but margins. It was a safe harbor for poets, artists, drifters, clamdiggers, gay men, lesbians, drag queens, hippies and dropouts of all kinds. There was even room for students who wanted to try on a new personality before the fall semester, like Mr. Bourdain, who seemed to be making a concerted effort to flunk out of Vassar College.

The Tony of “Tony,” played by Dominic Sessa, stumbles onshore lovesick and alone, in pursuit of a girl named Nancy. In real life, Mr. Bourdain rolled into town with a pack of pals that included Nancy Putkoski, who had been his girlfriend on and off for some time. (They married in 1985 and divorced 20 years later.)

“They were high school sweethearts,” recalled John Yingling, the founder of Spiritus Pizza, as he sat on a bench looking at summer crowds parading down Commercial Street, the town’s main drag.

Spiritus was the hub of Mr. Bourdain’s social wheel. Mr. Yingling’s sister went to Vassar, too, and she began bringing her circle with her on summer trips to Provincetown. Nancy, who brought Mr. Bourdain along for three summers, worked at Spiritus.

She was a great favorite there. Mr. Bourdain was another story. With a troublemaker’s grin, curly long hair and the torso of a snake, he looked like the singer in a band that a college station in Boston might have played late at night.

“He was a pain-in-the-ass kid around here, to me, a lot of times,” Mr. Yingling said.

There must have been moments when Mr. Bourdain’s roommates shared the feeling. They had jobs. He did not. They paid the rent on a cottage. He slept there.

“We all went to the beaches and ponds each morning, smoked pot, sniffed a little coke, dropped acid and sunbathed nude, as well as indulging in other healthy teenage activities,” he wrote in “Kitchen Confidential.”

His idyllic freeloading ended one night when a roommate came home from her job at the Flagship in a bad mood. The dishwasher hadn’t turned up, and dinner service had resembled a typhoon out of “Moby-Dick.” As she later relayed it to Mr. Yingling, her conversation with Mr. Bourdain went like this:

“I hate the restaurant business. But you know who our new dishwasher is?”

“No, who?”

“You!”

The next day, Mr. Bourdain tied on an apron. “And he never turned back,” Mr. Yingling said.

Now a private home, the Flagship sat in a long, skinny, shingled building that juts out past the sea wall on pilings. The one detail said to survive is the bar, which was built out of an old, scarred wooden dory. I tried everything short of breaking and entering to get a look at it. I failed.

Inside the Flagship, which went by the alias the Dreadnaught in “Kitchen Confidential,” the cooks were busy frying seafood and broiling chops and steaks.

Mr. Bourdain’s unruly soul seemed to find purpose and order in the channeled mania of the kitchen. He became, as he later told The Guardian, more than happy — “in fact, intensely satisfied.” When he moved from the dish sink to the salad station, the deep fryer and finally, for a few late-season shifts, the fearsome broiler, “I was overjoyed,” he said.

As part of the crew, Mr. Bourdain settled into one of Provincetown’s many margins. He also observed it, studying the mores of kitchen society with an anthropologist’s eye while his body rode its adrenaline highs. Years later, when he wrote about the life, he sounded like Margaret Mead with a sense of humor and a backpack full of amphetamines.

The effect was galvanic, said Adam Platt, the former restaurant critic for New York magazine, “similar to Martin Luther pounding his theses on the church door.” Our current obsession with what goes on backstage at restaurants — the whole teeming underworld of calloused hands, burn-scarred forearms and raging personality disorders — began then. It’s a straight line from “The Bear” back to “Kitchen Confidential.”

Before Mr. Bourdain died, when the lawless ways of restaurant kitchens came under fire for fostering serious physical and sexual abuse, he said he regretted valorizing that culture. He also came to a less celebratory perspective on drug use in Provincetown restaurants, which was notorious, even by the standards of the ’70s.

“Many of our friends from those days didn’t make it,” he said during a conversation with Mr. Yingling when he revisited Massachusetts in 2014 for his TV series “Parts Unknown.” He talked in that episode about his own heroin use and an epidemic of the drug elsewhere in the state.

In that first summer, though, he saw nothing but upside in the pirate’s life.

The next spring, he came back to the Flagship to apply again for his post at the broiler. Unfortunately for him, the place had a new owner: Ciriaco Cozzi, who also ran Ciro’s, an Italian restaurant on a nearby lane paved with clamshells and scented with garlic.

Mr. Cozzi set his standards high. Ciro’s bought whole veal legs that were broken down into scallopine and cutlets, the hand-chopped trimmings worked into meatballs. Garlic was sliced moments before it hit the pan. Using few shortcuts, a crackerjack team of cooks somehow pushed out around 500 dinners a night, seven nights a week.

“Ciro’s at that time was the busiest, most fantastic restaurant in Provincetown,” said Mr. Yingling, who let Mr. Bourdain sleep in a crawl space over his walk-in refrigerator at Spiritus during this audition.

Mr. Bourdain was awe-struck by the cooks at Ciro’s, called Mario’s in his memoir. “They moved in a pack, with their own dialect,” he wrote, “a high-pitched, ultra-femme, affected drawl, salted with terms from eighteenth-century English literature and Marine Corps drill instructor-speak — a lush, intimidating, sardonic secret language, which was much imitated.”

The admiration was not mutual. After he burned himself on a frying pan in a disastrous tryout, Mr. Bourdain was kicked back down to salads.

“We looked at him and sort of sneered, because he seemed very callow and, on the one hand, full of himself and, on the other hand, unsure,” said Alexej Getmanov, the Ciro’s cook known in the book as Dimitri. Mr. Bourdain told him that their disdain got under his skin and prompted him to attend the Culinary Institute of America, starting in February 1977. “He said, ‘Well, I’ll show them.’”

Ciro’s is now owned by the Luster family, two of whom, James and Larry, worked with Mr. Bourdain. Now under its original name, Ciro & Sal’s, the restaurant still breaks down whole legs of veal, even more rare today than it was then. The lane still smells like garlic.

Few other businesses from Mr. Bourdain’s era are still going. There’s the Provincetown Portuguese Bakery, where malasadas are fried in the window. The Lobster Pot, where his childhood friend Sam Goldman worked, is as busy as ever, but it wasn’t a hangout.

“We never ate there; it was for tourists & day-trippers,” Nancy Bourdain, his ex-wife, wrote in an email. (She declined an interview request.) “I think we subsisted on food from local year-round spots like Tips for Tops’n, the Portuguese Bakery & Cookie’s Tap (kale soup with linguiça), lots of pizza, & cooking at home. We saved our money for going out to the local bars (Piggy’s & the Governor Bradford), other ‘stuff,’ & rent.”

Versions of kale soup are still all over, even though the Portuguese community that brought it to the Cape is nearly gone. But looking for recipes that shaped Mr. Bourdain’s young palate is beside the point. We aren’t interested in him today because of the dishes he created as a chef so much as the way he wrote about the work, and the appreciation he showed, in his television career, for people who did their own particular thing in their own particular way.

In this regard, one book might be the Rosetta Stone for Bourdain scholars: Howard Mitcham’s “Provincetown Seafood Cookbook,” published in 1975.

Deaf, alcoholic and so dedicated to marine life that he kept a pet sea clam in a jar, Mr. Mitcham was the closest thing Provincetown had to a name chef. A copy of “Provincetown Seafood Cookbook” was presented to Mr. Bourdain when he started cooking at the Flagship. This custom lives on, I learned. Mac Hay, an owner of Mac’s Fish House Provincetown, said he gives the book to all his head chefs. “You need to understand the simplicity of this food,” he tells them.

Mr. Bourdain absorbed the book’s culinary wisdom, but it was the writing that captivated him. The text is energetic, passionate, oracular, wide-ranging, deeply grounded in the town’s seafaring history and the culture of its chowder-eating Yankees, the Portuguese fishermen who dried salt cod in their yards, and an Italian painter who sutured stuffed squid with needle and thread. The kind of eating Mr. Mitcham liked best was lusty, messy and unpretentious. His prose seems to rise from the muck of the harbor.

Mr. Bourdain clearly saw a kindred spirit and maybe, too, a model for how a cook with an omnivorous curiosity could apply it to another medium. He celebrated the book at length in “Kitchen Confidential,” and adapted two of its recipes for “Appetites: A Cookbook,” published in 2016.

“Provincetown Seafood Cookbook” was long out of print by then. Copies were going for $50 and up at Tim’s Used Books off Commercial Street. The owner, Tim Barry, got together with Seven Stories Press to reissue it.

The publisher asked for a preface by a well-known figure. Mr. Barry emailed a request to Mr. Bourdain, who was off shooting “Parts Unknown” on the other side of the globe. His reply came the next day: When do you need it?

“He was totally professional, and we didn’t change one word,” Mr. Barry said, sitting in a garden below the narrow raised boardwalk that leads to his shop.

Seven Stories published the reissue, with an introduction by Mr. Bourdain calling it “a true classic, one of the most influential of my life,” in June 2018. He had been found dead in a hotel room in France 16 days earlier.

Pete Wells is a reporter covering food. He was previously The Times’s restaurant critic from 2012 until 2024 and, before that, the editor of the Food section.

The FCC Is Coming for Robot Vacuums. How Soon Will It Be a Problem?

Wired July 30, 2026

This week, the US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of foreign-made advanced mobile robots. Humanoid and quadruped robots are specifically named, indicating the true target is robotic versions of people and animals, but something else happens to be an “advanced mobile robot”: robot vacuums.

So what does this ban mean? Though it's effective immediately, nothing changes for now. Robot vacuums won't get removed from the market, and your current robot vacuum won't stop working. The ban will instead stop new models from getting FCC approval to be sold in the United States. The vacuums available now won't be affected, but new models likely won't make it to the US if they're manufactured outside the country. And, unfortunately, a lot of great robot vacuum brands aren't based in the States.

Here's everything to know about what will happen next.

The FCC updated its Covered List this week to include foreign-made advanced mobile robots, which include robot vacuums. The Covered List, which comes from Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, is a “list of communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

It may feel like overkill for just a robot vacuum, but the definition of an advanced robotic device from the National Security Determination, an interagency body of the Executive Branch, clearly includes them. That definition includes the following highlights:

The National Security Determination said that connected vehicles, vehicles on rail lines, aircraft, and unmanned underwater vehicles are not included in the ban, along with stationary robots. But foreign-made robot vacuums, along with similar robots like robotic pool cleaners and automated lawn mowers, look to be on the chopping block.

The announcement comes after the FCC labeled all of these devices a security risk, since, according to the National Security Determination, “the networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system.”

The concern is primarily with the cameras and sensors built into these devices—some even have microphones built into the base station for voice commands. It is a security risk to bring any device into your home that has a camera and the ability to connect to the internet—especially if your Wi-Fi isn't secure. But it's interesting to see the ban stop at robot vacuums and not, say, smart speakers or devices with always-on cameras. The FCC documentation actually lists live cameras as an example, as well as an example of a humanoid robot being hacked, but no example for robot vacuums.

For the most part, it looks like robot vacuums just got unlucky. They're using the same sensors as other robots but aren't streaming live feeds of their surroundings. They do map your home, but that map isn't useful for anything besides knowing where the couch is and which rooms have carpet or hard floors. I wouldn't call these the most dangerous device with a camera in my home by any means, but it seems the government disagrees. This is not the only thing that's been banned lately, either—in May, the FCC also banned foreign-made routers, so we might continue to see bans for various household technology products roll out as the year goes on.

For now, you can shop robot vacuums (and other, similar automated home cleaning robots) as you normally would. FCC approval has already been given to all the robots on the market, so we can expect changes to take place in the future rather than immediately.

I reached out to the makers of my top robot vacuum picks, Shark and Eufy, along with popular robot makers Dreame and Roborock. Shark and Dreame didn't respond, and Roborock declined to comment. Eufy replied with the following statement:

“We are aware of the FCC’s recent update. Based on our current understanding, the new rule does not affect the continued availability, use, or support of products we currently sell in the United States. Those products remain available and will continue to receive updates and customer support.”

So don't worry about getting rid of your robot vacuum if you already have one you love. If you're in the market for a new model, I'd recommend shopping the newest models from brands that could be affected, like Dreame and Eufy, in case future models are blocked from arriving in the States.

It will also be interesting to see which companies avoid the ban—Shark is based in the US, for example, but it's unclear where the company's robot manufacturing is located. Matic is another US-based brand that could potentially evade the ban. But the buying options will be much, much more limited as time goes on.

The ban is disappointing news with IFA Berlin starting September 4, where we often see new robot vacuums announced. I'm not sure anything we'll see there this year will reach the US. A reduced market also isn't good for consumers—having fewer options never helps a category and might ultimately raise prices on less powerful vacuums because of limited supply. Only time will tell what the fallout will be.

A Leaked Memo Ties Cyberattacks on Minnesota Water Utilities to Iran

Wired July 30, 2026

Since the US launched its war against Iran in late February, the country’s hackers have struck back with retaliatory intrusions that have ranged from paralyzing medical supplies company Stryker to breaching the personal email of FBI director Kash Patel. Now, after an unprecedented wave of disruptive cyberattacks hit water utilities in Minnesota, a memo circulated within the water industry ties those attacks to Iran, too, in the widest and most disruptive strike yet inflicted by the country’s hackers against the US since the war began.

A communication obtained by WIRED on Thursday and sent to members of the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or WaterISAC, an industry group for water utilities to share cybersecurity information, links to Iran a series of cyberattacks that targeted dozens of Minnesota water and wastewater utilities.

The WaterISAC note states that the Minnesota Fusion Center, a state-level intelligence-sharing entity, issued an alert “regarding ongoing malicious cyber activity impacting public drinking water systems across Minnesota” and adds that the fusion center has found that those attacks were “aligned” with a hacking campaign first described in April by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as having been carried out by “Iran-affiliated” hackers. (Both the WaterISAC and Minnesota Fusion Center reports were marked as unclassified but “for official use only.”)

Confirmation of Iran’s responsibility for hacking the water utilities represents a kind of state-sponsored targeting of civilian infrastructure that has rarely been seen outside of Russia’s war against Ukraine, says Joe Slowik, a former Los Alamos National Labs cybersecurity researcher working on contract for the Department of Energy. “Now we have documented disruption and even modification of safety and protection parameters in critical infrastructure,” Slowik says. “Seeing this sort of tradecraft expand to Iran, and seeing it across multiple sites, it should really be making people concerned right now.”

Slowik adds that there’s no reason to believe that the attacks would stop with the incidents in Minnesota. “There are plenty of other sites that have the same targeted technology,” he says. “There’s plenty of areas for this to still be executed by an adversary that has shown a willingness to do so.”

A new CISA advisory related to the attacks released Thursday warns that “these threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes” and warns utilities to disconnect PLCs from the internet, password-protect access with strong passwords, and “allow-list” only trusted devices to connect to them.

Earlier this week, Minnesota state officials revealed that more than 30 municipal water and wastewater systems had been targeted in hacker breaches that had in some cases disabled telecommunications between the industrial control system technologies and water utility equipment. In at least one municipality, the 1,700-person city of Braham, the hacking reportedly led to a brief outage of the city’s water plant, though there’s not yet evidence of any resulting water shortages or a threat to the safety of Minnesota’s water supply. The latest CISA advisory notes that the attacks have, however, “resulted in boil-water notices”—suggesting fears of water contamination— and “sustained manual operations.”

In the days since that wave of incidents became public, Iran has emerged as the leading suspect behind the attacks, despite the lack of any official confirmation of the country’s involvement or any statement from an Iranian hacker group claiming responsibility. In a report published Monday, cybersecurity firm Tenable wrote that signs suggested CyberAv3ngers, an Iranian hacker group tied to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, may be responsible for the water utility breaches, noting that “the operational pattern is consistent with” the group or hacking groups associated with it. Separately, The New York Times reported Thursday that US and state officials and others familiar with the hacking incidents had concluded the Minnesota attacks were “likely” carried out by Iranian state-sponsored hackers, but without naming a specific group.

In its report on the Minnesota water cyberattacks, Tenable pointed to an advisory from CISA that was initially released in April but was updated last week, warning that Iran-linked actors were targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) used for automation and coordination in critical infrastructure to cause “operational disruption and financial loss.” That advisory specifically pointed the finger at an “Iranian-affiliated” hacker group and noted that CyberAv3ngers specifically had carried out similar targeting of PLCs.

The updated advisory, however, still doesn’t mention the Minnesota attacks—only the timing of its update on July 22 suggests a connection to the more recent hacking of the state’s water utilities. The WaterISAC memo is the first official document to explicitly draw that connection, tying the attack to Iran.

The WaterISAC memo states that, according to the Minnesota Fusion Center, the hackers who targeted the water utilities compromised remotely accessible PLCs, just as in the earlier hacking campaign described by CISA, “with the likely desired impact to cause loss of system pressure and potential contamination of the water supply.” The memo adds that the facilities “were able to mitigate further compromise, but the full impact is still being assessed.”

WaterISAC’s director of infrastructure cyber defense, Jennifer Lyn Walker, wrote in a statement that the organization had not provided the leaked memo to WIRED, nor did it “assess attribution at any time.”

“WaterISAC always maintains information sharing protocols and safeguards information shared by our members, partners and the broader information sharing community,” Walker wrote.

In the wake of the cyberattacks earlier this week, Minnesota officials said that all drinking water is still safe, and statements from multiple targeted municipalities emphasized that failsafes had protected the systems. “While the incident affected certain automated controls, established contingency procedures were immediately implemented, allowing Public Works staff to maintain normal water and wastewater operations,” South St. Paul officials wrote in a statement.

The CISA advisory that was updated last week, which specifically cited water and wastewater systems operators as part of the “intended audience” of its warning, noted that the attackers were exfiltrating and manipulating the project files that govern automated industrial systems. The alert, which issued with a consortium of US federal agencies including the FBI, the National Security Agency, Cyber Command, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of Energy, originally warned in April that likely Iranian hackers were tampering with PLCs to change information on the displays of industrial control systems, which can in some scenarios cause system disruption, damage, or dangerous conditions for utilities. “In a few cases, this activity has resulted in operational disruption and financial loss,” the advisory reads.

That advisory also notes that similar activity, including the targeting of PLCs, was carried out by CyberAv3ngers. That group first emerged in a hacking campaign in late 2023, after Hamas’ October 7 attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza that followed. In that first wave of cyberattacks, CyberAv3ngers targeted devices sold by industrial control systems firm Unitronics, which are typically used in water and wastewater facilities, setting devices to read “Gaza” and display an image of the CyberAv3ngers logo. While the attacks appeared to be mere vandalism, cybersecurity firms that tracked the attacks such as Dragos and Claroty told WIRED that the hackers had in fact rewritten the Unitronics’ devices’ code, leading to disruption of water-related services from Israel to Ireland to a US facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Even after the US State Department offered a $10 million bounty for information about the group and the US Treasury sanctioned six IRGC officials alleged to be linked to it, CyberAv3ngers’ attacks continued to escalate. According to Dragos, it went on to breach a US oil and gas company in 2024 and then to carry out a widespread hacking campaign infecting industrial control and internet-of-things devices with a piece of malware known as IOControl.

Whether CyberAv3ngers is behind the cyberattacks on the Minnesota water utilities remains far from clear. In an interview with WIRED, Yhonatan Harari, a researcher at the cybersecurity firm Claroty, said the company had found other evidence that the attacks might have been carried out by Handala, a distinct hacker group that claimed responsibility for the Stryker cyberattack in March, the breach of Kash Patel’s email later the same month, and numerous other disruptive hacking incidents.

Despite that uncertainty, Harari says that all signs point to Iran as the culprit. “We’re not sure yet if it’s CyberAv3ngers or Handala,” Harari says, “but in a very high likelihood we can say it’s Iranian actors.”

The string of attacks on the Minnesota utilities does, however, closely fit the modus operandi of CyberAv3ngers, which has established itself as a rare state-sponsored hacker group that has shown its willingness to not only target but also sabotage industrial control systems—and water in particular.

“They definitely have the capability; they have the intent,” Dragos cybersecurity researcher Kyle O’Meara told WIRED about CyberAv3ngers last year. “They have the interest in learning how to shut things off and potentially cause harm.”

Additional reporting by Lily Hay Newman.

Updated 7/31/2026 at 10:05 am EDT: Added comment from WaterISAC.
